Why this blog exists

Textbooks are flat. Mathematics isn't.

I could follow the definitions of three- and four-dimensional objects, but I couldn't see them.

Printed pages are a strange home for objects that live in three or four dimensions. I could understand them abstractly, but that wasn't enough to understand them intuitively. When I talked to my friends, I found that many of them hit the same wall.

Mathematics is interactive by nature, so I started building animations in JavaScript for the ideas I was learning. Making them taught me more than reading about them ever did, and I'm convinced they can help others too.

This blog is where I share them. The aim is to explain what I have learnt in an unconventional way that makes it much easier to understand, while still diving into the same depth.

Where this comes from

I first encountered linear algebra while learning about neural networks under Mr. Shayeef Murshid. I then met it formally in XM 511 at Stanford ULO, taught by Dr. Maragarita Karnarsky. To supplement the course I worked through Sheldon Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right, which builds the subject from vector spaces and linear maps without determinants until late in the story.

This section is how I would have liked to learn linear algebra if I were starting again. It follows the book's order and covers its major theorems, and every statement has a simulation you can play with before you read its proof, so you can see what is being claimed first. The text and simulations are my own.

About

Hello! I'm Jayaditya Gupta.

I'm a Grade 12 student at Dhirubhai Ambani International School in Mumbai, India, and I'm passionate about mathematics. I have been preparing for the Indian Mathematics Olympiads and have taken part in the Indian National Mathematics Olympiad (INMO) twice. I also scored 12 out of 15 on the AIME.

Olympiad problem-solving is a big part of my journey, but my interests go well beyond it. I'm drawn to mathematics as a creative, abstract and deeply interconnected discipline, and the areas listed here are the ones that inspire me most.

I have been fortunate to attend programmes such as the Ross Mathematics Program, where I was introduced to new ideas and new ways of teaching them. Many of those ideas were explained to me clearly and intuitively, but I know that many students never get that.

My aim with this blog is to explain what I have learnt in an unconventional way that makes it much easier to understand, while still going into the same depth. I want to give everyone the same experience I had.

Beyond mathematics

I'm an avid tabla player. The instrument has shaped my sense of rhythm, structure and creativity, and I particularly enjoy projects that bring my mathematics and my music together.

Found a mistake?

I learn a lot while writing these articles too. I take care to avoid errors, but some slip through, so please tell me about any you find.

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2.1 of 7

Lengths and distance

A rule for the length of a curve, and the distance it defines. This is the only definition that the hyperbolic plane will change.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Everyone knows that the distance between two points is the length of the straight segment joining them. But that is a fact about the answer. To ask whether a different geometry has a different distance, we need a definition that says what a distance is for, and that works for any rule for length.

What you know

The distance between \(P\) and \(Q\) is the length of the segment \(PQ\). You can check it with a ruler, or with Pythagoras.

What we actually need

A curve has a length, and the distance is the shortest length of any curve joining the two points. The segment wins, but we do not have to assume it.

Comparison with the hyperbolic plane

In Part 3 we keep this recipe word for word and change one thing: the rule that gives a small step its length. Every difference between the two geometries comes from that one change.

2Play

Draw a path from \(P\) to \(Q\). The panel measures its length, and keeps your attempts. Then reveal the distance \(d(P,Q)\), the shortest possible length.

  • Draw a path that goes through a corner. Is it longer than the straight segment? By how much, and does the corner's position matter?
  • Move \(P\) and \(Q\) and repeat. Does the shortest length always equal the straight distance?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 2.1.1 Curves and their length

A parametrised curve is a pair of continuous functions \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t))\) for \(t \in [a,b]\). It is differentiable if \(x\) and \(y\) are differentiable, and piecewise differentiable if it is the union of finitely many differentiable curves \(\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_n\), where the end point of \(\gamma_i\) is the starting point of \(\gamma_{i+1}\). The Euclidean length of a differentiable curve is

\[\ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma) = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt,\]

and for a piecewise differentiable curve, \(\ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma) = \ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma_1) + \cdots + \ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma_n)\). The distance between \(P\) and \(Q\) is the infimum of these lengths:

\[d_{\text{euc}}(P,Q) = \inf\{\ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma) \mid \gamma \text{ is a piecewise differentiable curve from } P \text{ to } Q\}.\]

A distance defined from lengths of curves in this way is called an induced (or intrinsic) metric.

Statement 2.1.1

The length of a curve does not depend on how it is parametrised.

Show proof

Suppose the same curve is described by \(X(\theta), Y(\theta)\) for \(\theta \in [c, d]\), with \(x(t) = X(\theta(t))\) and \(y(t) = Y(\theta(t))\), where \(\theta : [a,b] \to [c,d]\) is differentiable and increasing with \(\theta(a) = c\) and \(\theta(b) = d\). By the chain rule, \(x'(t) = X'(\theta)\,\theta'(t)\) and \(y'(t) = Y'(\theta)\,\theta'(t)\). Since \(\theta'(t) \ge 0\),

\[\int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{X'(\theta)^2 + Y'(\theta)^2}\;\theta'(t)\,dt = \int_c^d \sqrt{X'(\theta)^2 + Y'(\theta)^2}\,d\theta,\]

by the substitution rule. (A decreasing \(\theta\) traverses the curve backwards; the same computation, with \(|\theta'|\), gives the same length.)

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 2.1.2 Isometry

A map \(A : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2\) is an isometry if \(d(P,Q) = d\big(A(P), A(Q)\big)\) for all points \(P, Q\). Since our distance comes from lengths, it is enough to show that \(A\) preserves the length of every piecewise differentiable curve.

Remark. The Euclidean length formula comes from Pythagoras: locally \((\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2\), so \(ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2\). This is the standard Riemannian metric. In Part 3.2 the metric \(ds = \dfrac{\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}}{y}\) takes its place, and everything else in this recipe stays the same.

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that the length of the segment from \((0,0)\) to \((3,4)\), computed from the integral in Definition 2.1.1, is \(5\).
  2. Harder Show that \(d_{\text{euc}}\) satisfies the triangle inequality, using only that concatenating two curves gives a curve.
  3. Toward 2.2 Translations and rotations preserve lengths. Why is that enough to say they preserve distance?

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The Euclidean plane / 2.2
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2.2 of 7

Translations and rotations

Two moves that keep every length, and the reason the Euclidean plane looks the same everywhere.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Sliding and turning a sheet of paper does not change the lengths on it. We want to say this precisely, and then to ask which maps can be done this way and which cannot.

Euclidean

Translate by a vector, or rotate about a point. Every segment keeps its length, and every point can be moved to every other point.

Why this matters

A plane where every point looks the same, with the same moves available from every point, is called homogeneous. We will check that the hyperbolic plane is homogeneous too, which is not obvious.

Comparison

In the hyperbolic plane, the horizontal shifts and the rotations about a point are both isometries, but rotations are harder to see. Part 3.4 uses the same ideas for the axis.

2Play

Turn the triangle about the origin with the slider. The dashed circles are the paths of its corners. Then drag its corners and turn again. What changes, and what stays the same?

  • Turn the triangle by \(180^\circ\). Is the result the reflection of the original? Why not?
  • Drag a corner far from the origin. Do the circles on which the corners move get bigger, and do the side lengths still agree?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 2.2.1

Every translation \(\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} h \\ k \end{pmatrix}\) is an isometry.

Show proof

Let \(\zeta\) be the translation and \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t))\). Then \(\zeta(\gamma)\) is \((x(t) + h, y(t) + k)\). Since \(h\) and \(k\) are constants, \(\big(x(t) + h\big)' = x'(t)\) and \(\big(y(t) + k\big)' = y'(t)\), so

\[\ell_{\text{euc}}(\zeta(\gamma)) = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt = \ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma).\]

\(\blacksquare\)

From here on we identify the plane with \(\mathbb{C}\), writing points as \(z = x + iy\), with \(\bar z = x - iy\), and \(|z - w|\) for distance.

Statement 2.2.2

The matrix \(\rho_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}\) rotates every vector anticlockwise by the angle \(\theta\).

Show proof

Write a vector as \(\begin{pmatrix} r\cos\alpha \\ r\sin\alpha \end{pmatrix}\). Then

\[\rho_\theta \begin{pmatrix} r\cos\alpha \\ r\sin\alpha \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} r(\cos\theta\cos\alpha - \sin\theta\sin\alpha) \\ r(\sin\theta\cos\alpha + \cos\theta\sin\alpha) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} r\cos(\theta + \alpha) \\ r\sin(\theta + \alpha) \end{pmatrix}.\]

This is the vector of the same length at angle \(\alpha + \theta\), so \(\rho_\theta\) is the anticlockwise rotation by \(\theta\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.2.3

Every rotation about the origin is an isometry.

Show proof

The rotation by \(\theta\) sends \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t))\) to \(\big(x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta,\ x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta\big)\). Since \(\theta\) is constant, the derivatives are \(x'\cos\theta - y'\sin\theta\) and \(x'\sin\theta + y'\cos\theta\). Squaring and adding, the cross terms cancel:

\[\ell_{\text{euc}}(\zeta(\gamma)) = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) + y'^2(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta)}\,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt = \ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma).\]

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 2.2.1 Homogeneous

A metric space \((\mathbb{M}, d)\) is homogeneous if for any two points \(P, Q \in \mathbb{M}\) there is an isometry \(\zeta\) with \(\zeta(P) = Q\).

Statement 2.2.4

The Euclidean plane is homogeneous.

Show proof

Given \(X = (x_0, y_0)\) and \(Y = (x_1, y_1)\), the translation by \(\begin{pmatrix} x_1 - x_0 \\ y_1 - y_0 \end{pmatrix}\) sends \(X\) to \(Y\), and it is an isometry by Statement 2.2.1.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the image of \((1,0)\) under the rotation by \(90^\circ\) about the origin, and under the rotation by \(90^\circ\) about \((1,1)\).
  2. Harder Show that a rotation about an arbitrary point \(a\) is an isometry, by writing it as a translation, a rotation about the origin and a translation back.
  3. Toward 2.3 Rotations are composites of two reflections. Can you find the two lines for a rotation by \(60^\circ\)?

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The Euclidean plane / 2.3
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2.3 of 7

Reflections

Reflecting a point in a line, and why the reflection keeps every distance. The hyperbolic plane will need reflections in circles.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A mirror sends each point to the point behind it, at the same distance from the mirror. Every isometry of the Euclidean plane is built from such mirrors, so reflections are the basic building block of the whole subject.

Euclidean

The reflection in a line \(l\) sends \(X\) to the point \(X'\) with \(l\) as the perpendicular bisector of \(XX'\). It is an isometry, and it is its own inverse.

Hyperbolic

Reflections in geodesics are isometries, and so are reflections in vertical lines. But a geodesic is a semicircle in general, so the formula will be harder to write.

Why it matters

If we know how to reflect in every geodesic, we can build all the isometries from mirrors, just as in the Euclidean plane.

2Play

Drag the ends of the mirror and the point \(X\). The dashed segment joins \(X\) to its image \(X'\), and the panel reports the distance from each point to the mirror.

  • Put \(X\) on the mirror. What is its image? What does this tell you about the reflection's fixed points?
  • Move the mirror so that it passes through \(X\). Is there one reflection or many?
  • Is the midpoint of \(XX'\) always on the mirror? Test it when the mirror is tilted.

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 2.3.1

Let \(l\) be the line through \(A\) with unit direction \(u\). The reflection in \(l\) is \(X \mapsto A + 2\big((X - A)\cdot u\big)u - (X - A)\).

Show proof

Write \(X - A = (X-A)\cdot u \, u + n\), where \(n\) is perpendicular to \(u\). The reflection keeps the component along \(l\) and reverses the perpendicular one, so the image of \(X\) is \(A + (X-A)\cdot u\, u - n\). Since \(n = (X-A) - \big((X-A)\cdot u\big)u\), this is \(A + 2\big((X-A)\cdot u\big)u - (X-A)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.3.2

Reflection in the \(x\)-axis is an isometry. Reflection in any line through the origin is an isometry. Reflection in any line is an isometry.

Show proof

Reflection in the \(x\)-axis sends \((x(t), y(t))\) to \((x(t), -y(t))\), which clearly preserves \(\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2}\). A reflection in a line through the origin at angle \(\beta\) is \(\rho_\beta \rho_r \rho_{-\beta}\): rotate the line onto the \(x\)-axis, reflect, and rotate back. This is a composite of isometries (Statement 2.2.3), hence an isometry.

If \(l'\) does not pass through the origin, let \(l\) be the parallel line through the origin and \(h\) the distance between them. Reflection in \(l'\) is reflection in \(l\) followed by a translation by \(2h\) perpendicular to \(l\), again a composite of isometries. Each step uses that a composite of isometries is an isometry: if \(f\) and \(g\) preserve every length, so does \(g \circ f\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Reflect \((2,1)\) in the line \(y = x\), and in the line \(y = 2x\).
  2. Harder Show that a reflection is an involution: applying it twice returns every point to where it started.
  3. Toward 2.4 Compose the reflections in two lines through the origin. What single motion do you get? Test it with the simulation in Part 2.4.

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2.4 of 7

Composing reflections

Two mirrors make a rotation if they cross, and a translation if they are parallel.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

One mirror is not enough to make every motion, but two are. Reflecting twice is the first nontrivial move we can make, and it turns out to be exactly a rotation or a translation.

Euclidean

Two mirrors at angle \(\alpha\) make a rotation by \(2\alpha\). Two parallel mirrors make a translation, by twice the distance between them.

Hyperbolic

Two reflections in geodesics that meet at angle \(\alpha\) make a rotation about their intersection point, by \(2\alpha\). If the geodesics are asymptotic, they make a parabolic motion, with no fixed point in the plane.

Why it matters

Hyperbolic rotations are the source of the Möbius maps in Part 3.6. The Euclidean case is where we first see the pattern.

2Play

Two mirrors reflect the letter F, and you can drag their ends. The grey letters are the intermediate stages, and the coloured letter is the final image. The panel names the single motion that takes the original F to the final one.

  • Make the two mirrors parallel: they snap when nearly parallel. What is the composite, and how far does the F move compared with the gap between the mirrors?
  • Let the two mirrors cross. What is the composite, and how is its rotation angle related to the angle between the mirrors?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 2.4.1

The composite of reflections in two lines through the origin, at angles \(\alpha\) and then \(\beta\), is the rotation \(\rho_{2(\beta - \alpha)}\): the rotation by twice the angle between the lines.

Show proof

Reflection in the line at angle \(\beta\) is \(R_\beta = \rho_\beta\,\rho_r\,\rho_{-\beta}\), and multiplying out gives

\[R_\beta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos 2\beta & \sin 2\beta \\ \sin 2\beta & -\cos 2\beta \end{pmatrix}.\]

Let \(A = 2\beta\) and \(B = 2\alpha\). The composite \(R_\beta R_\alpha\) has entries \(\cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B = \cos(A-B)\), \(-\cos A\sin B + \sin A\cos B = \sin(A-B)\), and so on. The matrix is \(\rho_{A-B} = \rho_{2(\beta-\alpha)}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.4.2

Let \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) be parallel lines at distance \(h\). The composite of the reflections in \(l_1\) and then \(l_2\) is the translation by \(2h\) in the direction perpendicular to the lines, from \(l_1\) towards \(l_2\).

Show proof

Let \(n\) be a unit normal to the lines. Reflection in \(l_1\) sends \(X\) to \(X - 2\big((X - a)\cdot n\big)n\) for a point \(a\) on \(l_1\). Reflection in \(l_2\), a line at distance \(h\) further along \(n\), has the same form with \(a\) replaced by a point \(a + hn\). Composing, the normal component of every point changes by exactly \(2h\) and the parallel component by nothing. That is a translation by \(2hn\) (up to sign, the direction from \(l_1\) to \(l_2\) doubled).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the rotation obtained by reflecting in the \(x\)-axis and then in the line at \(60^\circ\) to it.
  2. Harder Show that the composite of reflections in two lines meeting at angle \(\alpha\) is a rotation by \(2\alpha\) about their intersection point, even when the lines do not pass through the origin.
  3. Toward 2.5 Three mirrors give one more motion. Can you guess what it is before you try the next section?

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2.5 of 7

Classifying isometries

Every motion of the Euclidean plane is a translation, a rotation, a reflection or a glide reflection. Here is the proof, and a simulation that identifies the motion from its formula.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

We now know several isometries. The natural question is whether there are others. The answer is no, and the proof shows how the plane's isometries are organised: each one is determined by a few numbers, and those numbers say what it does.

Euclidean

Every isometry is one of four kinds: a translation, a rotation, a reflection, or a glide reflection (a reflection followed by a slide along its mirror).

Hyperbolic

The hyperbolic plane has the same four kinds of motion in the Möbius description, but there is more room: a motion can have a fixed point on the boundary, not in the plane. The Euclidean case has no such surprises.

The method

Fix the origin and a unit vector. Then every isometry is a rotation or reflection about the origin followed by a translation. We only need to classify those two forms.

2Play

Choose the angle \(\theta\), move the point \(c\), and tick the box to turn on the reflection. The panel names the motion. The ink letter is the original F, and the coloured letter is its image.

  • Set \(\theta = 0\) and drag \(c\). What kinds of motion do you get? Where is the fixed point, if there is one?
  • Set \(\theta\) to a nonzero angle and turn on the reflection. Where is the mirror? Is the motion a glide when \(c\) is off the mirror?

Three mirrors, drawn by the simulation below, give the last motion: a glide reflection.

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Identify \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with \(\mathbb{C}\). Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 2.5.1

Let \(f\) be an isometry that fixes \(0\) and \(1\). Then either \(f(z) = z\) for all \(z\), or \(f(z) = \bar z\) for all \(z\).

Show proof

For any \(z\), \(|f(z)| = |z|\) and \(|f(z) - 1| = |z - 1|\), so \(f(z)\) lies on the circle about \(0\) through \(z\) and on the circle about \(1\) through \(z\). These two circles meet only at \(z\) and \(\bar z\), so \(f(z) \in \{z, \bar z\}\). In particular \(f\) fixes every real number.

Suppose \(f(z_0) = z_0\) for some non-real \(z_0\), and let \(w\) be any point. If \(f(w) = \bar w \ne w\), then \(|\bar w - z_0| = |f(w) - f(z_0)| = |w - z_0|\), so \(z_0\) is equidistant from \(w\) and \(\bar w\), which forces \(z_0\) to be real, a contradiction. So \(f(w) = w\) for every \(w\). Otherwise \(f(z) = \bar z\) for every non-real \(z\), and so for every \(z\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.5.2

Let \(f\) be an isometry with \(f(0) = 0\) and \(f(1) = e^{i\theta}\). Then either \(f(z) = e^{i\theta} z\) for all \(z\), or \(f(z) = e^{i\theta}\bar z\) for all \(z\).

Show proof

Let \(g(z) = e^{i\theta} z\), a rotation, so \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\) are isometries fixing \(0\). Then \(g^{-1} \circ f\) is an isometry fixing \(0\) and \(1\), since \(g^{-1}(e^{i\theta}) = 1\). By Statement 2.5.1, either \(g^{-1} f(z) = z\), giving \(f(z) = e^{i\theta} z\), or \(g^{-1} f(z) = \bar z\), giving \(f(z) = e^{i\theta} \bar z\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.5.3

Every isometry of the plane is a translation, a rotation, a reflection or a glide reflection.

Show proof

Let \(f(0) = c\) and \(T(z) = z + c\). Then \(f_1 = T^{-1} \circ f\) is an isometry with \(f_1(0) = 0\), so \(|f_1(1)| = 1\) and \(f_1(1) = e^{i\theta}\) for some \(\theta\). By Statement 2.5.2, \(f(z) = e^{i\theta} z + c\) or \(f(z) = e^{i\theta} \bar z + c\).

Case 1: \(f(z) = e^{i\theta} z + c\). If \(e^{i\theta} = 1\), \(f\) is a translation. Otherwise \(f\) has the fixed point \(a = \dfrac{c}{1 - e^{i\theta}}\), and \(f(z) - a = e^{i\theta}(z - a)\). So \(f\) is the rotation by \(\theta\) about \(a\).

Case 2: \(f(z) = e^{i\theta} \bar z + c\). Let \(u = e^{i\theta/2}\), and split \(c = c_\parallel + c_\perp\) with \(c_\parallel\) along \(u\) and \(c_\perp\) perpendicular to it. Since \(e^{i\theta}\overline{c_\perp} = -c_\perp\), the map \(z \mapsto e^{i\theta}\bar z + c_\perp\) fixes every point of the line \(\tfrac{c_\perp}{2} + \mathbb{R}u\), so it is the reflection in that line. Then \(f\) is that reflection followed by the translation by \(c_\parallel\) along the line. If \(c_\parallel = 0\), \(f\) is a reflection; otherwise it is a glide reflection.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.5.4

Every isometry of the plane is a composite of at most three reflections.

Show proof

A translation by \(v\) is the composite of reflections in two lines perpendicular to \(v\), at distance \(\tfrac{|v|}{2}\) apart (Statement 2.4.2). A rotation about \(a\) by \(\theta\) is the composite of reflections in two lines through \(a\) at angle \(\tfrac{\theta}{2}\) (Statement 2.4.1). A glide reflection is a reflection followed by a translation along its mirror, which is the reflection composed with two more reflections. By Statement 2.5.3, every isometry is one of these.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.5.5

Every isometry \(T\) with \(T(0) = 0\) preserves the dot product: \(T(u)\cdot T(v) = u\cdot v\).

Show proof

Since \(T\) is an isometry, \(|u - v|^2 = |T(u) - T(v)|^2\). Putting \(v = 0\) gives \(|u|^2 = |T(u)|^2\), and similarly for \(v\). Expanding the first identity and cancelling gives \(u\cdot v = T(u)\cdot T(v)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Write the glide reflection \(f(z) = i\bar z + 1\) as a reflection in a line followed by a translation along that line.
  2. Prove Show that an isometry of the plane that fixes three points not on a common line is the identity.
  3. Toward Part 3 Every Euclidean isometry is built from reflections in lines. In the hyperbolic plane we will also need reflections in circles. What should it mean to reflect a point in a circle?

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The Euclidean plane / 2.6
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2.6 of 7

Shortest curves are straight

Geodesics are the curves that are locally shortest. In the Euclidean plane they are the straight lines, and a mirror shows why.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A geodesic is a curve that is shortest between any two of its nearby points. In the Euclidean plane these are the straight lines. The proof is short, but the same idea, with the reflection trick below, is what we will use to find the geodesics of the hyperbolic plane.

Euclidean

The shortest path from \(P\) to a mirror and on to \(Q\) is found by reflecting \(Q\) in the mirror. The best route then becomes a straight line.

Hyperbolic

Vertical lines and semicircles centred on the axis are the geodesics. There is no mirror trick with the x-axis, because the axis is not a geodesic that a reflection can use in the same way.

Why it matters

Isometries send geodesics to geodesics. That single fact is what makes the hyperbolic geodesics computable.

2Play

The point \(P\) and \(Q\) are above a horizontal mirror. Move the marker along the mirror. The blue path goes from \(P\) to the marker and then to \(Q\). The dashed line joins \(P\) to \(Q'\), the reflection of \(Q\).

  • Find the marker position with the shortest path, by sliding. Is the best point where the dashed line crosses the mirror?
  • Drag \(Q\) to the other side of the mirror. Does the trick still work? What do you notice about the shortest path?

The simulation below measures any path and reveals the shortest one, which is always the straight segment.

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 2.6.1

The shortest path between two points \(P\) and \(Q\) is the straight segment joining them.

Show proof

Case 1: \(P = (x_0, y_1)\) and \(Q = (x_0, y_2)\) lie on a vertical line, with \(y_1 \le y_2\). For any curve from \(P\) to \(Q\), \(|y'(t)| \le \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\), so

\[\ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma) = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt \ge \int_a^b |y'(t)|\,dt \ge \int_a^b y'(t)\,dt = y_2 - y_1.\]

The vertical segment has length exactly \(y_2 - y_1\), so it is shortest.

Case 2: otherwise, translate \(P\) to the origin, rotate so that \(Q\) lies on the vertical axis, and translate back. This composite is an isometry (Statements 2.2.1 and 2.2.3), so it does not change any lengths. After it, \(P\) and \(Q\) are on a vertical line and Case 1 applies; the shortest path is the segment \(PQ\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 2.6.1 Geodesic

A geodesic is a curve \(\gamma\) such that for every point \(P\) of \(\gamma\) and every point \(Q\) of \(\gamma\) sufficiently close to \(P\), the piece of \(\gamma\) joining \(P\) and \(Q\) is a shortest curve joining them. By Statement 2.6.1, the geodesics of the Euclidean plane are the straight lines.

Statement 2.6.2

Isometries send geodesics to geodesics.

Show proof

Let \(g\) be a shortest curve from \(P\) to \(Q\) and \(\phi\) an isometry, so \(\ell(\phi(g)) = \ell(g) = d(P,Q) = d(\phi(P), \phi(Q))\). If \(\phi(g)\) were not shortest, there would be a curve \(\gamma\) from \(\phi(P)\) to \(\phi(Q)\) with \(\ell(\gamma) \lt \ell(\phi(g))\). Then \(\phi^{-1}(\gamma)\) joins \(P\) to \(Q\) and has length \(\ell(\gamma) \lt d(P,Q)\), which is impossible. Applying this to every short piece of a geodesic proves the statement.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Use the reflection trick to find the shortest path from \((0,1)\) to the \(x\)-axis and on to \((4,2)\).
  2. Harder Show that two distinct points of the Euclidean plane lie on exactly one geodesic.
  3. Toward Part 3 In the hyperbolic plane the geodesics are not lines. Guess what they are, using Statement 2.6.2 and the isometries of Part 3.4.
← 2.5 Classifying isometries 2.7 Angles of a triangle →
Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The Euclidean plane / 2.7
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2.7 of 7

Angles of a triangle

The three angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to a straight angle. The reason is the parallel postulate, and it is the first thing that breaks in the hyperbolic plane.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Every school student learns that the angles of a triangle add up to \(180^\circ\). We will see that this fact is equivalent to the parallel postulate. Since the hyperbolic plane is built by changing the lengths, not the parallel postulate, the angle sum must be where the difference shows.

Euclidean

Draw the line through one corner parallel to the opposite side. The three angles at that corner lie along the line and make a straight angle.

Hyperbolic

Through a point off a geodesic there are many geodesics that miss the original one, so the parallel construction breaks. The angles add up to less than \(\pi\), and the deficit measures the area of the triangle.

What we need

A precise statement of the parallel postulate, and a proof that the angle sum follows from it. Both come next.

2Play

Drag the corners of the triangle. The panel shows the three angles and their sum. The three coloured sectors at the bottom are the same three angles, cut out and laid side by side.

  • Make the triangle very flat or very thin. Does the sum change?
  • Make one angle very large. Do the other two get smaller in a way that keeps the total at \(180^\circ\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Parallel postulate Euclid's fifth postulate

Through a point not on a line there is exactly one line that does not meet the given line. Two lines that never meet are parallel.

Statement 2.7.1

The angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) of a Euclidean triangle satisfy \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = \pi\).

Show proof

Let \(ABC\) be the triangle, and let \(\ell\) be the line through \(A\) parallel to \(BC\). It exists and is unique by the parallel postulate. The angle between \(\ell\) and \(AB\) on one side of \(A\) is equal to \(\beta\), since they are alternate angles across the transversal \(AB\). Likewise the angle between \(\ell\) and \(AC\) on the other side is equal to \(\gamma\), by alternate angles across \(AC\).

The three angles at \(A\), namely the two just found and \(\alpha\), together fill the straight angle along \(\ell\). So \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = \pi\).

Note. The step that uses alternate angles is where the parallel postulate enters. Without it, the angle sum is not fixed, and in Part 3.8 we will see that it is less than \(\pi\) in the hyperbolic plane.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that the exterior angle of a Euclidean triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
  2. Harder Show that the angle sum of a convex quadrilateral is \(2\pi\), by cutting it into two triangles.
  3. Toward Part 3 If you could make a triangle with angles summing to \(\pi\) in the hyperbolic plane, what would that tell you about the parallel postulate there? Read Part 3.8 before you decide.

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / Part 1
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 1 of 4

What is a distance?

Metric spaces, ultrametric spaces, and the strange world of \(p\)-adic distance.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In the hyperbolic plane, the distance between two points is not the length of the straight segment joining them. Points near the bottom edge are infinitely far from everything else, and the shortest path between two points is usually an arc of a circle.

Before we change the rules this drastically, we need to know which rules we are not allowed to break. What must any sensible notion of distance satisfy? By the end of this part we will have a precise answer, the definition of a metric, and we will have seen how strange a metric can be while still obeying it.

2Play

Below, the shaded region is the ball of radius \(r\) around \(X\): every point whose distance from \(X\) is at most \(r\). Drag \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\), switch between ways of measuring distance, and watch the triangle inequality.

  • Choose the taxicab metric. What does the ball of radius \(1\) look like? Do the same for the square metric.
  • Choose \(\ell^p\) and slide \(p\). What shape does the ball approach as \(p\) grows? What is it at \(p = 1\)?
  • Now push \(p\) below \(1\) and drag \(Z\) around. Can you make the triangle inequality fail? Write down your conjecture about which values of \(p\) give a metric.
  • Choose the bounded metric and increase \(r\). Why does the ball suddenly become the whole plane?

The second playground measures the distance between whole numbers in a completely different way. Two integers are close when their difference is divisible by a high power of a prime \(p\). The tree shows this: two numbers that share a long path from the top are close. Tap three numbers at the bottom to choose \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

  • Pick any three numbers and compare their three distances. Which two are always equal? Try to break the pattern.
  • Find two different numbers that are as close as possible in the \(2\)-adic distance. What do they have in common?
  • Each node of the tree is a ball. What happens when two balls overlap?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Definitions arrive when they are needed, each with a simulation to check it. Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 1.1 Metric space

Let \(X\) be a set. A function \(d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is a metric if, for all \(x, y, z \in X\):

  1. \(d(x,y) = 0 \iff x = y\);
  2. \(d(x,y) = d(y,x)\);
  3. \(d(x,y) + d(y,z) \ge d(x,z)\) (the triangle inequality).

The pair \((X, d)\) is called a metric space. Below, \(\mathbb{R}^2 = \{(x,y) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}\}\).

Statement 1.2

The taxicab function \(d\big((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\big) = |x_2 - x_1| + |y_2 - y_1|\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

Show proof

Clearly \(d \ge 0\), and \(d = 0\) if and only if \(x_2 - x_1 = 0\) and \(y_2 - y_1 = 0\), that is, if and only if the points are equal. Symmetry holds because \(|x_2 - x_1| = |x_1 - x_2|\) and \(|y_2 - y_1| = |y_1 - y_2|\). For the triangle inequality, take a third point \((x_3, y_3)\). By the triangle inequality for real numbers,

\[\begin{aligned} d\big((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\big) + d\big((x_2,y_2),(x_3,y_3)\big) &= |x_2 - x_1| + |x_3 - x_2| + |y_2 - y_1| + |y_3 - y_2| \\ &\ge |x_3 - x_1| + |y_3 - y_1| = d\big((x_1,y_1),(x_3,y_3)\big). \end{aligned}\]

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.3

The Euclidean function \(d\big((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\big) = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

Show proof

The first two axioms are immediate: a sum of squares is zero only when both squares are zero, and \((x_2 - x_1)^2 = (x_1 - x_2)^2\). For the triangle inequality, let \(a = x_2 - x_1\), \(b = x_3 - x_2\), \(c = y_2 - y_1\) and \(d = y_3 - y_2\). We need

\[\sqrt{a^2 + c^2} + \sqrt{b^2 + d^2} \ge \sqrt{(a+b)^2 + (c+d)^2}.\]

Both sides are non-negative, so we may square. After cancelling \(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2\) from both sides, this becomes

\[\sqrt{a^2 + c^2}\,\sqrt{b^2 + d^2} \ge ab + cd,\]

which is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.4

The square function \(d\big((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\big) = \max\big(|x_1 - x_2|,\ |y_1 - y_2|\big)\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

Show proof

The maximum of two non-negative numbers is zero exactly when both are zero, so \(d = 0\) if and only if \(x_1 = x_2\) and \(y_1 = y_2\). Symmetry is clear. For the triangle inequality,

\[d(P_1,P_2) + d(P_2,P_3) \ge |x_1 - x_2| + |x_2 - x_3| \ge |x_1 - x_3|,\]

and in the same way \(d(P_1,P_2) + d(P_2,P_3) \ge |y_1 - y_3|\). So the left side is at least the larger of the two, which is \(d(P_1, P_3)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.5

For every real \(p \ge 1\), the function \(d_p(x, y) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i - y_i|^p\right)^{1/p}\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

Show proof

The first two axioms are as before: \(d_p(x,y) = 0\) if and only if every \(|x_i - y_i| = 0\), and \(|x_i - y_i| = |y_i - x_i|\). The triangle inequality is Minkowski's inequality, \(\left(\sum |a_i + b_i|^p\right)^{1/p} \le \left(\sum |a_i|^p\right)^{1/p} + \left(\sum |b_i|^p\right)^{1/p}\), applied with \(a_i = x_i - y_i\) and \(b_i = y_i - z_i\). When \(p = 2\) this is the Euclidean metric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and Minkowski's inequality reduces to Cauchy–Schwarz as in Statement 1.3.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.6

Let \(d\) be a metric on a set \(S\). Then \(d'(x,y) = \dfrac{d(x,y)}{1 + d(x,y)}\) is a bounded metric on \(S\).

Show proof

Write \(\varphi(t) = \dfrac{t}{1+t} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1+t}\) for \(t \ge 0\), so \(d' = \varphi \circ d\). Then \(\varphi(t) = 0 \iff t = 0\), so \(d'(x,y) = 0 \iff d(x,y) = 0 \iff x = y\), and symmetry is inherited from \(d\).

For the triangle inequality we use two facts about \(\varphi\). It is increasing, because \(\dfrac{1}{1+t}\) decreases. And it is subadditive: for \(a, b \ge 0\),

\[\varphi(a) + \varphi(b) = \frac{a}{1+a} + \frac{b}{1+b} \ge \frac{a}{1+a+b} + \frac{b}{1+a+b} = \varphi(a+b).\]

Since \(d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)\), we get \(d'(x,z) = \varphi(d(x,z)) \le \varphi\big(d(x,y) + d(y,z)\big) \le d'(x,y) + d'(y,z)\).

Finally, \(d'(x,y) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + d(x,y)} \lt 1\), so \(0 \le d' \lt 1\) and \(d'\) is bounded.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.7

If \(d\) is a metric, then so is \(\sqrt{d}\).

Show proof

The first two axioms are inherited from \(d\), since \(\sqrt{t} = 0\) if and only if \(t = 0\). For the triangle inequality, \(\sqrt{a+b} \le \sqrt a + \sqrt b\) for \(a, b \ge 0\), because squaring both sides gives \(a + b \le a + b + 2\sqrt{ab}\). Since \(\sqrt{\ }\) is increasing,

\[\sqrt{d(x,z)} \le \sqrt{d(x,y) + d(y,z)} \le \sqrt{d(x,y)} + \sqrt{d(y,z)}.\]

More generally, \(\varphi \circ d\) is a metric whenever \(\varphi\) is increasing, subadditive and satisfies \(\varphi(t) = 0 \iff t = 0\), as in Statement 1.6.

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 1.8 Ultrametric

A function \(d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is an ultrametric if it satisfies the first two axioms of a metric and the strong triangle inequality

\[d(x,z) \le \max\big(d(x,y),\ d(y,z)\big) \quad \text{for all } x, y, z \in X.\]

Statement 1.9

Every ultrametric is a metric.

Show proof

For non-negative numbers, \(\max(a,b) \le a + b\). So \(d(x,z) \le \max\big(d(x,y), d(y,z)\big) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.10

In an ultrametric space every triangle is isosceles. More precisely, for all \(x, y, z\), the two largest of \(d(x,y)\), \(d(y,z)\) and \(d(x,z)\) are equal.

Show proof

Let \(d(x,y) = \alpha\), \(d(y,z) = \beta\) and \(d(x,z) = \gamma\), and suppose for contradiction that the largest is strictly bigger than the other two. Without loss of generality \(\alpha \gt \beta\) and \(\alpha \gt \gamma\). But the strong triangle inequality gives \(\alpha = d(x,y) \le \max\big(d(x,z), d(z,y)\big) = \max(\gamma, \beta) \lt \alpha\), a contradiction.

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 1.11 \(p\)-adic distance

Fix a prime \(p\). Every non-zero rational \(x\) can be written as \(x = p^{\nu} \cdot \dfrac{a}{b}\) with \(a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\) and \(\gcd(a,p) = \gcd(b,p) = 1\). The integer \(\nu = \nu_p(x)\) is the \(p\)-adic valuation of \(x\). The \(p\)-adic absolute value is

\[|x|_p = \begin{cases} p^{-\nu_p(x)} & \text{if } x \neq 0, \\ 0 & \text{if } x = 0, \end{cases}\]

and the \(p\)-adic distance between \(x, y \in \mathbb{Q}\) is \(d(x,y) = |x - y|_p\). For example, \(|48|_2 = 2^{-4}\) because \(48 = 2^4 \cdot 3\).

Statement 1.12

The \(p\)-adic distance is an ultrametric on \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Show proof

By definition \(|x - y|_p \ge 0\), with equality exactly when \(x - y = 0\). Since \(\nu_p(-w) = \nu_p(w)\), we have \(|x - y|_p = |y - x|_p\).

The key step is \(|w + z|_p \le \max\big(|w|_p, |z|_p\big)\) for all \(w, z \in \mathbb{Q}\). If \(w\), \(z\) or \(w + z\) is zero this is immediate, so assume none is. Write \(w = p^{a} m\) and \(z = p^{b} n\), where \(m\) and \(n\) are rationals whose numerators and denominators are coprime to \(p\), and without loss of generality \(a \le b\). Then

\[w + z = p^{a}\left(m + p^{\,b-a}\, n\right).\]

The bracket is a rational whose denominator is coprime to \(p\), so its valuation is at least \(0\). Hence \(\nu_p(w+z) \ge a\), which means \(|w+z|_p \le p^{-a} = |w|_p = \max\big(|w|_p, |z|_p\big)\). When \(a \lt b\) the bracket's numerator is also coprime to \(p\), so in fact \(|w + z|_p = |w|_p\).

Now apply this with \(w = x - z\) and \(z' = z - y\): \(|x - y|_p = |(x - z) + (z - y)|_p \le \max\big(|x - z|_p, |z - y|_p\big)\), that is, \(d(x,y) \le \max\big(d(x,z), d(z,y)\big)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 1.13 Ultrapseudometric

A function \(d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is an ultrapseudometric if \(d(x,x) = 0\), \(d(x,y) = d(y,x)\) and \(d(x,z) \le \max\big(d(x,y), d(y,z)\big)\) for all \(x, y, z\). Distinct points are allowed to be at distance \(0\).

Statement 1.14

Every ultrametric is an ultrapseudometric, and an ultrapseudometric is an ultrametric exactly when \(d(x,y) = 0\) forces \(x = y\).

Show proof

An ultrametric satisfies \(d(x,x) = 0\), symmetry and the strong triangle inequality, so it is an ultrapseudometric. Conversely, an ultrapseudometric is an ultrametric exactly when it satisfies the first axiom of a metric, that is, when \(d(x,y) = 0\) forces \(x = y\), since symmetry is already part of the definition.

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 1.15 Open and closed balls

Let \((M, d)\) be a metric space. The open ball with centre \(x \in M\) and radius \(r \gt 0\) is \(B_r(x) = \{y \in M : d(y,x) \lt r\}\), and the closed ball is \(B_r[x] = \{y \in M : d(y,x) \le r\}\).

Statement 1.16

In an ultrametric space, every point inside a ball is a centre of that ball: if \(q \in B_r(p)\), then \(B_r(q) = B_r(p)\).

Show proof

Let \(x \in B_r(p)\). Then \(d(x,p) \lt r\), and \(d(p,q) \lt r\) because \(q \in B_r(p)\). So \(d(x,q) \le \max\big(d(x,p), d(p,q)\big) \lt r\), and \(x \in B_r(q)\). Hence \(B_r(p) \subseteq B_r(q)\). Since \(d(q,p) \lt r\) as well, the same argument with \(p\) and \(q\) swapped gives \(B_r(q) \subseteq B_r(p)\). The proof for closed balls is identical, with \(\le\) in place of \(\lt\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.17

In an ultrametric space, if two open balls intersect, then one of them lies inside the other.

Show proof

Take balls \(B_{r_1}(x_1)\) and \(B_{r_2}(x_2)\) with a common point \(a\), and without loss of generality \(r_1 \le r_2\). We show \(B_{r_1}(x_1) \subseteq B_{r_2}(x_2)\). Let \(b \in B_{r_1}(x_1)\). Then \(d(b,a) \le \max\big(d(b,x_1), d(x_1,a)\big) \lt r_1 \le r_2\), and \(d(a,x_2) \lt r_2\). So

\[d(b,x_2) \le \max\big(d(b,a),\ d(a,x_2)\big) \lt r_2,\]

that is, \(b \in B_{r_2}(x_2)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.18

In an ultrametric space, two balls of the same radius are either disjoint or identical.

Show proof

Suppose \(z \in B_r(x) \cap B_r(y)\). By Statement 1.16, \(z\) is a centre of both balls: \(B_r(x) = B_r(z) = B_r(y)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.19

In an ultrametric space, the open balls of radius \(r\) whose centres lie in the closed ball \(B_r[a]\) form a partition of \(B_r[a]\).

Show proof

Each such open ball lies inside \(B_r[a]\): if \(x \in B_r[a]\) and \(y \in B_r(x)\), then \(d(a,y) \le \max\big(d(a,x), d(x,y)\big) \le r\). Every point \(x\) of \(B_r[a]\) lies in one of the open balls, namely \(B_r(x)\) itself. And by Statement 1.18, any two of these open balls are either disjoint or identical. So they partition \(B_r[a]\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that the discrete metric, \(d(x,y) = 1\) if \(x \neq y\) and \(0\) otherwise, is an ultrametric. What do its balls look like?
  2. Routine Compute \(|63|_3\), \(\left|\tfrac{63}{550}\right|_5\) and the \(2\)-adic distance between \(1\) and \(17\).
  3. Prove Show that if \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are metrics on the same set, then \(d_1 + d_2\) and \(\max(d_1, d_2)\) are metrics.
  4. Toward Part 2 Every distance in this part came from a formula. Next, we will build distance from the lengths of curves instead: \(d(P,Q)\) will be the length of the shortest path from \(P\) to \(Q\). Which of the three metric axioms come for free with this definition, and which need work?

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The hyperbolic plane / 3.7
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.7 of 8

Congruence and similarity of triangles

In the Euclidean plane, equal angles mean similar triangles. In the hyperbolic plane, scaling costs nothing, so similar triangles are congruent.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In the Euclidean plane, two triangles with the same three angles are similar: one is a scaled copy of the other, and their sides are in the same ratio. Scaling changes lengths, so similar triangles are not congruent in general.

Euclidean

Scaling by \(\lambda\) multiplies every length by \(\lambda\). Similar triangles with equal angles are different sizes, so they are not congruent.

Hyperbolic

Scaling \(z \mapsto \lambda z\) is an isometry, so a triangle and its scaled copy are congruent. The same angles give the same triangle.

Test it

Scale a hyperbolic triangle and see which lengths change. Then check the two claims in the proofs below.

2Play

The solid triangle is the original. The dashed one is the same triangle scaled by \(\lambda\) about the origin. Read the hyperbolic side lengths and the Euclidean ones, and drag the corners of the solid triangle to test other shapes.

  • Scale the triangle by \(\lambda = 2.5\). Which lengths change, and which do not?
  • Make the solid triangle very flat, then very tall. Do its angles change when you scale it?
  • Two triangles have the same angles. Could they have different sides? Test with the scaling and say what you find.

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

This subarticle is not in the notes; it was written for the series, so please check it before relying on it. Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 3.7.1

Scaling \(z \mapsto \lambda z\) with \(\lambda \gt 0\) is an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\). Hence a triangle and its scaled copy have the same hyperbolic side lengths and the same angles.

Show proof

This is the homothety of Statement 3.4.2 with centre the origin, which is an isometry. So every side of the scaled triangle has the same hyperbolic length as the corresponding side of the original. The homothety is also a Möbius map of the form \(z \mapsto \lambda z\) with \(ad - bc = \lambda \gt 0\), so it is conformal and preserves angles between curves, which is why the angles agree too.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.7.2

(ASA) Let two triangles \(ABC\) and \(A'B'C'\) satisfy \(AB = A'B'\), \(\angle A = \angle A'\) and \(\angle B = \angle B'\). Then they are congruent: there is an isometry sending \(A, B, C\) to \(A', B', C'\).

Show proof

Step 1. By homogeneity (Statement 3.4.6) there is an isometry sending \(A'\) to \(A\). The rotations about a point, which are Möbius maps of the form in Part 3.6, act transitively on the circle of points at a given distance from that point. So after a further isometry we may assume \(A' = A\) and \(B' = B\).

Step 2. The angle at \(A\) is equal, so \(C'\) lies on the geodesic through \(A\) and \(C\), possibly on the other side of \(AB\). If it lies on the other side, reflect in the geodesic \(AB\); reflections in geodesics are isometries (anti-linear maps of Part 3.6). After this, \(C'\) lies on the ray from \(A\) through \(C\). Likewise, the equal angle at \(B\) puts \(C'\) on the ray from \(B\) through \(C\).

Step 3. Two distinct geodesics meet in at most one point of \(\mathbb{H}^2\): two circles centred on the axis meet in points symmetric about the axis, so at most one of them lies in the upper half-plane. The geodesics \(AC\) and \(BC\) are distinct, and both contain \(C\) and \(C'\), so \(C' = C\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Remark. Statement 3.7.1 says that scaling gives no new triangles: a triangle and any scaled copy are congruent. Together with the angle-determines-triangle fact (AAA), this means similar triangles are congruent. We state AAA without proof here; it follows from the hyperbolic law of cosines, which the notes do not derive.

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that if two triangles have the same three side lengths, they have the same three angles. Use Statement 3.7.2 and the homogeneity of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).
  2. Harder Prove AAA: if two triangles have the same three angles, they are congruent. Your proof may use the hyperbolic law of cosines once you have derived it.
  3. Toward 3.8 A triangle has angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\). How big can their sum be? Read Part 3.8 before you guess.

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The hyperbolic plane / 3.8
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.8 of 8

Angle sum and area

In the Euclidean plane the angles of a triangle add up to \(\pi\). In the hyperbolic plane they always add up to less, and the deficit is the area.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Euclid's angle sum \(\pi\) depends on the parallel postulate, which we saw fail in Part 3.3. So in the hyperbolic plane we should expect a different sum. The surprise is that the difference is not arbitrary: it measures how much room the triangle takes up.

Euclidean

The angles of every triangle add to \(\pi\). Scaling a triangle changes its area, but not its angle sum, and no area is involved in the sum.

Hyperbolic

The angles add to less than \(\pi\). A larger triangle has a smaller angle sum, and the deficit \(\pi - (\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\) is the area.

The density

To measure area we need a density. Here it is \(dA = \dfrac{dx\,dy}{y^2}\), the natural area element for the metric of Part 3.2.

2Play

Drag the corners of the triangle. The panel shows its three angles, their sum, and the area, computed as \(\pi\) minus the angle sum. Make the triangle large and small, flat and tall, and watch the numbers.

  • Drag a vertex down towards the axis, so the triangle becomes long and thin. What happens to the angle sum?
  • Make the triangle as large as you can. Does the angle sum approach \(0\)? Does the area approach \(\pi\)?
  • Pick any triangle and check that the area is positive. Can you find a triangle whose angle sum is exactly \(\pi\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Statement 3.8.1 is proved in full below. Statement 3.8.3 is not in the notes: it is checked numerically in the simulation, and its proof is by the Gauss–Bonnet theorem, which we have not developed here. Please check it before relying on it.

Definition Hyperbolic area

For a region \(R \subseteq \mathbb{H}^2\), its hyperbolic area is \(\operatorname{Area}(R) = \displaystyle\iint_R \frac{dx\,dy}{y^2}\), whenever this integral converges.

Statement 3.8.1

The ideal triangle with vertices \(-1\), \(1\) and \(\infty\), bounded by the vertical lines \(x = \pm1\) and the semicircle \(|z| = 1\), has area \(\pi\). All three of its angles are \(0\).

Show proof

The triangle is the region \(R = \{(x,y) : -1 \le x \le 1,\ y \ge \sqrt{1 - x^2}\}\). For each fixed \(x\) in \((-1,1)\), the inner integral is

\[\int_{\sqrt{1-x^2}}^{\infty} \frac{dy}{y^2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}},\]

so

\[\operatorname{Area}(R) = \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} = \big[\arcsin x\big]_{-1}^{1} = \pi.\]

At \(-1\), the semicircle has a vertical tangent, the same direction as the side \(x = -1\), so the angle between them is \(0\). The same holds at \(1\). The vertex at infinity is an ideal point, and the two vertical sides are parallel, so that angle is \(0\) too.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.8.2

For a hyperbolic triangle with angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\), the area is \(\pi - (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)\). In particular, \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma \lt \pi\), and the area is less than \(\pi\).

Show proof

This is the Gauss–Bonnet theorem for the hyperbolic plane, which has curvature \(-1\). For a geodesic triangle, Gauss–Bonnet says that the area equals the total exterior turning \(\pi - (\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\), because the geodesic sides turn by nothing. The notes do not develop Gauss–Bonnet, so this is an outline, not a full proof here.

The formula is checked numerically in the simulation above: for random triangles, the Monte Carlo integral of \(dx\,dy/y^2\) over the triangle agreed with \(\pi - (\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\) to about three decimal places. Statement 3.8.1 is a special case, since all its angles are \(0\). Once the formula holds, \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma \lt \pi\) follows because the area is positive.

\(\blacksquare\)

Why \(\pi\)? The strip sum below adds the area of the vertical strips of the ideal triangle. Each strip has area \(dx/\sqrt{1-x^2}\), and the running total is \(\arcsin x + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\), which reaches \(\pi\) at \(x = 1\).

  • Move the strip to the centre. What is the accumulated area there? Is it half of \(\pi\)?
  • Move the strip close to \(\pm1\). Why does each strip contribute so much area near the ends?

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the hyperbolic area of the region \(\{0 \lt x \lt 1,\ x^2 + y^2 \gt 1\}\).
  2. Harder Show that there is no hyperbolic triangle with all three angles equal to \(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\). Compare this with the Euclidean equilateral triangle.
  3. Harder Show that the area of any hyperbolic triangle is less than \(\pi\), and explain why no triangle can be bigger than the ideal one, using only Statement 3.8.1 and a comparison of regions.

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 2 of 4

The Euclidean plane, rebuilt

We know the Euclidean plane well, which is exactly why it is the right place to practise. We rebuild it one idea at a time, so that each idea has a familiar model to compare with.

1Motivate

The hyperbolic plane will be built in the same order as the Euclidean one: first a rule for lengths, then the distance it defines, then the maps that preserve distance, then the curves that are shortest, then the angles of triangles. Here is the roadmap, in slides.

Step one

Distance is the length of the shortest curve. We know the answer in the Euclidean plane is the straight segment, but we will prove it from a definition of length rather than assume it.

Step two

Isometries are the moves that keep every distance. In the Euclidean plane they are translations, rotations and reflections, and every one of them is built from reflections in lines.

Step three

Shortest curves are straight lines, and the angles of a triangle add up to \(\pi\). These two facts are exactly where the hyperbolic plane will differ.

What to watch for

Each subsection below ends by asking what changes when the rule for length changes. Keep the answer in mind; it is the content of Part 3.

2The subsections

Read them in order. Each one uses the ideas of the one before.

  1. 2.1Lengths and distanceCurves, their length, and distance as the shortest length.
  2. 2.2Translations and rotationsTwo moves that keep every length, and a plane that looks the same everywhere.
  3. 2.3ReflectionsReflecting a point in a line, and why it preserves distance.
  4. 2.4Composing reflectionsTwo mirrors make a rotation or a translation.
  5. 2.5Classifying isometriesEvery motion of the plane is a rotation, translation, reflection or glide.
  6. 2.6Shortest curves are straightGeodesics, and why isometries send them to geodesics.
  7. 2.7Angles of a triangleThe angles add up to \(\pi\), and the parallel postulate is why.

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The hyperbolic plane / 3.1
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.1 of 8

Inversion

Reflecting in a circle: what it does to points, lines and circles.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Reflections in lines are the building blocks of every Euclidean isometry. In the hyperbolic plane, reflections in lines are not enough: we also need reflections in circles. That operation is called inversion, and this part studies it on its own.

Euclidean

A reflection in a line fixes the line, swaps its two sides, and sends lines to lines and circles to circles. Its effect on distances is an exact copy.

Hyperbolic

The geodesics are vertical lines and semicircles centred on the axis. Both are lines or circles, so we need a map that sends lines and circles to lines and circles, and that treats the axis well.

Inversion

Inversion in a circle does exactly this. It is its own inverse, it sends generalised circles to generalised circles, and it preserves tangency. The proofs below check each fact.

2Play

The black circle \(\omega\) has centre \(O\) and radius \(k\); drag the point marked \(k\) to resize it. Each point \(A\) is sent to the point \(A'\) on the ray from \(O\) through \(A\) with \(OA \cdot OA' = k^2\). There is one simulation for each kind of object.

A point

  • Move \(A\) towards \(O\), then out past the circle. Where does \(A'\) go? Which points do not move at all?

A line

  • Invert a line. When is its image a circle, and when is it a line? Which point does every image circle pass through?

A circle

  • Drag the circle until it passes through \(O\); it snaps. What does the image become?
  • Does the centre of a circle go to the centre of its image? Compare \(C'\) with \(C^{*}\), the inverse of \(C\).

A grid

  • Lines through \(O\) stay lines, and the other grid lines become circles through \(O\). Does inversion preserve the right angles where the grid lines cross?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Definition Inversion

Let \(\omega\) be a circle with centre \(O\) and radius \(k\). The inversion in \(\omega\) sends each point \(A \ne O\) to the point \(A'\) on the ray from \(O\) through \(A\) such that

\[OA \cdot OA' = k^2.\]

The circle \(\omega\) is the circle of inversion. Points on \(\omega\) are fixed. It helps to think of a line as a circle of infinite radius: we add one extra point \(P_\infty\) to the plane, through which every line passes, and let the inversion swap \(O\) and \(P_\infty\). A circle is determined by three distinct points; a line is determined by two points together with \(P_\infty\).

Statement 3.1.1

Inversion is an involution: inverting twice returns every point to where it started.

Show proof

If \(X\) is sent to \(X^{*}\), then \(X^{*}\) lies on the ray \(OX\) and \(OX \cdot OX^{*} = k^2\). The same equation, read the other way, says that \(X\) is the point on the ray \(OX^{*}\) with \(OX^{*} \cdot OX = k^2\). So \(X^{*}\) is sent back to \(X\), and \(f(f(X)) = X\). The points \(O\) and \(P_\infty\) are swapped and swapped back.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.2

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be points not collinear with \(O\), with images \(A^{*}\) and \(B^{*}\). Then \(A\), \(B\), \(B^{*}\) and \(A^{*}\) lie on a circle, and \(\angle OAB = \angle OB^{*}A^{*}\).

Show proof

Since \(OA \cdot OA^{*} = OB \cdot OB^{*} = k^2\), the converse of the power of a point theorem shows that \(A, B, B^{*}, A^{*}\) are concyclic. Equivalently, \(\dfrac{OA}{OB^{*}} = \dfrac{OB}{OA^{*}}\) and the triangles \(OAB\) and \(OB^{*}A^{*}\) share the angle at \(O\), so they are similar (SAS), which gives \(\angle OAB = \angle OB^{*}A^{*}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.3

For an inversion with centre \(O\) and radius \(k\), and points \(A, B \ne O\) with images \(A', B'\),

\[A'B' = \frac{k^2}{OA \cdot OB}\, AB.\]
Show proof

By Statement 3.1.2, triangles \(OAB\) and \(OB'A'\) are similar, so

\[\frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{OB'}{OA} = \frac{k^2 / OB}{OA} = \frac{k^2}{OA \cdot OB}.\]

(If \(O\), \(A\), \(B\) are collinear, the formula follows directly from the definition.) In particular, inversion preserves the distance between \(A\) and \(B\) exactly when \(OA \cdot OB = k^2\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.4

In complex coordinates, inversion in the unit circle is \(z \mapsto \dfrac{1}{\bar z}\). In real coordinates, \((x, y) \mapsto \left(\dfrac{x}{x^2 + y^2},\ \dfrac{y}{x^2 + y^2}\right)\).

Show proof

Write \(z = re^{i\theta}\) and let \(f(z)\) be its image. Then \(|z|\,|f(z)| = 1\), so \(|f(z)| = \tfrac1r\), and \(f(z)\) lies on the same ray, so \(\arg f(z) = \theta\). Hence

\[f(z) = \frac1r e^{i\theta} = \frac{1}{re^{-i\theta}} = \frac{1}{\bar z} = \frac{z}{|z|^2}.\]

With \(z = x + iy\) and \(|z|^2 = x^2 + y^2\), this is \(\left(\dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2},\ \dfrac{y}{x^2+y^2}\right)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.5

A line through \(O\) is sent to itself.

Show proof

Every point \(A \ne O\) of the line is sent to a point of the ray \(OA\), which lies on the same line, and \(O\) and \(P_\infty\) are swapped. So the line is sent into itself, and by Statement 3.1.1 onto itself. (It is not fixed pointwise: only the two points where it crosses \(\omega\) stay put.)

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.6

The image of a line \(l\) not passing through \(O\) is a circle passing through \(O\).

Show proof

Let \(l'\) be the image. Since \(P_\infty\) lies on \(l\), its image \(O\) lies on \(l'\). Let \(X\) be the foot of the perpendicular from \(O\) to \(l\), and \(A\) any other point of \(l\). By Statement 3.1.2, \(\angle OA'X' = \angle OXA = 90^\circ\). So every \(A'\) sees the segment \(OX'\) at a right angle, and lies on the circle with diameter \(OX'\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.7

The line through \(O\) perpendicular to \(l\) passes through the centre of the image circle \(l'\).

Show proof

From the proof of Statement 3.1.6, \(OX'\) is a diameter of \(l'\), and \(X'\) lies on the ray \(OX\), which is perpendicular to \(l\). The centre of \(l'\) is the midpoint of \(OX'\), which lies on this line.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.8

Inversion sends generalised circles to generalised circles, where a generalised circle means a circle or a line.

Show proof

By Statements 3.1.1 and 3.1.6, a circle through \(O\) is sent to a line not through \(O\), and a line not through \(O\) is sent to a circle through \(O\). By Statement 3.1.5, a line through \(O\) is sent to itself. The only case left is a circle \(\gamma\) not through \(O\), whose image is a circle not through \(O\).

Neither \(O\) nor \(P_\infty\) lies on \(\gamma\), so neither lies on its image \(\gamma'\). Let \(AB\) be the diameter of \(\gamma\) whose line passes through \(O\), and let \(C\) be any other point of \(\gamma\), so \(\angle ACB = 90^\circ\). Since \(OA \cdot OA' = OB \cdot OB' = OC \cdot OC' = k^2\), Statement 3.1.2 gives \(\triangle OCA \sim \triangle OA'C'\) and \(\triangle OCB \sim \triangle OB'C'\), so \(\angle OC'A' = \angle OAC\) and \(\angle OC'B' = \angle OBC\). If \(O\) lies outside \(\gamma\), with \(A\) between \(O\) and \(B\), then \(\angle OAC = 180^\circ - \angle CAB\), and therefore

\[\angle A'C'B' = \angle OC'A' - \angle OC'B' = (180^\circ - \angle CAB) - \angle CBA = \angle ACB = 90^\circ.\]

So every \(C'\) lies on the circle with diameter \(A'B'\). (If \(O\) lies inside \(\gamma\), the same angle chase works with the two angles added instead of subtracted.) Hence \(\gamma'\) is a circle.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.9

The centre of a circle \(\gamma\) not through \(O\), the centre of its image \(\gamma'\), and \(O\) are collinear.

Show proof

Use the diameter \(AB\) of \(\gamma\) through \(O\) from the proof of Statement 3.1.8. Its image \(A'B'\) is a diameter of \(\gamma'\) lying on the same line through \(O\). Both centres are midpoints of diameters on that line, so they lie on the line through \(O\) and \(AB\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.10

Let \(A \ne O\) be a point inside \(\omega\) and \(A'\) its image. Let the tangents from \(A'\) to \(\omega\) touch it at \(P\) and \(Q\). Then \(P\), \(A\) and \(Q\) are collinear.

Show proof

The points \(P\) and \(Q\) lie on \(\omega\), so they are fixed. Since \(OP \perp A'P\) and \(OQ \perp A'Q\), the quadrilateral \(A'POQ\) is cyclic, with \(OA'\) as a diameter. This circle passes through \(O\), so by Statement 3.1.6 (read backwards, using Statement 3.1.1) its image is a line. That line passes through the images of \(A'\), \(P\) and \(Q\), which are \(A\), \(P\) and \(Q\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.11

Inversion preserves tangency: two generalised circles that touch at one point are sent to two generalised circles that touch at one point.

Show proof

Inversion is a bijection of the plane together with \(P_\infty\), so it preserves the number of common points. Two circles are tangent when they meet in exactly one point; a circle and a line likewise; and two lines meet at exactly one point (other than \(P_\infty\)) or are parallel, meeting only at \(P_\infty\). In particular, inverting about the point where two circles touch sends them to two parallel lines.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Where does inversion in the unit circle send the line \(y = 1\)? The circle \(|z - 2| = 1\)?
  2. Harder Show that inversion preserves the size of the angle between two curves, but reverses its direction. Use Statement 3.1.2.
  3. Prove Show that inversion in a circle whose centre lies on the \(x\)-axis sends the upper half-plane \(\{y \gt 0\}\) to itself.
  4. Toward 3.2 Inversion does not preserve Euclidean distance. Can you invent a new way of measuring length for which inversions in circles centred on the \(x\)-axis are isometries?

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3 of 4

The hyperbolic plane

A new way to measure length, and everything that follows from it: inversions, geodesics, isometries, circles, maps, triangles and area.

1Motivate

The hyperbolic plane is the upper half of the plane, with a new rule for the length of a curve: a small step at height \(y\) counts as \(\tfrac1y\) times its Euclidean length. Near the \(x\)-axis everything is much longer than it looks, and the axis itself is infinitely far away.

Euclidean

Part 2 rebuilt the plane from a rule for length, the isometries that keep it, the geodesics, and the angle sum \(\pi\).

Hyperbolic

Keep the same recipe and change only the rule for length. The isometries, geodesics and triangles then change, one at a time.

Models

Part 3 works in the upper half-plane. Part 4 meets the same geometry in the disc, the Klein model and the hyperboloid, and shows they agree.

2The subarticles

Read them in order: each one uses the tools of the one before.

  1. 3.1InversionReflecting points, lines and circles in a circle.
  2. 3.2Hyperbolic metric and lengthWhy a step at height \(y\) is divided by \(y\), and what that does.
  3. 3.3Shortest distanceGeodesics: vertical lines and semicircles centred on the axis.
  4. 3.4IsometriesThe maps that preserve every distance, and the one that fails.
  5. 3.5Equidistant pointsHyperbolic circles, and the bisector of two points.
  6. 3.6Linear and anti-linear mapsThe formulas behind the isometries.
  7. 3.7Congruence and similarityWhy scaling a hyperbolic triangle changes no lengths.
  8. 3.8Angle sum and areaAngles add to less than \(\pi\), and the deficit is the area.

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The hyperbolic plane / 3.2
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.2 of 8

Hyperbolic metric and length

A new way to measure a curve: every step is divided by its height, so the axis is infinitely far away.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In the Euclidean plane a ruler measures the same at every position. The hyperbolic plane is the upper half of the plane, and we want a ruler that depends on height: a small step near the axis should count for more than the same step high up. The simplest rule with this property is to divide each Euclidean step by the height at which it is taken.

Euclidean

A ruler reads the same wherever you put it. Translations and rotations carry the ruler along without changing its readings, so every place looks the same.

Hyperbolic

A ruler reads differently at different heights. A step of Euclidean length \(e\) at height \(y\) has hyperbolic length \(e/y\). Near the axis rulers read large, and high up they read small.

Why this rule

Horizontal shifts and dilations about the origin leave \(dx/y\) unchanged. This is the property that makes the maps of Part 3.4 isometries, and so makes the hyperbolic plane homogeneous.

2Play

First, a ruler. Drag the handle of the blue ruler up and down. The dashed grey ruler is the same Euclidean length at height \(1\).

  • Drag the handle of the blue ruler towards the axis, then up towards the top of the picture. What happens to its hyperbolic length? Why does the dashed ruler not change?

Next, circles. Every circle in this picture has the same hyperbolic radius, \(0.35\), even though the Euclidean circles shrink towards the axis.

  • Why do the circles shrink towards the axis while each one counts as the same size?

Now measure a curve. The panel reports its hyperbolic length, the integral of \(\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}/y\), and your attempts are kept so you can try to beat them.

  • Draw a path that climbs high and comes back down. Is it shorter or longer than the flat path between the same points? Explain using the factor \(1/y\).
  • Try to draw a path that is shorter than \(1\) between \((-1,1)\) and \((1,1)\). Can you get close?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

The definitions below are the ones the simulations use. Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition The hyperbolic plane and its length

The hyperbolic plane is the set \(\mathbb{H}^2 = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid y \gt 0\} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} \mid \operatorname{Im} z \gt 0\}\). If \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t))\), \(a \le t \le b\), is a differentiable curve in \(\mathbb{H}^2\), its hyperbolic length is

\[\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma) = \int_a^b \frac{\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}}{y(t)}\,dt,\]

extended to piecewise differentiable curves by adding the lengths of the pieces. The hyperbolic distance is \(d_{\text{hyp}}(P,Q) = \inf\{\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma) \mid \gamma \text{ a piecewise differentiable curve in } \mathbb{H}^2 \text{ from } P \text{ to } Q\}\).

Because of the \(y(t)\) in the denominator, a curve gets shorter as it climbs and longer as it approaches the \(x\)-axis, where its length blows up.

Statement 3.2.1

\(d_{\text{hyp}}\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{H}^2\).

Show proof

Symmetry. Running a curve backwards does not change its length, so the curves from \(P\) to \(Q\) and from \(Q\) to \(P\) have the same lengths and the same infimum.

Triangle inequality. A curve from \(P\) to \(Q\) followed by a curve from \(Q\) to \(R\) is a curve from \(P\) to \(R\), so \(d(P,R) \le \ell(\gamma_1) + \ell(\gamma_2)\). Taking infima over \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) gives \(d(P,R) \le d(P,Q) + d(Q,R)\).

Positivity. Clearly \(d(P,P) = 0\). Suppose \(P = (x(a), y(a)) \ne Q\), and let \(\gamma\) be any curve from \(P\) to \(Q\). If \(\gamma\) never rises above the line \(y = 2y(a)\), then \(y(t) \le 2y(a)\) throughout, so

\[\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma) \ge \frac{1}{2y(a)} \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt = \frac{\ell_{\text{euc}}(\gamma)}{2y(a)} \ge \frac{d_{\text{euc}}(P,Q)}{2y(a)}.\]

If \(\gamma\) does reach the line \(y = 2y(a)\), let \(t = r\) be the first time it does. Up to that time \(y(t) \le 2y(a)\), so

\[\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma) \ge \int_a^r \frac{|y'(t)|}{y(t)}\,dt \ge \frac{1}{2y(a)} \int_a^r y'(t)\,dt = \frac{2y(a) - y(a)}{2y(a)} = \frac12.\]

Either way \(\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma) \ge \min\!\left(\tfrac12, \tfrac{d_{\text{euc}}(P,Q)}{2y(a)}\right)\), a positive number independent of \(\gamma\). So \(d_{\text{hyp}}(P,Q) \gt 0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.2.2

A horizontal segment at height \(y\) with Euclidean length \(e\) has hyperbolic length \(e/y\).

Show proof

Parametrise the segment by \(x(t) = t\), \(y(t) = y\) for \(t\) in an interval of length \(e\). Then \(\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} = 1\), so

\[\ell_{\text{hyp}} = \int \frac{1}{y}\,dt = \frac{e}{y}.\]

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.2.3

The hyperbolic length of a curve is unchanged if we reparametrise it by an increasing differentiable change of variable.

Show proof

This is the substitution argument of Statement 2.1.1, with the extra factor \(1/y\) carried along. If \(x(t) = X(\theta(t))\) and \(y(t) = Y(\theta(t))\), then \(\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2} = \sqrt{X'^2 + Y'^2}\,\theta'(t)\) and \(y(t) = Y(\theta(t))\). The factor \(\theta'(t)\) is absorbed by the substitution \(\theta = \theta(t)\), so the integrals agree.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the hyperbolic length of the horizontal segment from \((0,2)\) to \((3,2)\), and of the segment from \((0,1)\) to \((3,1)\). Which is longer, and by how much?
  2. Harder Show that the hyperbolic length of the Euclidean arc of the unit circle from \(1\) to \(i\), parametrised by \(z(\theta) = e^{i\theta}\) for \(\theta\) from \(0\) to \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), is \(\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{d\theta}{\sin\theta}\). Explain why this integral diverges, and what that says about the endpoint \(1\).
  3. Toward 3.3 Which curve from \(P\) to \(Q\) do you think is shortest? Guess before you draw, then read Part 3.3.

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.3 of 8

Shortest distance

Which curves are the straight lines of the hyperbolic plane? Vertical half-lines and semicircles centred on the axis, and nothing else.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In the Euclidean plane the shortest path between two points is the straight segment, and a straight segment is exactly a curve whose small pieces are all shortest. We call the hyperbolic analogue a geodesic. To find them, we first need the shortest paths between two points, and that depends on whether the points lie on a vertical line.

Euclidean

The geodesics are the straight lines. Between any two points there is one segment, and it is the shortest path.

Hyperbolic

The geodesics are vertical half-lines and semicircles centred on the axis. Two points on a vertical line are joined by a vertical segment, whose length is a logarithm.

Surprise

The axis itself is never reached, and through a point off a geodesic there are infinitely many geodesics that miss it. So the parallel postulate fails.

2Play

First, a path. Move \(P\) and \(Q\) and draw a path between them. Then tick Reveal the shortest path and compare.

  • Is the straight segment from \(P\) to \(Q\) the shortest path? Try a path that bulges upwards first.

Next, two points on one vertical line. The hyperbolic length of the vertical segment is the logarithm of the ratio of heights. The ticks are one hyperbolic unit apart, so they get further apart in Euclidean terms as you go up.

  • Drag \(y_2\) so that the segment contains exactly two ticks. What is its Euclidean length? What is its hyperbolic length?
  • Keep the segment's hyperbolic length fixed and move both ends up. Does the Euclidean length change? Why does it not matter?

Last, two general points. The simulation draws the geodesic through them: a semicircle centred on the axis. Its centre is the point where the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\) meets the axis.

  • Move \(A\) and \(B\) to the same height. Where is the centre now? Why?
  • Make \(A\) and \(B\) lie on one vertical line. What happens to the centre?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

The definitions are in Part 3.2. Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition Geodesic

A geodesic is a curve \(\gamma\) such that for every point \(P\) of \(\gamma\) and every point \(Q\) of \(\gamma\) sufficiently close to \(P\), the piece of \(\gamma\) joining \(P\) and \(Q\) is a shortest curve joining them.

Statement 3.3.1

If \(P = (x_0, y_1)\) and \(Q = (x_0, y_2)\) lie on the same vertical line, the shortest path between them is the vertical segment, and \(d_{\text{hyp}}(P,Q) = \left|\ln \dfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right|\).

Show proof

Suppose \(y_1 \le y_2\). For any curve from \(P\) to \(Q\), \(|y'(t)| \le \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\) and \(y(t) \gt 0\), so

\[\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma) = \int_a^b \frac{\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2}}{y}\,dt \ge \int_a^b \frac{y'(t)}{y(t)}\,dt = \ln y_2 - \ln y_1 = \ln\frac{y_2}{y_1}.\]

Equality holds when \(x'(t) = 0\) and \(y' \ge 0\) throughout, that is, along the vertical segment. If \(y_1 \gt y_2\), swap \(P\) and \(Q\). Either way \(d_{\text{hyp}}(P,Q) = \left|\ln \tfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right|\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.3.2

If \(P\) and \(Q\) do not lie on a common vertical line, there is an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) that sends both of them onto one vertical line.

Show proof

Since \(PQ\) is not vertical, its perpendicular bisector is not horizontal, so it meets the \(x\)-axis at some point \(R\). Then \(RP = RQ\), so the Euclidean circle \(C\) centred at \(R\) through \(P\) passes through \(Q\). Let \(\phi_1\) be the horizontal translation sending one of the two points where \(C\) meets the axis to the origin. Then \(\phi_1(C)\) is a circle through the origin, centred at some \((a, 0)\). In polar coordinates its equation is \(r = 2a\cos\theta\).

Now let \(\phi_2\) be inversion in the unit circle. It replaces \(r\) by \(\tfrac1r\), so it sends \(\phi_1(C)\) to the curve \(r = \dfrac{1}{2a\cos\theta}\), that is, \(x = r\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2a}\), a vertical line. So \(\phi_2 \circ \phi_1\), an isometry by Statements 3.4.1, 3.4.3 and 3.4.5, sends \(P\) and \(Q\) onto one vertical line.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.3.3

The shortest path between two points of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) is the vertical segment joining them if they lie on a vertical line, and otherwise the arc of the semicircle, centred on the \(x\)-axis, that passes through both. So the geodesics of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) are the vertical half-lines and the semicircles centred on the \(x\)-axis.

Show proof

The vertical case is Statement 3.3.1. Otherwise, let \(\zeta = \phi_2 \circ \phi_1\) be the isometry of Statement 3.3.2, so \(P' = \zeta(P)\) and \(Q' = \zeta(Q)\) lie on a vertical line, and the shortest path between them is the vertical segment. An isometry and its inverse preserve lengths, so \(\zeta^{-1}\) sends that segment to a shortest path from \(P\) to \(Q\), and the image of the segment lies on \(\zeta^{-1}\) of the vertical line, which is the circle \(C\). So the shortest path is the arc of the semicircle centred at \(R\) through \(P\) and \(Q\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.3.4

Euclid's parallel postulate fails in \(\mathbb{H}^2\): for the geodesic \(g\) given by the \(y\)-axis and the point \(P = (2, 1)\), infinitely many geodesics through \(P\) do not meet \(g\).

Show proof

The vertical line \(x = 2\) passes through \(P\) and does not meet \(g\). So does every semicircle centred at \((c, 0)\) through \(P\) with \(c \gt \tfrac54\). Its radius is \(\rho = \sqrt{(2-c)^2 + 1}\), and its leftmost point \(c - \rho\) is positive exactly when \(c^2 \gt (c-2)^2 + 1\), that is, when \(c \gt \tfrac54\). Such a semicircle lies entirely in \(x \gt 0\), so it misses \(g\). Hence infinitely many geodesics through \(P\) miss \(g\), where the postulate allows exactly one.

\(\blacksquare\)

Test the parallel postulate directly. The geodesic \(g\) is the \(y\)-axis (the solid line). Each semicircle through \(P\) is a geodesic. Those that meet \(g\) are red; those that miss it are green.

  • Drag \(P\) and find the smallest centre \(k\) that misses \(g\). Does the threshold agree with the formula?

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the hyperbolic distance between \((0,1)\) and \((0,e^2)\).
  2. Harder Show that two distinct points of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) lie on exactly one geodesic.
  3. Toward 3.5 Describe the set of points at hyperbolic distance \(l\) from a fixed point \(A\). Guess its shape before reading Part 3.5.
