Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.4 of 8

Isometries

The maps that move the hyperbolic plane without changing a single distance, and the ones that do.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

An isometry is a map that preserves distance. Two triangles are congruent exactly when some isometry carries one onto the other, so the isometries are the moves that the geometry allows.

Euclidean

The isometries are translations, rotations, reflections and glide reflections. Part 2.5 proved that these are all of them.

Hyperbolic

The horizontal shifts, the dilations about the origin, the reflections in vertical lines, and inversions in circles centred on the axis. Each one is checked separately below.

The warning

Inversion in a circle centred off the axis looks harmless, but it is not an isometry. The last simulation shows why.

2Play

Each map gets its own simulation. The solid triangle is the original, and the dashed one is its image. The panel compares the three side lengths before and after. Drag any corner of the original to test other shapes.

Shift \(z \mapsto z+1.2\)

Dilation \(z \mapsto 1.7z\)

Inversion \(z \mapsto 1/\bar z\) in the unit circle

Möbius map \(z \mapsto (1.2z+0.5)/(0.4z+1)\)

Off-centre inversion (not an isometry)

  • For the shift, the dilation and the inversion, which lengths are unchanged? Why does the Möbius map also work?
  • For the off-centre inversion, which distances change, and what happens near the axis?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

An isometry is a map \(f\) with \(d(P,Q) = d(f(P), f(Q))\) for all \(P, Q\). Since distance is the infimum of lengths, it is enough to show that \(f\) preserves the length of every curve.

Statement 3.4.1

Horizontal translations \((x, y) \mapsto (x + h, y)\) and reflections in vertical lines \((x, y) \mapsto (2x_0 - x, y)\) are isometries of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).

Show proof

Each map sends \(\mathbb{H}^2\) to itself and does not change \(y(t)\). It changes \(x(t)\) by a constant or by a sign, so \(x'(t)^2\) and \(y'(t)\) are unchanged. Hence the integrand of \(\ell_{\text{hyp}}\) is unchanged, and so is the length of every curve.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.4.2

A homothety \(\zeta(x,y) = \big(\lambda(x - x_0) + x_0,\ \lambda(y - y_0) + y_0\big)\) with \(\lambda \gt 0\), centred at a point \((x_0, 0)\) on the \(x\)-axis, is an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).

Show proof

With \(y_0 = 0\), the image of \(\gamma\) is \(\big(\lambda(x(t) - x_0) + x_0,\ \lambda y(t)\big)\), with derivatives \(\lambda x'(t)\) and \(\lambda y'(t)\). So

\[\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\zeta(\gamma)) = \int_a^b \frac{\lambda\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}}{\lambda\, y(t)}\,dt = \ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma).\]

(If \(y_0 \ne 0\), the denominator would be \(\lambda(y - y_0) + y_0\) and the \(\lambda\)'s would no longer cancel. That is why the centre must lie on the axis.)

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.4.3

Inversion in the unit circle, \((x, y) \mapsto \left(\dfrac{x}{x^2 + y^2},\ \dfrac{y}{x^2 + y^2}\right)\), is an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).

Show proof

It sends \(\mathbb{H}^2\) to itself, since the second coordinate keeps its sign. Let \(X(t) = \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}\) and \(Y(t) = \dfrac{y}{x^2+y^2}\). By the quotient rule, using \(\tfrac{d}{dt}(x^2 + y^2) = 2xx' + 2yy'\),

\[X' = \frac{x'(y^2 - x^2) - 2xyy'}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, \qquad Y' = \frac{y'(x^2 - y^2) - 2xyx'}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.\]

Squaring and adding, the cross terms cancel and \((y^2 - x^2)^2 + 4x^2y^2 = (x^2 + y^2)^2\), so \(X'^2 + Y'^2 = \dfrac{x'^2 + y'^2}{(x^2 + y^2)^2}\). Therefore

\[\ell_{\text{hyp}}(\zeta(\gamma)) = \int_a^b \frac{\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2}\,/\,(x^2 + y^2)}{y\,/\,(x^2 + y^2)}\,dt = \ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma).\]

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.4.4

Inversion in any circle whose centre lies on the \(x\)-axis is an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).

Show proof

Let the centre be \((x_0, 0)\) and the radius \(r\). The inversion is \(z \mapsto x_0 + \dfrac{r^2}{\overline{z - x_0}}\), the composite of four maps: translate horizontally by \(-x_0\), invert in the unit circle, apply the homothety with ratio \(r^2\) about the origin, and translate back by \(x_0\). Each step is an isometry by Statements 3.4.1, 3.4.2 and 3.4.3, and so is their composite by Statement 3.4.5.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.4.5

The composite of two isometries of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) is an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).

Show proof

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be isometries and \(\gamma\) a curve. Since \(f\) preserves lengths, \(\ell_{\text{hyp}}(f(\gamma)) = \ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma)\). Applying the same fact to \(g\) and the curve \(f(\gamma)\) gives \(\ell_{\text{hyp}}(g(f(\gamma))) = \ell_{\text{hyp}}(f(\gamma)) = \ell_{\text{hyp}}(\gamma)\). So \(g \circ f\) preserves lengths, and hence distances.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.4.6

\(\mathbb{H}^2\) is homogeneous: for any two points \(P, Q\) there is an isometry sending \(P\) to \(Q\).

Show proof

Let \(P = (x_1, y_1)\) and \(Q = (x_2, y_2)\). The homothety about the origin with ratio \(\tfrac{y_2}{y_1}\) sends \(P\) to \(\left(\tfrac{x_1 y_2}{y_1},\ y_2\right)\). The horizontal translation by \(x_2 - \tfrac{x_1 y_2}{y_1}\) then sends it to \(Q\). Both are isometries (Statements 3.4.1 and 3.4.2), and so is their composite.

\(\blacksquare\)

Remark. Inversion in a circle whose centre is not on the axis is not an isometry in general: it can send points of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) below the axis, which is why the simulation flags it. The statement above is only for centres on the axis.

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the image of \(i\) under the composite of the homothety \(z \mapsto 2z\) and the inversion \(z \mapsto 1/\bar z\), and check that the composite is an isometry by applying it to the points \(i\) and \(2i\).
  2. Harder Show that inversion in the circle \(|z - 1| = 1\) is not an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\), by finding two points whose hyperbolic distance changes.
  3. Toward 3.6 Every isometry we have seen has the form \(z \mapsto \dfrac{az+b}{cz+d}\) or \(z \mapsto \dfrac{c\bar z+d}{a\bar z+b}\). Which of the moves above fit this shape?

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The hyperbolic plane / 3.5
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.5 of 8

Locus of equidistant points

Circles that look like Euclidean circles from far away, and a bisector that is itself a geodesic.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A Euclidean circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a centre. Two questions follow naturally in the hyperbolic plane: what is the set of points at a fixed hyperbolic distance \(l\) from a point \(A\), and what is the set of points equidistant from two points \(P\) and \(Q\)?

Euclidean

The circle has its centre at the point it is defined around. The points equidistant from two points form a line, the perpendicular bisector.

Hyperbolic circle

It is still a Euclidean circle, but its Euclidean centre is higher than \(A\). The hyperbolic centre and the Euclidean centre are different points.

Hyperbolic bisector

The equidistant set is a single geodesic: the bisector is again a semicircle centred on the axis, not a straight line.

2Play

Drag \(A\) and change the radius \(l\). The shaded region is the set of points at hyperbolic distance \(l\) from \(A\), and the green arcs are the geodesics of length \(l\) leaving \(A\).

  • Is the hyperbolic circle a Euclidean circle? Is \(A\) its Euclidean centre?
  • Keep \(l\) fixed and drag \(A\) down towards the axis. What happens to the Euclidean size of the circle? Why?

Now the bisector. The dotted set is every point \(X\) with \(d(X,P) = d(X,Q)\). Drag \(P\) and \(Q\), and use the slider to draw the circles of equal radius \(\rho\) about each. Their intersection points are on the dotted set.

  • Move \(P\) and \(Q\) so they are at different heights. Is the dotted set still a Euclidean straight line? Does it look like a geodesic?
  • Set \(\rho\) so the two circles just touch. Where is the touching point, and why is it on the dotted set?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 3.5.1

Let \(A = (x_0, y_0)\) and \(l \gt 0\). The set of points at hyperbolic distance \(l\) from \(A\) is the Euclidean circle with diameter \(BC\), where \(B = (x_0,\ y_0 e^{-l})\) and \(C = (x_0,\ y_0 e^{l})\).

Show proof

By Statement 3.3.1, \(B\) and \(C\) are the two points at distance \(l\) from \(A\) on the vertical line through \(A\). Let \(\Gamma\) be the circle with diameter \(BC\). Every point at distance \(l\) from \(A\) lies on some geodesic through \(A\), so it is enough to show that the two points at distance \(l\) from \(A\) along any other geodesic through \(A\) lie on \(\Gamma\).

Such a geodesic is a semicircle through \(A\) centred at a point \(F\) on the axis, with endpoints \(D\) and \(E\). Let \(G = (x_0, 0)\) be the foot of the vertical through \(A\). Since \(DE\) is a diameter, \(\angle DAE = 90^\circ\), and \(AG\) is the altitude of the right triangle \(DAE\), so

\[EA^2 = EG \cdot ED \qquad\text{and}\qquad AG^2 = GD \cdot GE.\]

Invert in the circle with centre \(E\) and radius \(EA\). It is an isometry by Statement 3.4.4, since \(E\) lies on the axis, and it fixes \(A\). It sends the vertical line through \(A\) to the geodesic \(DE\), and it sends \(B\) and \(C\) to points \(B'\) and \(C'\) of \(DE\) at distance \(l\) from \(A\), lying on the rays \(EB\) and \(EC\).

Now \(BG \cdot GC = y_0 e^{-l} \cdot y_0 e^{l} = y_0^2 = AG^2 = GD \cdot GE\). This says that \(B\) is the orthocentre of the triangle \(DCE\): the triangles \(DGB\) and \(CGE\) are similar right triangles, so \(DB \perp CE\). The point \(C'\) lies on \(CE\) and on the semicircle with diameter \(DE\), so \(\angle DC'E = 90^\circ\), and \(C'\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(CE\). Hence \(D\), \(B\), \(C'\) are collinear and \(\angle BC'C = 90^\circ\), so \(C'\) lies on the circle with diameter \(BC\). The same argument with \(B\) and \(C\) swapped puts \(B'\) on \(\Gamma\).

In coordinates, \(\Gamma\) has Euclidean centre \(\big(x_0,\ y_0\cosh l\big)\) and Euclidean radius \(y_0\sinh l\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.5.2

The Euclidean centre \((x_0, y_0\cosh l)\) of the hyperbolic circle in Statement 3.5.1 lies strictly above \(A\) when \(l \gt 0\). So the hyperbolic centre \(A\) is not the Euclidean centre.

Show proof

The Euclidean centre is at height \(y_0\cosh l\), and \(\cosh l \gt 1\) for \(l \gt 0\), so it is strictly above \(A\), whose height is \(y_0\). Since the hyperbolic circle is a Euclidean circle, its Euclidean centre is a Euclidean notion; \(A\) is the centre only in the sense that it is the point the circle is defined around.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.5.3

Let \(P_0 = (0, y_0)\) and \(P_1 = (0, y_1)\) with \(y_1 \gt y_0\), and let \(g\) be a complete geodesic through \(P_0\). Then \(P_0\) is the point of \(g\) closest to \(P_1\) if and only if \(g\) is the semicircle of radius \(y_0\) centred at the origin, that is, \(g\) meets the \(y\)-axis at right angles.

Show proof

Let \(d = d_{\text{hyp}}(P_0, P_1)\). By Statement 3.5.1, the hyperbolic circle \(\Gamma\) about \(P_1\) of radius \(d\) is a Euclidean circle centred on the \(y\)-axis, and \(P_0\) is its lowest point, so its tangent at \(P_0\) is horizontal.

If \(P_0\) is the point of \(g\) closest to \(P_1\), no point of \(g\) is inside \(\Gamma\), so \(g\) touches \(\Gamma\) at \(P_0\) and has a horizontal tangent there. The centre of \(g\) is on the \(x\)-axis directly below the point with horizontal tangent, so it is the origin, and the radius is \(y_0\).

Conversely, if \(g\) is the semicircle of radius \(y_0\) about the origin, every point of \(g\) has height at most \(y_0\), while every point of \(\Gamma\) other than \(P_0\) has height greater than \(y_0\). So \(g\) meets the closed disc bounded by \(\Gamma\) only at \(P_0\), and every other point of \(g\) is further from \(P_1\) than \(d\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.5.4

Let \(P = (0, y_1)\) and \(Q = (0, y_2)\). Every point of the semicircle \(|z| = \sqrt{y_1 y_2}\) is equidistant from \(P\) and \(Q\). This semicircle is a geodesic meeting \(PQ\) at right angles, through its midpoint.

Show proof

Let \(r = \sqrt{y_1 y_2}\) and let \(\sigma(z) = r^2/\bar z\). This is inversion in the circle \(|z| = r\), so it is an isometry by Statement 3.4.4 (its centre is the origin, on the axis). Points of the circle are fixed by \(\sigma\), since \(|X| = r\) gives \(r^2/\bar X = X\). And \(\sigma(iy_1) = \dfrac{r^2}{-iy_1} = iy_2\), so \(\sigma\) swaps \(P\) and \(Q\).

So for any \(X\) on the circle, \(d(X,P) = d(\sigma X, \sigma P) = d(X,Q)\). The circle \(|z| = r\) is a geodesic by Statement 3.3.3, and it meets the \(y\)-axis at right angles at \((0,r)\), which is the hyperbolic midpoint of \(P\) and \(Q\) because \(\ln\tfrac{r}{y_1} = \ln\tfrac{y_2}{r}\).

Note. The simulation shows that no other points are equidistant from \(P\) and \(Q\). The converse is not proved in these notes, so treat it as an observed fact until you prove it.

\(\blacksquare\)

Proof in action. Statement 3.5.4 uses the inversion in the circle \(|z| = \sqrt{y_1y_2}\). It swaps \(P\) and \(Q\), and it is an isometry, so it carries the distance from \(X\) to \(P\) onto the distance from \(\sigma X\) to \(Q\). Move \(X\) and watch the two distances.

  • Put \(X\) on the dashed semicircle. What are \(\sigma X\) and \(X\)?
  • Move \(P\) and \(Q\) to different heights. Does \(\sigma\) still swap them?

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the Euclidean centre and radius of the hyperbolic circle of radius \(\ln 2\) about \(A = (0, 1)\).
  2. Harder Prove the converse of Statement 3.5.4: if \(d(X,P) = d(X,Q)\), then \(X\) lies on the semicircle \(|z| = \sqrt{y_1 y_2}\). Start from the distance formula \(\cosh d = 1 + \dfrac{|z-w|^2}{2\operatorname{Im} z \operatorname{Im} w}\).
  3. Toward 3.6 Which maps move a hyperbolic circle onto a hyperbolic circle? Test one of the maps from Part 3.6 on this simulation.

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / The hyperbolic plane / 3.6
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 3.6 of 8

Linear and anti-linear fractional maps

A two-parameter family of formulas that does all the moving, and what it does to the axis.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In Part 3.4 we found isometries one at a time. Here is a single formula that contains many of them. The idea is to write every isometry as a fraction of two linear expressions in \(z\), and to check which coefficients keep the upper half-plane in place.

Euclidean

The similarities of the plane are the maps \(z \mapsto az + b\), with \(a\) and \(b\) complex. They have a rotation-and-dilation part and a shift.

Hyperbolic

The isometries are fractions \(z \mapsto (az+b)/(cz+d)\) with real coefficients and \(ad - bc = 1\). Four numbers, one condition, and every move comes from them.

Reflections

Reflections need a twin formula with \(\bar z\). The anti-linear maps handle the orientation-reversing moves.

2Play

Choose a preset, then move the sliders. The solid curves are vertical lines and semicircles centred on the axis, and the dashed curves are horizontal lines. The letter F shows what happens to a shape. The condition \(ad - bc = 1\) is kept on every move.

  • Whatever you choose, what do the solid curves turn into? And the dashed ones?
  • Switch on the anti-linear version and watch the letter F near \(i\). What has changed?
  • Drive \(a\) to its smallest value, then move \(b\) and \(c\). Does the picture ever leave the upper half-plane? Why not, when \(ad - bc = 1\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Definition Möbius transformation

A Möbius transformation is a map \(z \mapsto \dfrac{az + b}{cz + d}\) with \(a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{C}\) and \(ad - bc \ne 0\). From now on \(a, b, c, d\) are real.

Statement 3.6.1

If \(a, b, c, d\) are real with \(ad - bc \gt 0\), the map \(z \mapsto \dfrac{az+b}{cz+d}\) sends \(\mathbb{H}^2\) to itself.

Show proof

Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(c\bar z + d\),

\[\operatorname{Im}\frac{az + b}{cz + d} = \frac{\operatorname{Im}\big((az + b)(c\bar z + d)\big)}{|cz + d|^2} = \frac{(ad - bc)\operatorname{Im} z}{|cz + d|^2},\]

which is positive whenever \(\operatorname{Im} z \gt 0\). Dividing all four coefficients by \(\sqrt{ad - bc}\) does not change the map, so we may assume \(ad - bc = 1\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.6.2

For real \(a, b, c, d\) with \(ad - bc = 1\), both

\[z \mapsto \frac{az + b}{cz + d} \qquad\text{and}\qquad z \mapsto \frac{c\bar z + d}{a\bar z + b}\]

are isometries of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).

Show proof

Case \(a \ne 0\). Compose the horizontal translation by \(\tfrac{b}{a}\), inversion in the unit circle \(w \mapsto \tfrac{1}{\bar w}\), the homothety with ratio \(\tfrac{1}{a^2}\) about the origin, and the horizontal translation by \(\tfrac{c}{a}\):

\[z \;\mapsto\; z + \frac ba = \frac{az + b}{a} \;\mapsto\; \frac{a}{a\bar z + b} \;\mapsto\; \frac{1}{a(a\bar z + b)} \;\mapsto\; \frac{1}{a(a\bar z + b)} + \frac ca.\]

Using \(1 + bc = ad\),

\[\frac{1}{a(a\bar z + b)} + \frac ca = \frac{1 + ac\bar z + bc}{a(a\bar z + b)} = \frac{ad + ac\bar z}{a(a\bar z + b)} = \frac{c\bar z + d}{a\bar z + b}.\]

This is the anti-linear map. Composing it with one more inversion in the unit circle gives \(\dfrac{az + b}{cz + d}\), the linear map.

Case \(a = 0\). Then \(-bc = 1\), so \(c \ne 0\). The coefficients \((c,\ b + d,\ c,\ d)\) satisfy \(cd - (b+d)c = -bc = 1\) and have first entry \(c \ne 0\), so by the first case \(z \mapsto \dfrac{cz + b + d}{cz + d}\) is an isometry. Composing with the horizontal translation by \(-1\) gives

\[\frac{cz + b + d}{cz + d} - 1 = \frac{b}{cz + d} = \frac{az + b}{cz + d},\]

the linear map. One more inversion in the unit circle gives the anti-linear one.

The maps \(z \mapsto \dfrac{az+b}{cz+d}\) are called linear fractional, and \(z \mapsto \dfrac{c\bar z+d}{a\bar z+b}\) anti-linear fractional.

\(\blacksquare\)

Remark. The notes also state the converse, that every isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) has one of these two forms. We have not proved it here, so it is a claim to verify, not a result proved in this series.

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find real \(a, b, c, d\) with \(ad - bc = 1\) such that \(z \mapsto \dfrac{az + b}{cz + d}\) sends \(i\) to \(2 + 3i\).
  2. Harder Show that \(z \mapsto \dfrac{\cos\theta\, z - \sin\theta}{\sin\theta\, z + \cos\theta}\) fixes \(i\), and check that it is an isometry for every \(\theta\).
  3. Toward 3.7 Two triangles have the same angles. Are they congruent, or can one be a scaled copy of the other? Read Part 3.7 to find out.

Home / Linear Algebra / 7.1
Linear Algebra · Part 7.1

Adjoints and normal operators

Every linear map has a partner that runs the other way. Its null space is the orthogonal complement of the range, and the operators that commute with their partner are the ones whose behaviour is easiest to see.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

On \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual dot product, a matrix \(A\) can be moved across the dot product: \(\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^{T}v\rangle\). The transpose is the partner of \(A\), and the question is what plays that role for a linear map between general inner product spaces.

Moving the map

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the map \(T\) can be applied to \(u\) and then dotted with \(v\), or \(T^{*}\) can be applied to \(v\) and then dotted with \(u\). The two numbers agree, and that is the whole definition of \(T^{*}\).

A dot product is a vector

A linear functional on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is always "dot with a fixed vector". The adjoint is built from exactly this fact: for each \(w\), the map \(v \mapsto \langle Tv, w\rangle\) is a functional, so it has a vector that represents it.

Commuting with the partner

A rotation of the plane and a symmetric matrix both commute with their transposes. Those are the operators the next two posts study, and this post names the class.

2Play

Drag the two columns of \(T\), which are the images of the standard basis vectors. Move the blue vector \(w\) and turn the test direction \(x\). The orange arrow is \(Tx\), and the green arrow is \(T^{*}w\), which is the vector that matches \(w\) through the inner product.

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Move \(w\) to a new place. Does \(\langle Tx, w\rangle\) equal \(\langle x, T^{*}w\rangle\) for the test \(x\) you picked? Does it still hold for all \(x\)?
  • Which vectors \(x\) make \(Tx\) point along \(w\)? Which make \(\langle Tx, w\rangle = 0\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 7.1.1 Adjoint

Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\). The adjoint of \(T\) is a map \(T^{*} \in \mathcal{L}(W,V)\) such that \(\langle Tv, w\rangle = \langle v, T^{*}w\rangle\) for all \(v \in V\) and \(w \in W\).

Definition 7.1.2 Self-adjoint

An operator \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) is self-adjoint if \(T^{*} = T\).

Definition 7.1.3 Normal

An operator \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) is normal if \(TT^{*} = T^{*}T\).

Statement 7.1.1 The adjoint exists and is unique

For every \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) there is exactly one map \(T^{*}\) satisfying the defining equation, and it is linear.

for each w there is one vector

Show proof

Existence. Fix \(w \in W\). The map \(\varphi(v) = \langle Tv, w\rangle\) is linear in \(v\). Let \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) be an orthonormal basis of \(V\) and put \(u = \sum_j \overline{\varphi(e_j)}\, e_j\). Because the inner product is conjugate-linear in its second slot, \(\langle v, u\rangle = \sum_j \varphi(e_j)\langle v, e_j\rangle = \varphi\bigl(\sum_j \langle v,e_j\rangle e_j\bigr) = \varphi(v)\). Define \(T^{*}w = u\). Then \(\langle Tv, w\rangle = \langle v, T^{*}w\rangle\) for all \(v\).

Uniqueness. If \(u\) and \(u'\) both work for \(w\), then \(\langle v, u-u'\rangle = 0\) for every \(v\). Taking \(v = u-u'\) gives \(u = u'\).

Linearity. For scalars \(a,b\), \(\langle v, T^{*}(aw_1+bw_2)\rangle = \langle Tv, aw_1+bw_2\rangle = \bar a\langle Tv,w_1\rangle + \bar b\langle Tv,w_2\rangle = \langle v, aT^{*}w_1+bT^{*}w_2\rangle\) for all \(v\), so uniqueness gives linearity.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.1.2 Null space of the adjoint

For \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), \(\operatorname{null}T^{*} = (\operatorname{range}T)^{\perp}\), and \(\operatorname{range}T^{*} = (\operatorname{null}T)^{\perp}\).

drag the columns, turn w

Show proof

Take \(w \in W\). If \(T^{*}w = 0\), then \(\langle Tv, w\rangle = \langle v, T^{*}w\rangle = 0\) for every \(v\), so \(w\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}T\). Conversely, if \(w \perp \operatorname{range}T\), then \(\langle v, T^{*}w\rangle = \langle Tv, w\rangle = 0\) for all \(v\); choosing \(v = T^{*}w\) gives \(\lVert T^{*}w\rVert^{2} = 0\). So \(\operatorname{null}T^{*} = (\operatorname{range}T)^{\perp}\).

For the second equation, apply the first to \(T^{*}\) in place of \(T\). Since \(T^{**} = T\) (both sides satisfy \(\langle T^{*}w, v\rangle = \langle w, Tv\rangle\)), this gives \(\operatorname{null}T = (\operatorname{range}T^{*})^{\perp}\). Taking orthogonal complements in the finite-dimensional space \(V\) gives \(\operatorname{range}T^{*} = (\operatorname{null}T)^{\perp}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.1.3 The matrix of the adjoint

Fix orthonormal bases \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) of \(V\) and \(f_1,\dots,f_m\) of \(W\). Then the matrix of \(T^{*}\) with respect to these bases is the conjugate transpose of the matrix of \(T\).

turn the phase of entry 12

Show proof

Since \(f_1,\dots,f_m\) is orthonormal, \(Te_k = \sum_j \langle Te_k, f_j\rangle f_j\). So the \((j,k)\) entry of the matrix of \(T\) is \(\langle Te_k, f_j\rangle\). Similarly the \((k,j)\) entry of the matrix of \(T^{*}\) is \(\langle T^{*}f_j, e_k\rangle\). By the defining equation this equals \(\langle f_j, Te_k\rangle\), which is the complex conjugate of \(\langle Te_k, f_j\rangle\). So the matrix of \(T^{*}\) is the conjugate transpose.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.1.4 Normal operators, by lengths

An operator \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) is normal if and only if \(\lVert Tv\rVert = \lVert T^{*}v\rVert\) for every \(v \in V\).

drag the columns, turn v

Show proof

For every \(v\), \(\lVert Tv\rVert^{2} = \langle Tv, Tv\rangle = \langle T^{*}Tv, v\rangle\) and \(\lVert T^{*}v\rVert^{2} = \langle TT^{*}v, v\rangle\). So \(\lVert Tv\rVert^{2} - \lVert T^{*}v\rVert^{2} = \langle Av, v\rangle\), where \(A = T^{*}T - TT^{*}\). The operator \(A\) is self-adjoint, because \((T^{*}T)^{*} = T^{*}T\) and \((TT^{*})^{*} = TT^{*}\).

So the statement reduces to: a self-adjoint \(A\) with \(\langle Av,v\rangle = 0\) for all \(v\) must be zero. For any \(u, w\), expanding gives \(0 = \langle A(u+w), u+w\rangle = \langle Au,u\rangle + \langle Aw,w\rangle + \langle Au,w\rangle + \langle Aw,u\rangle\). Here \(\langle Aw,u\rangle = \langle w, Au\rangle = \overline{\langle Au,w\rangle}\), so \(\operatorname{Re}\langle Au,w\rangle = 0\) for all \(u,w\). Replacing \(w\) by \(iw\) in the complex case gives \(\operatorname{Im}\langle Au,w\rangle = 0\) too, so \(\langle Au,w\rangle = 0\). (In the real case the first step already suffices.) Taking \(w = Au\) gives \(Au = 0\).

Hence \(T^{*}T = TT^{*}\) exactly when \(\lVert Tv\rVert = \lVert T^{*}v\rVert\) for all \(v\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Let \(T : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2\) send \((x,y,z)\) to \((x+2y, z-y)\). Write the matrix of \(T^{*}\) and check the equation \(\langle Tv,w\rangle = \langle v,T^{*}w\rangle\) on \(v = (1,0,1)\) and \(w = (2,-1)\).
  2. Harder Show that \((ST)^{*} = T^{*}S^{*}\) whenever the composition makes sense, and that \(T^{*}T = 0\) forces \(T = 0\).
  3. Toward 7.2 Let \(T\) be normal and \(Tv = \lambda v\). Apply Statement 7.1.4 to \(T - \lambda I\) to show that \(T^{*}v = \bar\lambda v\). Why does this make the eigenvectors of a normal operator useful?

Home / Linear Algebra / 2.2
Linear Algebra · Part 2.2

Bases and dimension

A basis is a list that spans and is independent, so every vector has exactly one address in it. Every space has a basis, every basis of a space has the same length, and that length is the dimension.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A coordinate system on the plane is a choice of two arrows that reach everywhere, with no redundancy. Once we fix them, each point has one pair of numbers that describes it. The same idea works in any vector space, and the number of arrows needed does not depend on which arrows we chose.

Euclidean

The standard vectors \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). So are \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\). Both bases have two vectors.

Beyond the plane

The polynomials \(1, x, x^2, \dots, x^n\) form a basis of the polynomials of degree at most \(n\). Any polynomial of that degree has exactly one expression in them.

The count

Two bases of the same space always have the same number of vectors. That number is the dimension, and the statements below prove it is well defined.

2Play

Drag \(b_1\) and \(b_2\). The coloured lattice shows every combination \(c_1 b_1 + c_2 b_2\) with integer coefficients. Drag the target \(w\) and read off its coefficients. When the two vectors are parallel, the lattice collapses onto a line and the list stops being a basis.

What to notice before reading the proof:

drag b1, b2 and the target w

  • Move \(b_2\) to lie on the line through \(b_1\). What happens to the coefficients of a target that is not on that line?
  • Pick a target and watch its coefficients as you move one basis vector. Which coefficients change, and which stay put?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 2.2.1 Basis

A basis of \(V\) is a list of vectors in \(V\) that is linearly independent and spans \(V\). A vector space is finite-dimensional if it has a finite spanning list.

Statement 2.2.1 Basis is unique representation

A list \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) is a basis of \(V\) if and only if every vector of \(V\) has exactly one representation as a linear combination of the list.

drag b1, b2 and the target w

Show proof

If the list is a basis, it spans, so every vector has at least one representation. If a vector had two, subtracting them would give a nontrivial zero combination, contradicting independence. Hence exactly one.

Conversely, if every vector has exactly one representation, then the list spans (since representations exist) and the zero vector has only one representation, the trivial one. So the list is independent, and it is a basis.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.2.2 Spanning lists contain bases

Every spanning list of a vector space contains a basis of that space.

drag the four vectors of the list

Show proof

Among all spanning sublists of the given spanning list, choose one of smallest length. We claim this sublist is independent. If not, the dependence lemma (Statement 2.1.2) gives a vector in it lying in the span of the others. Removing that vector keeps the span, since the removed vector is a combination of what remains. This yields a shorter spanning sublist, contradicting minimality.

A spanning, independent sublist is a basis.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.2.3 Independent lists extend to bases

If \(V\) is finite-dimensional, then every linearly independent list in \(V\) can be extended to a basis of \(V\).

drag u1 or add u2; the standard vectors are tried

Show proof

Let \(w_1,\dots,w_m\) be a spanning list of \(V\), which exists by finite-dimensionality. Start with the independent list \(u_1,\dots,u_n\). Go through \(w_1,\dots,w_m\) in order, adjoining \(w_j\) to the current list exactly when \(w_j\) is not in its span.

The current list stays independent. If \(w_j\) is not in the span of the current list and \(a w_j + \sum b_i u_i = 0\) with \(a \ne 0\), then \(w_j\) is a combination of the rest, a contradiction; so \(a=0\), and then all \(b_i=0\) by independence of the current list. At the end every \(w_j\) lies in the span of the final list, so that list spans \(\operatorname{span}(w_1,\dots,w_m)=V\). It is therefore a basis extending the \(u_i\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.2.4 Independent lists are no longer than spanning lists

If \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) spans \(V\) and \(u_1,\dots,u_n\) is linearly independent in \(V\), then \(n \le m\).

drag the spanning vectors s1, s2, s3 and the independent p1, p2

Show proof

Build up the independent list one vector at a time while keeping a spanning list of length \(m\). Start with the spanning list \(v_1,\dots,v_m\). Put \(u_1\) in front: the new list \(u_1,v_1,\dots,v_m\) is dependent, because \(u_1\) is a combination of the \(v_j\). Since \(u_1 \neq 0\) by independence, the dependence lemma removes some \(v_j\) and keeps the span. The list now has \(m\) vectors, \(u_1\) among them, and spans \(V\).

Repeat. At step \(k\), the list has the form \(u_1,\dots,u_{k-1}\) together with \(m-k+1\) of the \(v_j\), and it spans \(V\). Adding \(u_k\) in front gives a dependent list, so the dependence lemma removes a vector. That vector cannot be one of the \(u_i\), because a \(u_i\) in the span of earlier vectors would contradict independence. So a \(v_j\) is removed. If \(k-1=m\) were reached with \(u_{m+1}\) to add, \(u_{m+1}\) would lie in the span of \(u_1,\dots,u_m\), a contradiction. Hence \(n \le m\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 2.2.2 Dimension

The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space \(V\), written \(\dim V\), is the length of any basis of \(V\).

Statement 2.2.5 Dimension is well defined

Any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same length.

drag the two bases B1 and B2

Show proof

Let \(B\) and \(B'\) be bases, of lengths \(m\) and \(n\). Since \(B\) spans and \(B'\) is independent, Statement 2.2.4 gives \(n \le m\). Exchanging the roles gives \(m \le n\). Hence \(m=n\), and \(\dim V\) is well defined.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.2.6 Dimension of a subspace

If \(V\) is finite-dimensional and \(U\) is a subspace of \(V\), then \(U\) is finite-dimensional and \(\dim U \le \dim V\).

drag the line's direction; pick a subspace

Show proof

Build a list in \(U\) by starting empty and adding a vector of \(U\) that is not in the span of the list so far, as long as one exists. The list stays independent, and it cannot be longer than \(\dim V\): an independent list in \(V\) has length at most the length of a basis of \(V\), by Statement 2.2.4. So the process stops, with an independent list in \(U\) that spans \(U\). That list is a basis of \(U\), so \(U\) is finite-dimensional and \(\dim U \le \dim V\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 2.2.7 Dimension of a sum

If \(U\) and \(W\) are finite-dimensional subspaces of \(V\), then \(U+W\) is finite-dimensional and \(\dim(U+W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U\cap W)\).

choose U and W, drag their directions

Show proof

Let \(u_1,\dots,u_k\) be a basis of \(U\cap W\). Extend it, by Statement 2.2.3 applied inside \(U\), to a basis \(u_1,\dots,u_k,v_1,\dots,v_p\) of \(U\). Extend it likewise inside \(W\) to a basis \(u_1,\dots,u_k,w_1,\dots,w_q\) of \(W\). Then \(\dim U = k+p\), \(\dim W = k+q\), and \(\dim(U\cap W)=k\).

We claim \(u_1,\dots,u_k,v_1,\dots,v_p,w_1,\dots,w_q\) is a basis of \(U+W\). It spans, since it contains spanning lists of \(U\) and of \(W\). For independence, suppose \(\sum a_i u_i + \sum b_j v_j + \sum c_l w_l = 0\). Set \(x = \sum b_j v_j\). Then \(x \in U\), and \(x = -\sum a_i u_i - \sum c_l w_l\) lies in \(W\), since each \(u_i \in W\). So \(x \in U\cap W\), and \(x = \sum d_i u_i\) for some \(d_i\). Then \(\sum d_i u_i - \sum b_j v_j = 0\), and since \(u_1,\dots,u_k,v_1,\dots,v_p\) is independent, all \(b_j=0\) and \(d_i=0\). The original relation becomes \(\sum a_i u_i + \sum c_l w_l = 0\), and independence of the basis of \(W\) forces all \(a_i, c_l = 0\).

The basis has \(k+p+q\) vectors, so \(\dim(U+W) = k+p+q = (k+p)+(k+q)-k = \dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find a basis of \(\{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x+y+z=0\}\), and give its dimension.
  2. Harder Let \(U\) and \(W\) be two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Use Statement 2.2.7 to show that \(U\cap W\) is at least a line.
  3. Toward 3.1 Once a basis is fixed, a linear map is determined by what it does to the basis. How many numbers does it take to specify a linear map from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^3\)?

Home / Linear Algebra / 9.1
Linear Algebra · Part 9.1

Bilinear and quadratic forms

A bilinear form takes two vectors and returns a number, linearly in each. The symmetric ones are exactly the self-adjoint operators in disguise, and the spectral theorem turns every quadratic form into a sum of weighted squares.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

The dot product on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) takes two vectors and returns a number. It is linear in each slot, so it is a bilinear form. Plugging the same vector into both slots gives \(x^2+y^2\), a quadratic form whose level sets are circles.

Forms as matrices

Once a basis is fixed, a bilinear form \(b\) becomes a matrix \(A\) with \(b(u,v)=u^{\top}Av\). Changing basis changes \(A\) to \(P^{\top}AP\).

Ellipses

The level set \(q(v)=1\) of a positive definite quadratic form is an ellipse. Its axes point along the eigenvectors of the matrix, and its size is set by the eigenvalues.

A saddle

If one eigenvalue is positive and the other negative, the level set is a hyperbola. The form is then neither positive nor negative definite.

2Play

Fix a matrix \(A\) and two vectors \(u\) and \(v\). The number \(b(u,v)=u^{\top}Av\) is the value of the form. The dashed line is the set of \(x\) with \(b(x,v)=0\). Drag \(u\) and \(v\) and watch that line rotate with \(v\).

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Why is the dashed line always perpendicular to \(Av\)? Which vector is \(Av\) when \(A\) is symmetric?
  • Set \(A\) to the identity and drag \(u\) and \(v\). Does the form change when you rotate both vectors together?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 9.1.1 Bilinear form

A bilinear form on \(V\) is a function \(b:V\times V\to\mathbf{F}\) that is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed. It is symmetric if \(b(u,v)=b(v,u)\) for all \(u,v\).

Definition 9.1.2 Quadratic form and positive definiteness

The quadratic form of a bilinear form \(b\) is \(q(v)=b(v,v)\). It is positive definite if \(q(v)\gt 0\) for every \(v\neq 0\).

Statement 9.1.1 Matrix of a bilinear form

Let \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) be a basis of \(V\), and let \(A_{ij}=b(e_i,e_j)\). Then \(b\bigl(\sum_ix_ie_i,\sum_jy_je_j\bigr)=\sum_{i,j}x_iA_{ij}y_j\). If \(f\) is another basis with change of basis matrix \(P\), so that \(f_k=\sum_iP_{ik}e_i\), then the matrix of \(b\) in the basis \(f\) is \(P^{\top}AP\).

The value \(b(u,v)\) computed from the matrix and from the double sum must agree. Drag and compare:

drag u and v

Show proof

Expand each argument using linearity: \(b(\sum_ix_ie_i,\sum_jy_je_j)=\sum_i x_i\,b(e_i,\sum_jy_je_j)=\sum_{i,j}x_iy_j\,b(e_i,e_j)\).

For the change of basis, \(b(f_k,f_l)=\sum_{i,j}P_{ik}P_{jl}\,b(e_i,e_j)=\sum_{i,j}P_{ik}A_{ij}P_{jl}=(P^{\top}AP)_{kl}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 9.1.2 Symmetric forms are self-adjoint operators

Let \(V\) be a real inner product space and \(b\) a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\). There is a unique \(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\) with \(b(u,v)=\langle Tu,v\rangle\) for all \(u,v\), and this \(T\) is self-adjoint. Conversely, every self-adjoint \(T\) defines a symmetric bilinear form this way.

Choose symmetric or non-symmetric entries. The two values of \(b\) and the inner products \(\langle Tu,v\rangle\) match in both cases, but \(T\) is self-adjoint only when the matrix is symmetric:

drag u and v

Show proof

Existence. Let \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) be an orthonormal basis. For fixed \(u\), the map \(v\mapsto b(u,v)\) is linear. Put \(w_u=\sum_jb(u,e_j)e_j\). Writing \(v=\sum_jv_je_j\), we get \(\langle w_u,v\rangle=\sum_jb(u,e_j)v_j=b(u,v)\).

Uniqueness and linearity. If two vectors \(w,w'\) both satisfy \(\langle w,v\rangle=b(u,v)=\langle w',v\rangle\) for all \(v\), then \(w-w'\) is orthogonal to everything, so \(w=w'\). Define \(Tu=w_u\). Then \(\alpha w_u+\beta w_{u'}\) satisfies the defining property for \(\alpha u+\beta u'\), because \(b\) is linear in its first slot. So \(T\) is linear.

Self-adjointness. \(\langle Tu,v\rangle=b(u,v)=b(v,u)=\langle Tv,u\rangle=\langle u,Tv\rangle\). Conversely, if \(T\) is self-adjoint, then \(b(u,v)=\langle Tu,v\rangle\) is bilinear and symmetric.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 9.1.3 Orthonormal diagonalisation

Let \(V\) be a real inner product space of dimension \(n\) and \(b\) a symmetric bilinear form with quadratic form \(q\). There is an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) and real numbers \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\) such that \(q\bigl(\sum_jx_je_j\bigr)=\sum_j\lambda_jx_j^2\) for all coordinates \(x_j\).

The level set \(q=1\) is drawn in blue. Its axes point along the orthonormal eigenvectors, and the eigenvalues give its shape:

move the entries; drag w

Show proof

Let \(T\) be the self-adjoint operator of 9.1.2, so \(q(v)=b(v,v)=\langle Tv,v\rangle\). By the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators on a real inner product space (Part 7.2), there is an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) of eigenvectors, \(Te_j=\lambda_je_j\), with real \(\lambda_j\).

For \(v=\sum_jx_je_j\), \(\langle Tv,v\rangle=\sum_{j,k}x_jx_k\lambda_j\langle e_j,e_k\rangle=\sum_j\lambda_jx_j^2\), because the basis is orthonormal.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 9.1.4 Positive definiteness and eigenvalues

With \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\) as in 9.1.3, the quadratic form \(q\) is positive definite if and only if every \(\lambda_j\) is positive.

Blue regions have \(q\gt 0\), red regions have \(q\lt 0\). The form is positive definite when the unit circle stays entirely blue:

move the entries

Show proof

If every \(\lambda_j\gt 0\) and \(v\ne 0\), then some \(x_k\neq 0\), so \(q(v)=\sum_j\lambda_jx_j^2\gt 0\).

Conversely, if \(\lambda_k\le 0\) for some \(k\), then \(q(e_k)=\lambda_k\le 0\), and \(e_k\neq 0\). So \(q\) is not positive definite.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Let \(b(u,v)=u_1v_1+2u_1v_2+3u_2v_1+u_2v_2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Write its matrix, and check whether \(b\) is symmetric.
  2. Harder Show that a symmetric \(2\times 2\) real matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{bmatrix}\) is positive definite if and only if \(a\gt 0\) and \(ac-b^2\gt 0\).
  3. Toward 9.2 Find all alternating bilinear forms on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Does every such form have a matrix that is symmetric? What do the skew-symmetric ones look like?

Home / Linear Algebra / 3.4
Linear Algebra · Part 3.4

Change of basis

A map is one thing and its matrix is another. The matrix depends on the basis we choose, and moving from one basis to another changes it by a conjugation \(P^{-1}AP\).

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A vector has coordinates only once we choose a basis to measure against. The same arrow in the plane is \((2,1)\) in the standard basis and something else in a skewed basis. A map has the same problem: its matrix is a table of coordinates, and the table changes when the basis does. This part asks how the tables are related.

Same vector, new coordinates

In the basis \((1,1), (1,-1)\), the vector \((2,1)\) has coordinates \((1.5,\ 0.5)\), because \(1.5(1,1) + 0.5(1,-1) = (2,1)\). The arrow did not move. Only the numbers describing it did.

Same map, new matrix

The rotation \((x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)\) has matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) in the standard basis. In the basis \((1,0), (1,1)\) the same rotation has matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\).

A matrix that converts

Writing the new basis vectors in standard coordinates gives a square table \(P\). Multiplying by \(P\) converts coordinates in the new basis into standard ones. Converting back needs \(P^{-1}\), which is the content of the first statement below.

2Play

The standard grid is fixed. The skewed grid is the new basis \(b_1, b_2\), and you can drag its two vectors. The arrows show the map \(A\) applied to each new basis vector. The readout computes \(P^{-1}AP\), and then recomputes the same matrix directly by solving for the coordinates of \(Ab_1\) and \(Ab_2\). The two agree for every basis.

drag b1, b2

  • Drag \(b_1\) until it is parallel to \(b_2\). Which readout breaks, and why is that the right failure?
  • Move the basis until the lower-left entry of \(P^{-1}AP\) is \(0\). What does that say about the direction of \(b_1\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 3.4.1 Coordinates, change-of-basis matrix

Let \(B = (b_1,\dots,b_n)\) be a basis of \(V\), and let \(B' = (b'_1,\dots,b'_n)\) be another basis. The change-of-basis matrix \(P\) is the \(n \times n\) matrix whose \(k\)th column is \([b'_k]_B\), the coordinates of \(b'_k\) in the basis \(B\). For a linear map \(T\) on \(V\), the matrix \([T]_B\) is the matrix whose \(k\)th column is \([Tb_k]_B\).

Statement 3.4.1 The change-of-basis matrix is invertible

Let \(B\) and \(B'\) be bases of \(V\), and let \(P\) be the change-of-basis matrix of Definition 3.4.1. Then \(P\) is invertible, and \(P^{-1}\) is the matrix whose \(k\)th column is \([b_k]_{B'}\).

drag b1, b2 and the test vector v

Show proof

The coordinate identity. For every \(v \in V\) we have \([v]_B = P[v]_{B'}\). Indeed, write \(v = \sum_k x'_k b'_k\), where \(x'\) is the coordinate vector \([v]_{B'}\). Then \(v = \sum_k x'_k \sum_j P_{jk} b_j\), so the \(j\)th coordinate of \(v\) in \(B\) is \(\sum_k P_{jk}x'_k\), which is the \(j\)th entry of \(P[v]_{B'}\). Exchanging the roles of \(B\) and \(B'\), let \(Q\) be the matrix whose \(k\)th column is \([b_k]_{B'}\); the same argument gives \([v]_{B'} = Q[v]_B\) for every \(v\).

Substituting one identity into the other gives \([v]_B = PQ[v]_B\) for every \(v\). Taking \(v = b_j\), whose coordinate vector \([b_j]_B\) is the standard basis vector \(e_j\), gives \(PQe_j = e_j\) for every \(j\). Hence \(PQ = I\). Similarly \([v]_{B'} = QP[v]_{B'}\) for every \(v\), and taking \(v = b'_j\) gives \(QP = I\). So \(P\) is invertible with \(P^{-1} = Q\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.4.2 Matrix in a new basis

Let \(T\) be an operator on a finite-dimensional space \(V\), let \(B\) and \(B'\) be bases of \(V\), and let \(P\) be the change-of-basis matrix of Definition 3.4.1. Then \([T]_{B'} = P^{-1}\,[T]_B\,P\).

drag b1, b2 to change the basis

Show proof

Write \(A = [T]_B\) and \(A' = [T]_{B'}\). By definition \([Tv]_{B'} = A'[v]_{B'}\) for every \(v\). The coordinate identity from the proof of Statement 3.4.1 applies to the vector \(Tv\) and to \(v\), so

\[ A[v]_B = [Tv]_B = P[Tv]_{B'} = PA'[v]_{B'}. \]

But \([v]_B = P[v]_{B'}\), so the left side is \(AP[v]_{B'}\). Therefore \((AP - PA')[v]_{B'} = 0\) for every \(v\). Taking \(v = b'_k\), so that \([v]_{B'} = e_k\), shows that the \(k\)th column of \(AP - PA'\) is zero. Hence \(AP = PA'\), and multiplying on the left by \(P^{-1}\) gives \(A' = P^{-1}AP\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Take \(B\) to be the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(B' = ((1,0),(1,1))\). Find \(P\), \(P^{-1}\), and the matrix of the rotation by \(90^\circ\) in the basis \(B'\), and check your answer against the slides.
  2. Harder Show that \(\operatorname{tr}(P^{-1}AP) = \operatorname{tr}A\) for every invertible \(P\). (Use the fact that \(\operatorname{tr}(XY) = \operatorname{tr}(YX)\).)
  3. Toward 4.1 Find a polynomial of degree \(2\) with real coefficients that is zero when applied to the rotation matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Why can no polynomial of degree \(1\) do this?

Linear Algebra · Part 9.2

Determinants

The determinant of an operator is the factor by which it scales volume. We define it without any matrices, as the scalar by which an operator acts on the one-dimensional space of alternating forms, and then check that it agrees with the familiar formula.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Two vectors in the plane span a parallelogram. Its area, with a sign that records whether the second vector is anticlockwise from the first, is \(u_1v_2-u_2v_1\). This number is linear in each vector, and it vanishes when the two vectors are equal.

Signed area

Swapping \(u\) and \(v\) reverses the orientation, so the sign flips. Making \(u=v\) collapses the parallelogram to a segment, so the area is zero.

An operator scales area

A linear map \(T\) sends the unit square to the parallelogram spanned by \(Te_1\) and \(Te_2\). The ratio of the signed areas is one number, and it does not depend on the square we started with.

When area vanishes

If the image parallelogram collapses to a segment, the operator has squashed a whole direction. That is exactly when it fails to be invertible.

2Play

Drag the vertices \(u\) and \(v\). The shaded parallelogram has signed area \(f(u,v)=u_1v_2-u_2v_1\). Green means positive, red means negative. Swap the roles of \(u\) and \(v\) in your head and watch the sign.

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Drag \(v\) so that it is parallel to \(u\). What is the area, and why does that match the alternating property?
  • Drag \(u\) past \(v\) so the orientation flips. What happens to the sign?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 9.2.1 Alternating \(n\)-linear form

Let \(\dim V=n\). An \(n\)-linear form is a function \(f:V^n\to\mathbf{F}\) that is linear in each argument. It is alternating if \(f(v_1,\dots,v_n)=0\) whenever \(v_j=v_k\) for some \(j\neq k\).

Statement 9.2.1 Alternating forms form a line

For \(\dim V=n\), the alternating \(n\)-linear forms on \(V\) form a vector space of dimension \(1\).

The area form is the alternating form on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Drag the vectors and test the three properties used in the proof: linearity, sign under swap, and vanishing when the vectors are equal:

drag u and v

Show proof

Alternating forms are determined by one value. Let \(f\) be alternating, and \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) a basis. Expanding each argument in the basis gives \(f(v_1,\dots,v_n)=\sum a_{1i_1}\cdots a_{ni_n}f(e_{i_1},\dots,e_{i_n})\). Terms with a repeated index vanish. Replacing two arguments \(x\) and \(y\) by \(x+y\) in an alternating form gives \(f(\dots x\dots y\dots)+f(\dots y\dots x\dots)=0\), so swapping two arguments changes the sign. Therefore \(f(e_{\sigma(1)},\dots,e_{\sigma(n)})=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)f(e_1,\dots,e_n)\), and \(f\) is determined by \(f(e_1,\dots,e_n)\). So the space has dimension at most \(1\).

A nonzero alternating form exists. Let \(D(v_1,\dots,v_n)\) be the determinant (Leibniz formula) of the matrix whose \(j\)th column holds the coordinates of \(v_j\) in the basis. Each term of the Leibniz sum uses one entry from each column, so \(D\) is linear in each argument. If columns \(j\) and \(k\) are equal, pair each permutation \(\sigma\) with \(\sigma\circ(j\ k)\). These two terms have opposite signs and equal products, since the two columns agree. So the sum vanishes, and \(D\) is alternating. Also \(D(e_1,\dots,e_n)=1\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 9.2.2 Determinant of an operator

Let \(\dim V=n\), \(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\), and let \(f\) be a nonzero alternating \(n\)-linear form. The form \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto f(Tv_1,\dots,Tv_n)\) is alternating and \(n\)-linear, so by 9.2.1 it equals \(c\,f\) for a unique scalar \(c\). Define \(\det T=c\). This does not depend on \(f\): if \(f'=af\) with \(a\neq 0\), then \(f'(T\cdot)=a\,c\,f=c\,f'\).

Statement 9.2.2 The determinant of an operator is the determinant of its matrix

If \(A\) is the matrix of \(T\) in some basis, then \(\det T=\det A\), where \(\det A\) is the Leibniz determinant of \(A\).

Set the entries of \(T\). The unit square is sent to the parallelogram spanned by \(Te_1\) and \(Te_2\). Its signed area divided by the area of the square is \(\det T\):

move the entries of T

Show proof

Take \(f=D\), the Leibniz form with respect to the given basis, so \(f(e_1,\dots,e_n)=1\). The \(j\)th column of \(A\) holds the coordinates of \(Te_j\), so \(f(Te_1,\dots,Te_n)=\det A\). By definition, \(f(Te_1,\dots,Te_n)=(\det T)\,f(e_1,\dots,e_n)=\det T\). Hence \(\det T=\det A\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 9.2.3 Multiplicativity

For \(S,T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\), \(\det(ST)=\det S\cdot\det T\).

Here \(S\) is a rotation with a stretch and \(T\) is a triangular matrix. The image under \(ST\) has area equal to the product of the two scalings:

move the sliders

Show proof

Let \(f\neq 0\) be alternating. By definition, \(f(Sw_1,\dots,Sw_n)=\det S\cdot f(w_1,\dots,w_n)\) for all \(w_i\). Taking \(w_i=Tv_i\) and using the definition of \(\det T\), \(f(STv_1,\dots,STv_n)=\det S\cdot f(Tv_1,\dots,Tv_n)=\det S\cdot\det T\cdot f(v_1,\dots,v_n)\).

The left side is \(\det(ST)\,f(v_1,\dots,v_n)\) by definition. Taking \(v_i=e_i\) with \(f(e)\neq 0\) gives \(\det(ST)=\det S\det T\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 9.2.4 Invertibility

\(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\) is invertible if and only if \(\det T\neq 0\).

Drag the images \(Te_1\) and \(Te_2\). Watch the parallelogram collapse exactly when \(\det T\) becomes zero:

drag u = Te1 and v = Te2

Show proof

If \(T\) is invertible. Then \(\det T\cdot\det T^{-1}=\det(I)=1\), since \(f(Iv_1,\dots,Iv_n)=f(v_1,\dots,v_n)\). So \(\det T\ne 0\).

If \(T\) is not invertible. In finite dimensions \(T\) is then not surjective, so \(\operatorname{range}T\) has dimension less than \(n\). The \(n\) vectors \(Te_1,\dots,Te_n\) span \(\operatorname{range}T\), so they are linearly dependent: some \(Te_j\) is a combination of the others. Expanding \(f(Te_1,\dots,Te_n)\) by linearity in slot \(j\) gives a sum of terms in which some vector appears twice, so \(f(Te_1,\dots,Te_n)=0\). Hence \(\det T\cdot f(e_1,\dots,e_n)=0\), and \(\det T=0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 9.2.5 Determinant equals the product of eigenvalues

Let \(V\) be complex and \(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\). Then \(\det T=\prod_\lambda\lambda^{\dim G(\lambda,T)}\), the product of the eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

Take an upper-triangular \(2\times 2\) matrix with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\). The rectangle with sides \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) has signed area equal to the product, which equals the determinant:

move the eigenvalues and the entry

Show proof

Choose a basis in which \(T\) is upper triangular with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\), as in 8.2.4. In the Leibniz sum, a term \(\prod_i A_{\sigma(i),i}\) is nonzero only if \(\sigma(i)\le i\) for every \(i\), because the entries below the diagonal vanish. Then \(\sigma(1)=1\), \(\sigma(2)=2\), and so on, so only the identity survives. Hence \(\det A=\prod_k\lambda_k\).

By 9.2.2, \(\det T=\det A\). By 8.2.4(b), each eigenvalue \(\lambda\) occurs exactly \(\dim G(\lambda,T)\) times on the diagonal, so \(\prod_k\lambda_k=\prod_\lambda\lambda^{\dim G(\lambda,T)}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Compute \(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&3&4\\5&0&6\end{bmatrix}\) by expanding along the first row, then again along the second column. Check that the two answers agree.
  2. Harder Let \(\chi(z)=\det(zI-T)\) for \(T\) on a complex space. Show that \(\chi(z)=\prod_\lambda(z-\lambda)^{\dim G(\lambda,T)}\), and so \(\chi\) is the characteristic polynomial of 8.2.5.
  3. Beyond Let \(T\) be invertible. Show that \(\det(T^{-1})=1/\det T\), using only 9.2.3 and 9.2.4.

Home / Linear Algebra / 5.4
Linear Algebra · Part 5.4

Diagonalizable operators

The best basis is an eigenbasis: the matrix becomes diagonal and the operator just stretches each axis. We find when such a basis exists, and a test that uses the minimal polynomial, then close with Gershgorin's disc theorem for locating eigenvalues.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A diagonal matrix is the simplest possible picture of an operator: each basis vector is stretched by its own factor, and nothing mixes. The question is which operators can be put in that form by some choice of basis.

In the plane

A stretch along two perpendicular axes is diagonal. A stretch along two skew lines is also diagonal, in a basis made of those lines. A shear has only one invariant line, so no basis of lines can capture it.

Two directions

If two directions are scaled by different factors, they can never coincide, because they lie on different eigenlines. That independence is what makes a basis.

Locating eigenvalues

Even when we cannot compute eigenvalues exactly, a picture of discs can trap them. Gershgorin's theorem does exactly that for any complex square matrix.

2Play

The operator here is \(T=Q\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}Q^{\mathsf T}\), with \(Q\) a rotation. Its eigenspaces (as lines or the whole plane) are drawn in colour. Change \(a\), \(d\) and \(b\) and watch whether the eigenspaces can span the plane.

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Set \(a=d\) with \(b\ne0\). How many independent eigenvectors are there, and can they span the plane?
  • Set \(a=d\) and \(b=0\). What changes, and why?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 5.4.1 Diagonal matrix, diagonalizable operator

A matrix is diagonal if all its entries off the diagonal are \(0\). An operator \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\) is diagonalizable if \(V\) has a basis with respect to which \(\mathcal M(T)\) is diagonal. Recall that the eigenspace of \(\lambda\) is \(E_\lambda=\operatorname{null}(T-\lambda I)\) (Part 5.1).

Definition 5.4.2 Minimal polynomial (recalled)

The minimal polynomial \(m\) of \(T\) is the monic polynomial of least degree with \(m(T)=0\). We use one fact from Part 5.2: if \(p(T)=0\), then \(m\) divides \(p\).

Statement 5.4.3 Eigenbasis, diagonal matrix, eigenspaces

For \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\), the following are equivalent: (a) \(T\) is diagonalizable; (b) \(V\) has a basis consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\); (c) the eigenspaces of \(T\) span \(V\), that is, \(V=E_{\lambda_1}+\dots+E_{\lambda_m}\) for the distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\).

the eigenspaces decide everything

Show proof

(a) implies (b). If \(\mathcal M(T)\) is diagonal with respect to \(v_1,\dots,v_n\), then \(Tv_k=\lambda_kv_k\) for the diagonal entries \(\lambda_k\), so each \(v_k\) is an eigenvector and they form a basis.

(b) implies (a). If \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) are eigenvectors forming a basis, then \(Tv_k=\lambda_kv_k\) and the matrix is diagonal with entries \(\lambda_k\).

(b) implies (c). Each \(v_k\) lies in some eigenspace, and every vector of \(V\) is a sum of the \(v_k\). So \(V\) is contained in, and hence equal to, the sum of the eigenspaces.

(c) implies (b). If the eigenspaces span \(V\), their union is a list of eigenvectors that spans \(V\). A spanning list contains a basis, and every member of that basis is still an eigenvector.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.4.4 Distinct eigenvalues give a basis

If \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\) has \(\dim V\) distinct eigenvalues, then \(T\) is diagonalizable.

the shaded parallelogram is nondegenerate

Show proof

First, eigenvectors \(v_1,\dots,v_k\) for distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\) are linearly independent. Suppose not, and take a nontrivial relation \(\sum c_iv_i=0\) with the fewest nonzero coefficients. Relabel so that \(c_1,\dots,c_m\ne0\) and the rest vanish. Then \(m\ge2\), since each \(v_i\ne0\). Apply \(T-\lambda_mI\): the term with \(v_m\) disappears, leaving \(\sum_{i\lt m}c_i(\lambda_i-\lambda_m)v_i=0\). Its coefficient on \(v_1\) is \(c_1(\lambda_1-\lambda_m)\ne0\), so this is a nontrivial relation with fewer nonzero terms, a contradiction.

Now choose one eigenvector for each of the \(\dim V\) distinct eigenvalues. They are independent, and a list of \(\dim V\) independent vectors is a basis. By Statement 5.4.3, \(T\) is diagonalizable.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.4.5 Minimal polynomial test

An operator \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\) on a finite-dimensional space is diagonalizable if and only if its minimal polynomial is a product of distinct linear factors, \(m(z)=(z-\lambda_1)\cdots(z-\lambda_k)\) with \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\) distinct. In particular, the minimal polynomial has distinct roots, all in the field of scalars.

watch the minimal polynomial change

Show proof

Diagonalizable implies distinct roots. Let \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) be an eigenbasis with eigenvalues \(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n\), and let \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\) be the distinct values among the \(\mu_j\). Put \(q(z)=\prod_i(z-\lambda_i)\). The factors commute, and the factor with \(\lambda_i=\mu_j\) kills \(v_j\), so \(q(T)v_j=\prod_i(\mu_j-\lambda_i)v_j=0\) for every \(j\). Hence \(q(T)=0\). So \(m\) divides \(q\), and by unique factorization in the scalar field \(m\) is a product of some of the distinct factors \(z-\lambda_i\).

Distinct roots implies diagonalizable. Suppose \(m=\prod_{i=1}^k(z-\lambda_i)\) with distinct \(\lambda_i\). Let \(L_i(z)=\prod_{j\ne i}\dfrac{z-\lambda_j}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}\). The polynomial \(\sum_iL_i-1\) has degree at most \(k-1\) and vanishes at the \(k\) distinct points \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\), so it is zero. Hence \(\sum_iL_i(T)=I\). Next, \((z-\lambda_i)L_i(z)=c_i\,m(z)\) for a nonzero constant \(c_i\), so \((T-\lambda_iI)L_i(T)=c_i\,m(T)=0\). Thus each \(P_i=L_i(T)\) maps \(V\) into \(E_{\lambda_i}\). Every \(v\in V\) equals \(\sum_iP_iv\), so \(V=E_{\lambda_1}+\dots+E_{\lambda_k}\). By Statement 5.4.3, \(T\) is diagonalizable.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.4.6 Gershgorin disc theorem

Let \(A=(a_{jk})\) be an \(n\times n\) complex matrix. For each \(j\), let \(D_j\) be the closed disc centred at \(a_{jj}\) with radius \(r_j=\sum_{k\ne j}|a_{jk}|\). Every eigenvalue of \(A\) lies in at least one \(D_j\).

drag centres (diagonal) or spokes (off-diagonal)

Show proof

Let \(\lambda\) be an eigenvalue with eigenvector \(x\ne0\), and choose \(j\) with \(|x_j|=\max_k|x_k|\); this maximum is positive. Row \(j\) of \(Ax=\lambda x\) reads \(\sum_ka_{jk}x_k=\lambda x_j\), so \((\lambda-a_{jj})x_j=\sum_{k\ne j}a_{jk}x_k\). Taking absolute values and using \(|x_k|\le|x_j|\), \[|\lambda-a_{jj}|\,|x_j|\le\sum_{k\ne j}|a_{jk}|\,|x_k|\le|x_j|\sum_{k\ne j}|a_{jk}|=|x_j|\,r_j.\] Dividing by \(|x_j|>0\) gives \(|\lambda-a_{jj}|\le r_j\), so \(\lambda\in D_j\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\) is not diagonalizable, by finding its eigenspaces.
  2. Harder Use Gershgorin's theorem to show that a strictly diagonally dominant complex matrix has no zero eigenvalue when all diagonal entries are nonzero.
  3. Toward 5.5 Diagonalizable operators are exactly those whose minimal polynomial has no repeated factor. What extra structure does a complex operator with a repeated root have, and how would you describe its blocks?

Linear Algebra · Part 5.1

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

An eigenvector is a direction that an operator only stretches, and the stretch factor is an eigenvalue. Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues never line up, and over the complex numbers every operator has an eigenvalue.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Most vectors change direction when an operator acts on them. The special ones keep their line and are only stretched or shrunk. Finding those lines turns a complicated operator into a collection of stretches along simple directions, and the rest of the series is about when that can be done.

A line that stays a line

The shear \((x,y) \mapsto (x+y, y)\) fixes the \(x\)-axis: the vector \((1,0)\) goes to \((1,0)\). The vector \((0,1)\) goes to \((1,1)\), which leaves its line. So \((1,0)\) is a special direction for this shear and \((0,1)\) is not.

Stretch factors

The map \((x,y) \mapsto (2x, \tfrac12 y)\) stretches the \(x\)-axis by \(2\) and the \(y\)-axis by \(\tfrac12\). Those two stretch factors are its eigenvalues.

A rotation has none, over the reals

A quarter turn sends every nonzero real vector off its line. Over the complex numbers the same turn has eigenvectors \((1,i)\) and \((1,-i)\), with eigenvalues \(-i\) and \(i\).

2Play

The matrix \(T\) is drawn with a grey grid. Slide \(\lambda\) and watch the matrix \(T - \lambda I\). When it fails to be invertible, its null space is a line, and that line glows: it is the set of eigenvectors for \(\lambda\). Try the three presets, one of which has no real eigenvalue.

slide λ until a line lights up

  • For the symmetric matrix, which values of \(\lambda\) make \(T - \lambda I\) fail to be invertible? Read them off the readouts.
  • For the quarter turn, no slider position lights up a line. Why does that match the slides?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 5.1.1 Eigenvalue, eigenvector

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). A scalar \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\) if there is a nonzero \(v \in V\) with \(Tv = \lambda v\). Such a \(v\) is an eigenvector of \(T\) for \(\lambda\). The set of all \(v\) with \(Tv = \lambda v\) is the subspace \(\operatorname{null}(T - \lambda I)\), the eigenspace of \(\lambda\).

Statement 5.1.1 Eigenvalue as a non-injective shift

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\). Then \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\) if and only if \(T - \lambda I\) is not injective.

slide λ

Show proof

By Definition 5.1.1, \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue exactly when there is \(v \ne 0\) with \(Tv = \lambda v\). This is the same as \(v \ne 0\) with \((T - \lambda I)v = 0\), that is, \(\operatorname{null}(T - \lambda I) \ne \{0\}\). By Statement 3.1.1, the null space is \(\{0\}\) exactly when the map is injective. So \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue exactly when \(T - \lambda I\) is not injective.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.1.2 Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Suppose \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\) are distinct eigenvalues of \(T\), with eigenvectors \(v_1,\dots,v_m\). Then \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) is linearly independent.

move λ2 away from λ1

Show proof

Suppose the statement fails, and choose a counterexample with \(m\) as small as possible: a list \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) of eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\) that is linearly dependent. A single eigenvector is nonzero, so \(m \ge 2\). Take a dependence \(\sum_k a_kv_k = 0\), not all \(a_k\) zero.

Every \(a_j\) is nonzero. Otherwise \(\sum_{k \ne j} a_kv_k = 0\) would be a nontrivial dependence among \(m-1\) eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues, contradicting the minimality of \(m\).

Apply \(T\) to the dependence: \(\sum_k a_k\lambda_kv_k = 0\). Subtract \(\lambda_m\) times the original dependence:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{m-1} a_k(\lambda_k - \lambda_m)\,v_k = 0. \]

The list \(v_1,\dots,v_{m-1}\) is independent by minimality, so \(a_k(\lambda_k - \lambda_m) = 0\) for each \(k < m\). But \(a_k \ne 0\) and \(\lambda_k \ne \lambda_m\), a contradiction.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.1.3 At most as many eigenvalues as dimensions

Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then \(T\) has at most \(\dim V\) distinct eigenvalues.

drag each diagonal entry along its row

Show proof

Let \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\) be distinct eigenvalues of \(T\), and pick an eigenvector \(v_k\) for each \(\lambda_k\). By Statement 5.1.2 the list \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) is linearly independent. An independent list in \(V\) has length at most \(\dim V\), so \(m \le \dim V\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.1.4 Operators on complex spaces have eigenvalues

Let \(V\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space. Then every \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) has an eigenvalue.

drag the roots; each root labels an eigenline

Show proof

Let \(n = \dim V \ge 1\) and pick \(v \ne 0\) in \(V\). The \(n+1\) vectors \(v, Tv, \dots, T^nv\) cannot be independent, since a list longer than \(\dim V\) is dependent. So there are scalars \(a_0,\dots,a_n\), not all zero, with \(\sum_k a_kT^kv = 0\).

Let \(m\) be the largest index with \(a_m \ne 0\). If \(m = 0\), then \(a_0v = 0\) with \(a_0 \ne 0\), forcing \(v = 0\), which is false. So \(m \ge 1\). Let \(p(z) = \sum_{k \le m} a_kz^k\). Then \(p\) is nonconstant and \(p(T)v = 0\).

By Statement 4.1.4, \(p(z) = c(z-\lambda_1)\cdots(z-\lambda_m)\) with \(c \ne 0\). Since polynomials in \(T\) multiply like the polynomials, \(p(T) = c\,(T-\lambda_1I)\cdots(T-\lambda_mI)\). Put \(S = (T-\lambda_1I)\cdots(T-\lambda_mI)\). Then \(Sv = c^{-1}p(T)v = 0\), and \(v \ne 0\), so \(S\) is not injective.

If every factor \(T - \lambda_jI\) were injective, then their composition \(S\) would be injective. So some \(T - \lambda_jI\) is not injective, and by Statement 5.1.1, \(\lambda_j\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find all eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(T(x,y) = (2x+y,\ x+2y)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  2. Harder Let \(T\) be invertible and \(\lambda\) an eigenvalue of \(T\). Show that \(\lambda \ne 0\) and that \(\lambda^{-1}\) is an eigenvalue of \(T^{-1}\).
  3. Toward 5.2 Suppose \(Tv = \lambda v\) with \(v \ne 0\), and let \(p\) be a polynomial. What is \(p(T)v\)? Use the answer to relate the zeros of \(p\) to the eigenvalues of \(T\).

Home / Linear Algebra / 8.2
Linear Algebra · Part 8.2

Generalised eigenspace decomposition

Over the complex numbers, every operator splits the whole space into pieces, one for each eigenvalue, and each piece is a copy of a nilpotent operator shifted by a scalar. Counting dimensions gives multiplicities, and the same splitting proves the Cayley–Hamilton theorem.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

An eigenspace is only part of the story. In the plane, the eigenspace of a shear is a line, but the generalised eigenspace is the whole plane. The question is whether the generalised eigenspaces, taken together, always fill the space without overlap.

Two lines

An operator on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with eigenvalues \(2\) and \(3\) has two lines of eigenvectors. Every vector is a sum of one vector from each line, and the two lines meet only at \(0\).

A shear, again

The Jordan block \(\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\) has only one eigenline, but its generalised eigenspace for \(2\) is the whole plane. The eigenspace misses part of the picture.

Block form

If each generalised eigenspace is \(T\)-invariant, then \(T\) becomes block diagonal in a basis adapted to the splitting. Each block is a scalar plus a nilpotent operator.

2Play

Choose an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(T=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\) and move the power \(j\). The coloured set is \(\operatorname{null}(T-\lambda I)^j\). Compare the eigenspace (\(j=1\)) with the generalised eigenspace (\(j=2\)).

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Why is the generalised eigenspace for \(\lambda=2\) bigger than the eigenspace? What is \(\operatorname{null}(T-2I)^2\)?
  • For \(\lambda=3\), why does the picture collapse to a single point?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 8.2.1 Generalised eigenspace

For \(\lambda\in\mathbf{F}\), the generalised eigenspace of \(T\) for \(\lambda\) is \(G(\lambda,T)=\{v\in V:(T-\lambda I)^jv=0\text{ for some }j\ge 1\}\). It contains \(0\) and all generalised eigenvectors for \(\lambda\).

Definition 8.2.2 Multiplicity

The multiplicity of an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(T\) is \(\dim G(\lambda,T)\). Statement 8.2.4 shows this matches the count on the diagonal of a triangular matrix.

Statement 8.2.1 The generalised eigenspace is a null space

Let \(d=\dim V\). Then \(G(\lambda,T)=\operatorname{null}(T-\lambda I)^d\). In particular \(G(\lambda,T)\) is a subspace of \(V\), and it contains the eigenspace \(\operatorname{null}(T-\lambda I)\).

Compare the null spaces of \((T-\lambda I)^j\) with \(d=2\):

choose lambda, then move j

Show proof

Write \(S=T-\lambda I\). The union \(\bigcup_{j\ge1}\operatorname{null}S^j\) is \(G(\lambda,T)\). By 8.1.1 the null spaces increase with \(j\), and by 8.1.3 they are all equal to \(\operatorname{null}S^d\) for \(j\ge d\). So the union equals \(\operatorname{null}S^d\), which is a subspace. The eigenspace is \(\operatorname{null}S\subseteq\operatorname{null}S^d\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.2.2 Decomposition into generalised eigenspaces

Let \(V\) be a complex vector space and \(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\). Then \(V\) is the direct sum of the generalised eigenspaces of \(T\): \(V=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\mathbf{C}}G(\lambda,T)\), where only finitely many terms are nonzero.

Split a vector into its parts in the two generalised eigenspaces, and check that the parts behave as claimed:

drag v

Show proof

Splitting off one eigenspace. Let \(n=\dim V\ge 1\), let \(\lambda\) be an eigenvalue of \(T\) (one exists because \(V\) is a nonzero complex space; this is the fundamental theorem of algebra at work), and put \(S=T-\lambda I\), \(R=\operatorname{range}S^n\). Both \(\operatorname{null}S^n\) and \(R\) are \(T\)-invariant, since \(T\) commutes with \(S\).

They meet only in \(0\): if \(v=S^nw\) and \(S^nv=0\), then \(w\in\operatorname{null}S^{2n}=\operatorname{null}S^n\) by 8.1.3, so \(v=0\). By the fundamental theorem of linear maps, their dimensions add to \(n\). Hence \(V=G(\lambda,T)\oplus R\).

Induction. Induct on \(n\); the case \(n=0\) is trivial. Since \(G(\lambda,T)\ne 0\), the space \(R\) has dimension less than \(n\), so the induction hypothesis applies to \(T|_R\): \(R=\sum_\mu G(\mu,T|_R)\). Each \(G(\mu,T|_R)\) is contained in \(G(\mu,T)\), because the same vectors satisfy the same conditions. Also \(G(\lambda,T)\cap R=0\), so \(\lambda\) does not occur among the \(\mu\). Therefore \(V=G(\lambda,T)+\sum_\mu G(\mu,T)\subseteq\sum_{\text{all }\mu}G(\mu,T)\subseteq V\).

Directness. Suppose \(g_1+\cdots+g_m=0\) with \(g_i\in G(\mu_i,T)\) and the \(\mu_i\) distinct. The nonzero \(g_i\) are generalised eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues, so by 8.1.6 they are independent. Since their sum is zero, there are none. Hence the sum is direct.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.2.3 Block diagonal form

Let \(V\) be complex, and let \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r\) be the distinct eigenvalues of \(T\). Concatenate bases of \(G(\lambda_1,T),\dots,G(\lambda_r,T)\). The matrix of \(T\) in the resulting basis is block diagonal, and the \(j\)th block has the form \(\lambda_jI+N_j\), where \(N_j\) is nilpotent.

Set a block-diagonal matrix with two blocks, and check that each block is a scalar plus a nilpotent matrix:

move the sliders

Show proof

Each \(G(\lambda_j,T)\) is \(T\)-invariant, since \(T\) commutes with \((T-\lambda_jI)^d\). Taking the concatenated basis, \(T\) sends each basis vector of the \(j\)th block into the span of that block, so the matrix is block diagonal.

On \(G_j=G(\lambda_j,T)\), let \(N_j=(T-\lambda_jI)|_{G_j}\). By 8.2.1, \(N_j^{d}=0\) on \(G_j\), so \(N_j\) is nilpotent, and the block of \(T\) is \(\lambda_jI+N_j\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.2.4 Multiplicity is the diagonal count

(a) Complex \(V\) has a basis in which \(T\) has an upper-triangular matrix. (b) In any basis giving an upper-triangular matrix with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\), the number of indices \(k\) with \(\lambda_k=\lambda\) equals \(\dim G(\lambda,T)\).

Pick a diagonal value and compare its count on the diagonal with the dimension of its generalised eigenspace:

move the entries; the highlighted diagonal entry is inspected

Show proof

Part (a). First, a nilpotent operator \(N\) on a space \(W\) has a basis with strictly upper-triangular matrix. Let \(W_j=\operatorname{null}N^j\), so \(W_0=0\) and \(W_d=W\) for \(d=\dim W\) by 8.1.4. Build a basis by adding, for \(j=1,2,\dots\), vectors that extend a basis of \(W_{j-1}\) to one of \(W_j\). Each new vector \(x\in W_j\) satisfies \(Nx\in W_{j-1}\), which is spanned by the vectors added earlier. So the column of \(N\) for \(x\) has nonzero entries only in earlier positions, and the matrix is strictly upper triangular.

Now apply this to each \(N_j=(T-\lambda_jI)|_{G_j}\) of 8.2.3. Each block \(\lambda_jI+N_j\) is then upper triangular with diagonal \(\lambda_j\). Concatenating the blocks gives an upper-triangular matrix for \(T\), since the blocks are block diagonal.

Part (b). Let \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) be any basis with upper-triangular matrix, and let \(U_k=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\). Each \(U_k\) is \(T\)-invariant and \(Tv_k\equiv\lambda_kv_k\) modulo \(U_{k-1}\). Put \(g_k(\mu)=\dim G(\mu,T|_{U_k})\), with \(g_0=0\).

Since \(G(\mu,T|_{U_{k-1}})=G(\mu,T|_{U_k})\cap U_{k-1}\), the difference \(g_k(\mu)-g_{k-1}(\mu)\) is the dimension of the image of \(G(\mu,T|_{U_k})\) in \(U_k/U_{k-1}\), which is one-dimensional, so the difference is at most \(1\). If \(\lambda_k\neq\mu\), take \(x=av_k+u\) in \(G(\mu,T|_{U_k})\) with \(u\in U_{k-1}\). Modulo \(U_{k-1}\), \((T-\mu I)^jx\equiv(\lambda_k-\mu)^jav_k\), and this must be \(0\), so \(a=0\) and \(x\in U_{k-1}\). Thus the difference is \(0\) when \(\lambda_k\ne\mu\).

Summing over \(k\), \(g_n(\mu)\le\#\{k:\lambda_k=\mu\}\) for every \(\mu\). By 8.2.2, \(\sum_\mu g_n(\mu)=\sum_\mu\dim G(\mu,T)=n\), and the total of the counts is also \(n\). A sum of inequalities with equal totals is an equality termwise, so \(g_n(\mu)=\#\{k:\lambda_k=\mu\}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.2.5 Cayley–Hamilton theorem

Let \(V\) be complex, let \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r\) be the distinct eigenvalues of \(T\), and let \(d_j=\dim G(\lambda_j,T)\). Define the characteristic polynomial \(p(z)=\prod_{j}(z-\lambda_j)^{d_j}\). Then \(p(T)=0\).

For a \(2\times 2\) matrix the characteristic polynomial is \(z^2-(\operatorname{tr}T)z+\det T\). Check that \(p(T)=0\) for any choice of entries:

move the entries of T

Show proof

Fix \(j\), and let \(N=(T-\lambda_jI)|_{G_j}\), an operator on a space of dimension \(d_j\). It is nilpotent, so \(N^{d_j}=0\) by 8.1.4. Thus \((T-\lambda_jI)^{d_j}\) vanishes on \(G_j\).

Write \(p(z)=(z-\lambda_j)^{d_j}q_j(z)\), where \(q_j(z)=\prod_{i\neq j}(z-\lambda_i)^{d_i}\). Polynomials in \(T\) commute, so for \(v\in G_j\), \(p(T)v=q_j(T)(T-\lambda_jI)^{d_j}v=0\). Since \(V=\bigoplus_jG(\lambda_j,T)\) by 8.2.2, \(p(T)=0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine For \(T=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), find \(G(1,T)\) and the eigenspace \(\operatorname{null}(T-I)\). Check that they differ.
  2. Harder Let \(T\) be an operator on a complex space with \(T^2=T\). Use the decomposition to describe \(V\) as a direct sum of two generalised eigenspaces, and identify both.
  3. Toward 8.3 The decomposition gives each block as \(\lambda_jI+N_j\). Which operators \(N_j\) can occur, and what does a Jordan basis for \(N_j\) look like? This is the next part.
