Linear Algebra · Part 6.2

Orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt

Orthonormal lists behave like the coordinate axes: coefficients are read off by inner products, and norms are computed by Pythagoras. Gram–Schmidt turns any independent list into an orthonormal one with the same span, which gives orthonormal bases, triangular forms, and the Riesz representation.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

The standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is perfect: the coordinates of a vector are its dot products with the basis vectors, and its length is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates. Gram–Schmidt asks whether every space with an inner product has a basis that behaves the same way.

Two perpendicular unit vectors

If \(e_1,e_2\) are perpendicular and of length \(1\), then \(a_1e_1+a_2e_2\) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs \(a_1\) and \(a_2\).

Straightening a basis

Two independent vectors in the plane are generally at a slant. Subtracting from the second vector its part along the first leaves a vector perpendicular to the first.

Repeated

The same subtraction, applied one vector at a time, straightens any basis. That is the whole algorithm.

2Play

The first sim checks the Pythagorean identity for an orthonormal pair \(e_1,e_2\). The second animates Gram–Schmidt: press Play, or scrub the timeline, to watch \(v_1,v_2\) turn into \(e_1,e_2\). Both use the inner product with coupling \(g\), so the orthogonality is in that ruler.

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

Gram–Schmidt, step by step:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Scrub the Pythagorean sim so that \(a_1=a_2=1\). Does the hypotenuse depend on the orientation of the pair?
  • Drag \(v_2\) almost onto \(v_1\). What happens to the length of the remainder in step 2, and why does it matter?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 6.2.1 Orthonormal list

A list \(e_1,\dots,e_m\) in an inner product space is orthonormal if \(\langle e_j,e_k\rangle=0\) for \(j\ne k\) and \(\|e_k\|=1\) for every \(k\). Equivalently, \(\langle e_j,e_k\rangle=\delta_{jk}\).

Statement 6.2.2 Pythagorean identity for orthonormal lists

If \(e_1,\dots,e_m\) is orthonormal and \(a_1,\dots,a_m\in\mathbb F\), then \(\big\|\sum_k a_ke_k\big\|^2=\sum_k|a_k|^2\). In particular an orthonormal list is linearly independent.

the combination's length is the hypotenuse

Show proof

Expanding, \(\big\|\sum_ja_je_j\big\|^2=\sum_{j,k}a_j\overline{a_k}\langle e_j,e_k\rangle=\sum_{j,k}a_j\overline{a_k}\delta_{jk}=\sum_k|a_k|^2\).

For independence, suppose \(\sum_ka_ke_k=0\). Then \(\sum_k|a_k|^2=0\), so every \(a_k=0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.2.3 Gram–Schmidt procedure

Let \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) be linearly independent. Define \(e_1=v_1/\|v_1\|\) and, for \(k\ge2\), \(e_k=w_k/\|w_k\|\) where \(w_k=v_k-\sum_{j\lt k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j\). Then \(e_1,\dots,e_m\) is orthonormal, and \(\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_k)=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\) for every \(k\).

drag v1 and v2 · press Play

Show proof

We induct on \(k\). Suppose \(e_1,\dots,e_{k-1}\) is orthonormal with the same span as \(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}\). Independence of the \(v\)'s says \(v_k\notin\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_{k-1})\), so \(w_k\ne0\) and \(e_k\) is defined. For \(i\lt k\), \[\langle w_k,e_i\rangle=\langle v_k,e_i\rangle-\sum_{j\lt k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle\langle e_j,e_i\rangle=\langle v_k,e_i\rangle-\langle v_k,e_i\rangle=0,\] so \(e_k\) is orthogonal to the earlier vectors and has length \(1\). Thus \(e_1,\dots,e_k\) is orthonormal. Also \(e_k\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\), and \(v_k=\|w_k\|e_k+\sum_{j\lt k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j\in\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_k)\). With the inductive hypothesis, the spans agree.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.2.4 Orthonormal bases exist

Every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis.

the two results lie on the unit ball of the chosen norm

Show proof

Take any basis \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) of \(V\). It is linearly independent, so Statement 6.2.3 produces an orthonormal list \(e_1,\dots,e_n\). By 6.2.2 it is independent, so it is a list of \(n=\dim V\) independent vectors, hence a basis.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.2.5 Triangular form in an orthonormal basis

If \(V\) is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner product space and \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\), then there is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) with respect to which \(T\) has an upper-triangular matrix.

Gram–Schmidt keeps the triangular structure

Show proof

By Statement 5.3.6, \(V\) has a basis \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) for which \(Tv_k\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\) for all \(k\). Apply Gram–Schmidt (6.2.3) to get an orthonormal \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) with \(U_k:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_k)=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\). Then \(T\) maps each \(U_k\) into itself, because \(Tv_j\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_j)\subseteq U_k\) for \(j\le k\). In particular \(Te_k\in U_k=\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_k)\), and Statement 5.3.4 shows the matrix in the basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) is upper triangular.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.2.6 Riesz representation

Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space and \(\varphi:V\to\mathbb F\) linear. Then there is a unique \(v\in V\) with \(\varphi(u)=\langle u,v\rangle\) for all \(u\in V\).

drag x to test the identity

Show proof

Existence. Take an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) (6.2.4) and put \(v=\sum_k\overline{\varphi(e_k)}\,e_k\). For \(u=\sum_ja_je_j\), linearity in \(u\) and 6.2.2-style orthonormality give \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_ja_j\,\varphi(e_j)=\varphi(u)\).

Uniqueness. If \(\langle u,v\rangle=\langle u,v'\rangle\) for all \(u\), then \(\langle u,v-v'\rangle=0\) for all \(u\). Taking \(u=v-v'\) gives \(v=v'\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Apply Gram–Schmidt to \((1,1,0),(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\) in \(\mathbb R^3\) with the standard inner product, and check orthonormality.
  2. Harder Show that the Gram–Schmidt vectors are unchanged if each \(v_k\) is multiplied by a positive number, and that they change sign if a \(v_k\) is multiplied by \(-1\).
  3. Toward 6.3 Given a subspace \(U\), how would you find the vector in \(U\) closest to a given \(v\)? Gram–Schmidt on a basis of \(U\) is the first step.

Linear Algebra · Part 6.1

Inner products and norms

An inner product measures angles and lengths on an abstract vector space. From three axioms we get the Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle inequalities, the Pythagorean theorem and the parallelogram law, all in one framework.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In the plane, the dot product \(\langle x,y\rangle=x_1y_1+x_2y_2\) gives lengths \(\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}\) and angles through \(\langle x,y\rangle=\|x\|\,\|y\|\cos\theta\). Those formulas do not care about coordinates, so they extend to any vector space that has an inner product.

Euclidean

The dot product is the standard example. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is \(0\), and the Pythagorean theorem is \(\|x+y\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2\) in that case.

Another ruler

Weight the coordinates with a symmetric positive matrix \(G\) and set \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}Gy\). The unit circle becomes an ellipse, yet the same inequalities hold. The sims below use this family.

Why axioms

Once the axioms are fixed, every consequence follows by algebra alone. That is why the proofs below never mention coordinates.

2Play

Here the inner product is \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}Gy\) with \(G=\begin{pmatrix}1&g\\g&1\end{pmatrix}\). Slide \(g\) to change the ruler; the dashed ellipse is the set of vectors of length \(1\). Drag \(u\) and \(v\) and check the readouts against the statements below.

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Make \(v\) parallel to \(u\). Does the inequality become an equality? What is \(\langle u,v\rangle\) then?
  • Set \(g\) near \(0.9\). Does Cauchy–Schwarz still hold? Which pairs of vectors come closest to equality?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 6.1.1 Inner product

An inner product on a vector space \(V\) over \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\) is a function \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F\) such that: (i) \(\langle u,v\rangle\) is linear in \(u\), for fixed \(v\); (ii) \(\langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle}\); (iii) \(\langle v,v\rangle\ge0\), with equality only for \(v=0\).

Definition 6.1.2 Norm and orthogonality

The norm is \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\). Vectors \(u,v\) are orthogonal, written \(u\perp v\), when \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\).

Statement 6.1.3 Basic properties

For all \(u,v\in V\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb F\): (a) \(\langle u,\lambda v\rangle=\overline{\lambda}\langle u,v\rangle\); (b) \(\langle 0,u\rangle=0\); (c) \(\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|\); (d) \(\langle u,v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle\) when \(\mathbb F=\mathbb R\).

scale v by λ and compare both sides

Show proof

(a) By (ii), \(\langle u,\lambda v\rangle=\overline{\langle\lambda v,u\rangle}=\overline{\lambda\langle v,u\rangle}=\overline\lambda\,\overline{\langle v,u\rangle}=\overline\lambda\langle u,v\rangle\), using (i), (ii) and the fact that conjugation is multiplicative.

(b) By (i), \(\langle 0,u\rangle=\langle 0+0,u\rangle=2\langle 0,u\rangle\), so \(\langle 0,u\rangle=0\).

(c) By (i), (a) and the definition of the norm, \(\|\lambda v\|^2=\lambda\overline\lambda\langle v,v\rangle=|\lambda|^2\|v\|^2\). Take square roots.

(d) This is (ii) in the real case, where conjugation does nothing.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.1.4 Cauchy–Schwarz inequality

For all \(u,v\in V\), \(|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|\). Equality holds if and only if one of \(u,v\) is a scalar multiple of the other.

equality lights up when u and v are parallel

Show proof

If \(v=0\), both sides are \(0\) and \(v=0\cdot u\), so the claim holds. Assume \(v\ne0\), so \(\|v\|^2>0\). Put \(c=\langle u,v\rangle/\|v\|^2\) and \(w=u-cv\). Expanding with (i), (ii) and 6.1.3(a), \[0\le\|w\|^2=\|u\|^2-\overline c\langle u,v\rangle-c\langle v,u\rangle+|c|^2\|v\|^2=\|u\|^2-\frac{|\langle u,v\rangle|^2}{\|v\|^2}.\] Multiplying by \(\|v\|^2\) gives \(|\langle u,v\rangle|^2\le\|u\|^2\|v\|^2\), and taking square roots proves the inequality.

For the equality case, equality holds exactly when \(\|w\|^2=0\), that is, when \(w=0\), i.e. \(u=cv\). Conversely, if \(u=\lambda v\) then \(|\langle\lambda v,v\rangle|=|\lambda|\|v\|^2=\|\lambda v\|\,\|v\|\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.1.5 Triangle inequality

For all \(u,v\in V\), \(\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|\).

the sum is never longer than the two sides

Show proof

Expanding, \(\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\langle u,v\rangle+\langle v,u\rangle+\|v\|^2=\|u\|^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\), since \(\langle v,u\rangle=\overline{\langle u,v\rangle}\). Because \(\operatorname{Re}z\le|z|\), Statement 6.1.4 gives \(2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle\le2\|u\|\,\|v\|\). Hence \(\|u+v\|^2\le(\|u\|+\|v\|)^2\), and taking square roots finishes the proof.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.1.6 Pythagorean theorem

If \(u\perp v\), then \(\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2\).

use the chip to make v orthogonal to u

Show proof

As in the proof of 6.1.5, \(\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\). If \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\), the middle term vanishes.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.1.7 Parallelogram equality

For all \(u,v\in V\), \(\|u+v\|^2+\|u-v\|^2=2\|u\|^2+2\|v\|^2\).

the two diagonals of the parallelogram

Show proof

Expanding each term, \(\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\) and \(\|u-v\|^2=\|u\|^2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\). Adding the two gives \(2\|u\|^2+2\|v\|^2\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}Gy\) is an inner product on \(\mathbb R^2\) when \(G=\begin{pmatrix}1&g\\g&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(|g|\lt1\).
  2. Harder Prove that equality in the triangle inequality holds if and only if one of \(u,v\) is a nonnegative multiple of the other.
  3. Toward 6.2 The Pythagorean theorem extends to more than two summands when they are pairwise orthogonal. Which hypothesis is really needed, and what does the same argument give for an orthonormal list?

Home / Linear Algebra / 3.3
Linear Algebra · Part 3.3

Invertibility and isomorphisms

A linear map that loses nothing and reaches everything can be undone, and the undoing is linear too. For spaces of equal dimension, those two conditions turn out to be the same condition.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Some linear maps can be run backwards. A shear slides every point of the plane along a fixed direction, and another shear slides them back. Other maps cannot be run backwards. A projection throws away a whole direction, so two different inputs land on the same output and no backward map can tell them apart. The question of this part is which maps can be undone, and when the two conditions "nothing is lost" and "everything is reached" agree.

Undoing a shear

Shearing the plane is reversed by a shear in the opposite direction. The reversing map is linear as well, because it respects sums and scalar multiples.

A map that cannot be undone

Projecting \(\mathbb{R}^2\) onto the \(x\)-axis sends \((1,2)\) and \((1,-5)\) to the same point. No backward map can send that point to both, so the projection has no inverse.

Same dimension, same story

A map from \(\mathbb{R}^3\) to \(\mathbb{R}^2\) always loses something. When the two spaces have the same dimension, a map loses something exactly when it fails to reach everything, and the dimension count decides which case we are in.

2Play

Drag the two points \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) on the right. The map \(T\) takes the grid on the left to the tilted grid on the right. The shaded parallelogram on the left is the set of points that \(T\) sends to the parallelogram spanned by \(w_1\) and \(w_2\). Watch the inverse send the sum \(w_1+w_2\) to the sum of the two preimages.

drag w1 and w2 on the right

  • Drag \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) to two parallel points. What happens to the two preimages?
  • Push the shear up to \(2\). Why does the inverse disappear, and why does the number of solutions of \(Tx = w_1\) change?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 3.3.1 Invertible map, isomorphism

A linear map \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) is invertible if there is a linear map \(S \in \mathcal{L}(W,V)\) with \(ST = I_V\) and \(TS = I_W\). Such an \(S\) is an inverse of \(T\). An invertible linear map is an isomorphism, and \(V\) and \(W\) are isomorphic, written \(V \cong W\), when some isomorphism \(V \to W\) exists.

Statement 3.3.1 Invertible means bijective

A linear map \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) is invertible if and only if it is injective and surjective. In that case the inverse \(T^{-1} \colon W \to V\) is unique and linear.

drag w1 and w2, then push the shear

Show proof

Invertible implies bijective. Let \(S\) be an inverse of \(T\). If \(Tu = Tv\), then \(u = STu = STv = v\), so \(T\) is injective. For any \(w \in W\), the vector \(v = Sw\) satisfies \(Tv = TSw = w\), so \(T\) is surjective.

Bijective implies invertible. Suppose \(T\) is injective and surjective. For each \(w \in W\) there is exactly one \(v \in V\) with \(Tv = w\). Call it \(S(w)\), which defines a function \(S \colon W \to V\). Linearity of \(S\) comes from uniqueness: if \(S(w_1) = v_1\) and \(S(w_2) = v_2\), then \(T(v_1+v_2) = w_1+w_2\) and \(T(\lambda v_1) = \lambda w_1\), so \(S(w_1+w_2) = v_1+v_2\) and \(S(\lambda w_1) = \lambda v_1\). By construction \(S(Tv) = v\) for every \(v\), since \(v\) is the unique preimage of \(Tv\), so \(ST = I_V\). Also \(T(Sw) = w\), so \(TS = I_W\). Hence \(T\) is invertible with inverse \(S\).

Uniqueness. If \(S\) and \(S'\) are both inverses, then \(S = S(TS') = (ST)S' = S'\). We write \(T^{-1}\) for the inverse.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.3.2 Equal dimensions

Suppose \(V\) and \(W\) are finite-dimensional with \(\dim V = \dim W\), and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\). Then the following are equivalent: \(T\) is invertible, \(T\) is injective, \(T\) is surjective.

push the squash to zero

Show proof

By Statement 3.3.1 it is enough to show that \(T\) is injective if and only if it is surjective. By the fundamental theorem of linear maps (Statement 3.1.2), \(\dim V = \dim\operatorname{null} T + \dim\operatorname{range} T\).

\(T\) is injective exactly when \(\operatorname{null} T = \{0\}\) (Statement 3.1.1), that is, when \(\dim\operatorname{null} T = 0\). By the theorem this happens exactly when \(\dim\operatorname{range} T = \dim V = \dim W\).

\(T\) is surjective exactly when \(\operatorname{range} T = W\). Since \(\operatorname{range} T\) is a subspace of \(W\), it equals \(W\) exactly when it has the same finite dimension as \(W\). That last fact holds because a basis of a subspace \(U \subseteq W\) with \(\dim U = \dim W\) is a linearly independent list of length \(\dim W\) in \(W\), hence a basis of \(W\), so \(U = W\).

Both conditions are therefore equivalent to \(\dim\operatorname{range} T = \dim W\), so they are equivalent to each other.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.3.3 Same dimension, isomorphic

Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional. Then \(V \cong W\) if and only if \(\dim V = \dim W\).

choose a dimension on each side

Show proof

Isomorphic implies same dimension. Let \(T \colon V \to W\) be an isomorphism, let \(n = \dim V\), and let \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) be a basis of \(V\). The list \(Te_1,\dots,Te_n\) spans \(W\): given \(w\in W\), surjectivity gives \(v\) with \(Tv = w\), and writing \(v = \sum a_je_j\) gives \(w = \sum a_jTe_j\). It is independent: if \(\sum c_jTe_j = 0\), then \(T(\sum c_je_j) = 0\), so \(\sum c_je_j = 0\) by injectivity, and all \(c_j = 0\). So it is a basis of \(W\), and \(\dim W = n\).

Same dimension implies isomorphic. Let \(n = \dim V = \dim W\), with bases \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) of \(V\) and \(f_1,\dots,f_n\) of \(W\). Define \(T\) by \(T(\sum a_je_j) = \sum a_jf_j\). This is well defined because the coefficients \(a_j\) are unique, and it is linear because adding or scaling vectors adds or scales their coefficients. It is injective: if \(\sum a_jf_j = 0\), then every \(a_j = 0\), so the original vector is \(0\). It is surjective: every \(w = \sum b_jf_j\) equals \(T(\sum b_je_j)\). By Statement 3.3.1, \(T\) is an isomorphism.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that \(T(x,y) = (x+2y,\ y)\) is an invertible map \(\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2\), and find \(T^{-1}\).
  2. Harder Show that if \(\dim V < \dim W\), then no linear map \(V \to W\) is surjective.
  3. Toward 3.4 An isomorphism \(\mathbb{F}^n \to V\) is determined by a basis of \(V\). Two bases can give different isomorphisms from \(\mathbb{F}^n\). How are the two resulting maps related?

Home / Linear Algebra / 8.3
Linear Algebra · Part 8.3

Jordan form and square roots

Over the complex numbers every operator is a block diagonal matrix whose blocks are a scalar plus a single chain of ones. The same structure shows that every invertible operator has a square root, and it explains why the trace is the sum of the eigenvalues.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A diagonal matrix is the ideal, but not every operator can be diagonalised. What can always be reached is a matrix that is diagonal apart from a few superdiagonal ones, and those ones encode how eigenvectors fail to be enough.

A chain

For a nilpotent operator, a single chain \(w,\,Nw,\,N^2w,\dots\) ends in \(0\). Written in the basis \(N^{m-1}w,\dots,Nw,w\), the matrix has ones just above the diagonal.

Square roots in the plane

Every nonzero complex number has two square roots. The same is true for invertible operators: their eigenvalues have square roots, and the nilpotent parts can be handled separately.

The trace

Adding up the diagonal of a matrix gives the same number in every basis. That number is the sum of the eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity.

2Play

Here is a \(3\times 3\) nilpotent matrix with entries \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) above the diagonal. Drag the sliders and watch the chain generated by \(e_3\) appear and break. When the chain has length \(3\), the matrix in the chain basis is exactly a Jordan block.

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Set \(a=0\). Which vector of the chain disappears, and what does that say about the eigenvectors?
  • When the chain is a basis, why is the matrix in that basis the same for every choice of \(a,b,c\) with \(ab^2\ne 0\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 8.3.1 Jordan block

For \(\lambda\in\mathbf{F}\) and \(m\ge 1\), the Jordan block \(J(\lambda,m)\) is the \(m\times m\) matrix with \(\lambda\) on the diagonal, \(1\) on the superdiagonal, and \(0\) elsewhere. A Jordan form is a block diagonal matrix whose blocks are Jordan blocks.

Statement 8.3.1 Jordan basis for a nilpotent operator

Let \(N\) be nilpotent on a space \(W\) of dimension \(n\). Then \(W\) has a basis of chains \(\{w_i,Nw_i,\dots,N^{m_i-1}w_i\}\), with \(N^{m_i}w_i=0\) and \(\sum_i m_i=n\). In the basis \(N^{m_i-1}w_i,\dots,Nw_i,w_i\) for each \(i\), the matrix of \(N\) is block diagonal with blocks \(J(0,m_i)\).

Here \(N\) is the nilpotent matrix of the Play section, shown with its generator \(e_3\). The chain is a Jordan basis exactly when it has length \(3\):

move a, b and c

Show proof

Induct on \(n\). If \(n=0\) there is nothing to prove. Let \(n\ge 1\). Since \(N\) is nilpotent and \(W\neq 0\), \(N\) is not injective: if it were, \(N^m\) would be injective for every \(m\), which is impossible when \(N^m=0\).

Let \(W'=\operatorname{range}N\). It has dimension less than \(n\), is \(N\)-invariant, and \(N|_{W'}\) is nilpotent. By induction \(W'\) has a chain basis: vectors \(w_1,\dots,w_r\) and lengths \(m_1,\dots,m_r\) such that \(\{N^jw_i:0\le j\lt m_i\}\) is a basis of \(W'\) and \(N^{m_i}w_i=0\). The tops \(t_i=N^{m_i-1}w_i\) are independent and lie in \(\operatorname{null}N\). Extend them by vectors \(z_1,\dots,z_s\) to a basis of \(\operatorname{null}N\), so \(r+s=\dim\operatorname{null}N\).

Since each \(w_i\) is in the range of \(N\), choose \(x_i\) with \(Nx_i=w_i\). We claim that the vectors \(N^jx_i\) (for \(0\le j\le m_i\)) together with the \(z_l\) form a basis of \(W\). There are \(\sum_i(m_i+1)+s=\dim W'+\dim\operatorname{null}N=n\) of them, by rank–nullity, so it is enough to show independence.

Suppose \(\sum_i\sum_{j=0}^{m_i}a_{ij}N^jx_i+\sum_lb_lz_l=0\). Apply \(N\), using \(N^{j+1}x_i=N^jw_i\) and \(Nz_l=0\), and then use \(N^{m_i}w_i=0\). This gives \(\sum_i\sum_{j=0}^{m_i-1}a_{ij}N^jw_i=0\), so \(a_{ij}=0\) for \(j\lt m_i\). What remains is \(\sum_ia_{im_i}t_i+\sum_lb_lz_l=0\), and since these form a basis of \(\operatorname{null}N\), all coefficients vanish.

Reading the chain \(N^{m-1}w,\dots,Nw,w\) in that order, \(N\) sends each vector to the one before it and the first to \(0\), so the block is \(J(0,m)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.3.2 Jordan form over the complex numbers

Let \(V\) be complex and \(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\). There is a basis of \(V\) in which the matrix of \(T\) is block diagonal, each block being a Jordan block \(J(\lambda,m)\) with \(\lambda\) an eigenvalue of \(T\).

Change the eigenvalues and the superdiagonal entry in a block diagonal Jordan matrix. Setting the superdiagonal entry to \(0\) splits the first block into two eigenvectors:

move the sliders

Show proof

By 8.2.2, \(V=\bigoplus_jG(\lambda_j,T)\). By 8.2.3, the matrix of \(T\) in a basis adapted to this sum is block diagonal with blocks \(\lambda_jI+N_j\), where \(N_j\) is the nilpotent operator \((T-\lambda_jI)|_{G_j}\).

Apply 8.3.1 to each \(N_j\) to get a chain basis of \(G_j\) in which \(N_j\) is block diagonal with blocks \(J(0,m)\). In that basis \(T|_{G_j}=\lambda_jI+N_j\) is block diagonal with blocks \(\lambda_jI+J(0,m)=J(\lambda_j,m)\). Concatenating the bases over \(j\) gives the claimed basis.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.3.3 Identity plus nilpotent has a square root

If \(N\) is nilpotent on a complex space, then \(I+N\) has a square root: some \(R\) with \(R^2=I+N\).

Let \(N\) be strictly upper triangular, so \(N^3=0\). The square root is \(R=I+\tfrac12N-\tfrac18N^2\). The graph shows why: \(\sqrt{1+x}\) and \(1+\tfrac x2-\tfrac{x^2}8\) agree up to the \(x^2\) term.

move the entries and the point x

Show proof

A polynomial lemma. We build polynomials \(p_m\) with \(p_m(0)=1\) and \(p_m(x)^2-(1+x)\) divisible by \(x^m\). Start with \(p_1=1\). Given \(p=p_m\) with \(p^2-(1+x)=x^mq(x)\), set \(p_{m+1}=p+cx^m\) with \(c=-q(0)/2\). Then \(p_{m+1}^2-(1+x)=x^m\bigl(q+2cp+c^2x^m\bigr)\), and the bracket vanishes at \(0\) because \(p(0)=1\) and \(q(0)+2c=0\). So \(p_{m+1}^2-(1+x)\) is divisible by \(x^{m+1}\).

Take \(m=\dim W\), so \(N^m=0\) by 8.1.4. Write \(p=p_m\) and \(p(x)^2-(1+x)=x^mq(x)\). Substituting \(N\) for \(x\) is a ring homomorphism, so \(p(N)^2-(I+N)=N^mq(N)=0\). Take \(R=p(N)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.3.4 Invertible operators have square roots

Every invertible \(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\), with \(V\) complex, has a square root.

Take \(T=\lambda I+N\) with \(N=\begin{bmatrix}0&b\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\). The eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is any nonzero number, and the square root of \(\lambda\) can be imaginary:

move lambda and b

Show proof

Since \(T\) is invertible, \(0\) is not an eigenvalue. By 8.2.2, \(V=\bigoplus_jG_j\) with \(G_j=G(\lambda_j,T)\) and \(\lambda_j\ne 0\). On \(G_j\), write \(T=\lambda_jI+N_j\) with \(N_j\) nilpotent.

Choose a complex square root \(s_j\) of \(\lambda_j\), which exists in \(\mathbf{C}\). The operator \(N_j/\lambda_j\) is nilpotent, so by 8.3.3 there is \(R_j'\) on \(G_j\) with \(R_j'^2=I+N_j/\lambda_j\). Put \(R_j=s_jR_j'\). Then \(R_j^2=s_j^2(I+N_j/\lambda_j)=\lambda_jI+N_j=T|_{G_j}\).

Define \(R\) on \(V\) by \(R|_{G_j}=R_j\), which is well defined because \(V=\bigoplus_jG_j\). Then \(R^2\) and \(T\) agree on every \(G_j\), so \(R^2=T\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.3.5 The trace

For a square matrix \(A\), let \(\operatorname{tr}A\) be the sum of its diagonal entries. (a) \(\operatorname{tr}(P^{-1}AP)=\operatorname{tr}A\) for every invertible \(P\), so the trace \(\operatorname{tr}T\) of an operator, computed in any basis, is well defined. (b) If \(V\) is complex, then \(\operatorname{tr}T=\sum_\lambda \lambda\,\dim G(\lambda,T)\): the sum of the eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

Change the basis by a rotation and a stretch. The diagonal of the matrix changes, but its sum does not:

move the entries and the basis

Show proof

Part (a). Let \(A=(A_{ij})\) and \(B=(B_{ij})\). Then \(\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\sum_i\sum_jA_{ij}B_{ji}=\sum_j\sum_iB_{ji}A_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(BA)\). Hence \(\operatorname{tr}(P^{-1}AP)=\operatorname{tr}((AP)P^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}A\). Matrices of \(T\) in two bases differ by such a conjugation, so \(\operatorname{tr}T\) does not depend on the basis.

Part (b). Use the upper-triangular basis of 8.2.4(a). Its diagonal entries are the eigenvalues, and by 8.2.4(b) each \(\lambda\) occurs \(\dim G(\lambda,T)\) times. So the trace, which is the sum of the diagonal, equals \(\sum_\lambda\lambda\dim G(\lambda,T)\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find a Jordan basis for \(N=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\). Which Jordan blocks appear?
  2. Harder Show that \(N=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\) has no square root. Hint: if \(R^2=N\), then \(R^4=0\), so \(R\) is nilpotent on a \(2\)-dimensional space, and such an operator squares to zero.
  3. Toward 9.1 The trace is linear and basis independent. Is the trace of \(T^2\) the square of the trace of \(T\)? Check with a diagonal example, then with a nilpotent one.

Home / Linear Algebra / 3.1
Linear Algebra · Part 3.1

Linear maps, null spaces and ranges

A linear map respects addition and scaling, so once you know where a basis goes you know where everything goes. Its null space records what it throws away, its range records what it reaches, and the fundamental theorem says the two always add up to the dimension of the start.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A projection of the plane onto a line squashes every direction except the line. That squashing is the whole story of a linear map: some information is lost, and the rest is carried over. The bookkeeping of what is lost and what survives is exactly what this page is about.

Euclidean

Projecting \(\mathbb{R}^2\) onto a line sends a whole line of points to a single point. The lost direction is one line, and the image is another line.

Beyond the plane

Differentiation sends each polynomial of degree at most \(3\) to one of degree at most \(2\). Its null space is the constants, and its range is all polynomials of degree at most \(2\).

The count

The dimension lost plus the dimension reached equals the dimension we started with. The fundamental theorem below says this is always true.

2Play

The map below is the orthogonal projection of the plane onto the line in direction \(\theta\). Drag the angle. The line through the origin that the map crushes to \(0\) is the null space, and the line it keeps is the range.

What to notice before reading the proof:

drag the slider to turn the line

  • Which points of the plane go to \(0\)? Where are they on the picture?
  • As you turn the line, does the sum of the null-space dimension and the range dimension change?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 3.1.1 Linear map

A linear map from \(V\) to \(W\) is a function \(T : V \to W\) with \(T(u+v) = Tu + Tv\) and \(T(\lambda v) = \lambda Tv\) for all \(u,v \in V\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\). We write \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) for the set of linear maps.

Statement 3.1.1 A linear map is determined by a basis

Let \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) be a basis of \(V\). If \(T,S \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) satisfy \(Tv_j = Sv_j\) for every \(j\), then \(T=S\).

drag the basis b1, b2, their images, and the point v

Show proof

Let \(v \in V\). Write \(v = a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n\), which is possible since the list spans. Linearity applied repeatedly, first to the sum and then to each scalar multiple, gives \(Tv = \sum a_iTv_i\). The same computation for \(S\) gives \(Sv = \sum a_iSv_i\). Since \(Tv_i = Sv_i\) for every \(i\), we get \(Tv = Sv\). As \(v\) was arbitrary, \(T=S\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.2 Any choice of images gives a linear map

Let \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) be a basis of \(V\) and let \(w_1,\dots,w_n \in W\) be any vectors. Then there is a unique \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) with \(Tv_j = w_j\) for every \(j\).

drag the images w1, w2 of the standard basis

Show proof

Each \(v \in V\) has a unique representation \(v = \sum a_iv_i\) by Statement 2.2.1. Define \(Tv = \sum a_iw_i\). This is well defined because the representation is unique. It sends \(v_j\) to \(w_j\), since \(v_j\) has the representation with \(a_j=1\) and all others \(0\).

For linearity, let \(v = \sum a_iv_i\) and \(u = \sum b_iv_i\). Then \(u+v = \sum (a_i+b_i)v_i\) and \(\lambda v = \sum (\lambda a_i)v_i\). So \(T(u+v) = \sum(a_i+b_i)w_i = Tu+Tv\) and \(T(\lambda v) = \lambda Tv\). Uniqueness follows from Statement 3.1.1.

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 3.1.2 Null space and range

For \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), the null space is \(\operatorname{null} T = \{v \in V : Tv = 0\}\), and the range is \(\operatorname{range} T = \{Tv : v \in V\}\).

Statement 3.1.3 Null space and range are subspaces; injectivity

For \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), the set \(\operatorname{null} T\) is a subspace of \(V\) and \(\operatorname{range} T\) is a subspace of \(W\). Moreover, \(T\) is injective if and only if \(\operatorname{null} T = \{0\}\).

drag the images of e1 and e2; the unit square is mapped to a parallelogram

Show proof

Linearity gives \(T0 = T(0+0) = T0 + T0\), so \(T0 = 0\). Thus \(0\) lies in the null space. If \(Tu = Tv = 0\), then \(T(u+v) = 0\) and \(T(\lambda u) = 0\), so the null space is closed under the operations. For the range, \(0 = T0\) lies in it, and if \(Tu, Tv\) are in the range then \(Tu+Tv = T(u+v)\) and \(\lambda Tu = T(\lambda u)\) are too.

If \(T\) is injective and \(v \in \operatorname{null} T\), then \(Tv = 0 = T0\) gives \(v = 0\). Conversely, if \(\operatorname{null} T = \{0\}\) and \(Tu = Tv\), then \(T(u-v) = 0\), so \(u-v = 0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.4 Fundamental theorem of linear maps

If \(V\) is finite-dimensional and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), then \(\operatorname{range} T\) is finite-dimensional and \(\dim V = \dim\operatorname{null} T + \dim\operatorname{range} T\).

slide the dimension of V and the rank of T

Show proof

Let \(u_1,\dots,u_m\) be a basis of \(\operatorname{null} T\), extended to a basis \(u_1,\dots,u_m,v_1,\dots,v_k\) of \(V\). We claim that \(Tv_1,\dots,Tv_k\) is a basis of \(\operatorname{range} T\).

Spanning. Any \(v \in V\) can be written \(v = \sum a_iu_i + \sum b_jv_j\). Applying \(T\) kills the \(u_i\), so \(Tv = \sum b_jTv_j\).

Independence. If \(\sum b_jTv_j = 0\), then \(T(\sum b_jv_j) = 0\), so \(\sum b_jv_j\) lies in the null space and equals \(\sum a_iu_i\) for some \(a_i\). Then \(\sum a_iu_i - \sum b_jv_j = 0\) is a relation in the basis, so all \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) vanish.

Hence \(\dim\operatorname{range} T = k\), and \(\dim V = m + k = \dim\operatorname{null} T + \dim\operatorname{range} T\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.5 Too many to fit injectively

If \(\dim V > \dim W\), then no linear map from \(V\) to \(W\) is injective.

set the two dimensions and try to match them

Show proof

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\). Since \(\operatorname{range} T\) is a subspace of \(W\), \(\dim\operatorname{range} T \le \dim W\) by Statement 2.2.6. The fundamental theorem gives \(\dim\operatorname{null} T = \dim V - \dim\operatorname{range} T \ge \dim V - \dim W > 0\). So the null space is not \(\{0\}\), and by Statement 3.1.3 the map is not injective.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.1.6 Too few to cover the target

If \(\dim V < \dim W\), then no linear map from \(V\) to \(W\) is surjective.

set the two dimensions and try to reach every target

Show proof

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\). The fundamental theorem gives \(\dim\operatorname{range} T = \dim V - \dim\operatorname{null} T \le \dim V < \dim W\). A subspace of \(W\) of strictly smaller dimension is not all of \(W\), since equal subspaces of a finite-dimensional space have equal dimension. So \(\operatorname{range} T \ne W\), and \(T\) is not surjective.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Let \(T : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2\) send \((x,y,z)\) to \((x+y, z)\). Find \(\operatorname{null} T\) and \(\operatorname{range} T\), and check Statement 3.1.4.
  2. Harder Show that if \(\dim V < \dim W\), there is no surjective linear map \(V \to W\) whose null space is \(\{0\}\), by combining Statements 3.1.3 and 3.1.6.
  3. Toward 3.2 Once bases of \(V\) and \(W\) are fixed, a linear map becomes a rectangular array of numbers. How many numbers does a map from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) need?

Home / Linear Algebra / 3.2
Linear Algebra · Part 3.2

Matrices

Once bases are fixed, a linear map becomes a grid of numbers, and composing maps becomes multiplying grids. The grid also reveals a hidden fact: the number of independent columns always equals the number of independent rows.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

A rotation of the plane is one map, but its description depends on the coordinates you use. Pick a basis, record where each basis vector goes, and you have a matrix. Two maps composed are described by the product of their matrices, which is why matrix multiplication has the rule it does.

Euclidean

The matrix with columns \((0,1)\) and \((-1,0)\) rotates the plane by a quarter turn. Applying it twice is the half turn, given by the square of the matrix.

Beyond the plane

Differentiation on polynomials of degree at most \(2\), in the basis \(1,x,x^2\), is a \(3 \times 3\) grid. Its square is the second derivative.

The count

A grid with two rows and three columns has rows of length three and columns of length two. Counting the independent ones on each side gives the same number, and the last statement proves it.

2Play

The map \(T\) is fixed: it doubles the first coordinate and adds the second, \(T(x,y) = (2x+y, \tfrac{3}{2}y)\). Drag the domain basis \(v_1,v_2\) on the left and the target basis \(w_1,w_2\) on the right. The grid of numbers is the matrix of \(T\) relative to these two bases, and it changes as you move the bases.

What to notice before reading the proof:

left: domain basis v1, v2. right: target basis w1, w2

  • Make \(v_1,v_2\) the standard basis and \(w_1,w_2\) the standard basis. Do you recover the matrix of \(T\) in standard coordinates?
  • Move the target basis but leave the domain basis alone. Which entries of the matrix change?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 3.2.1 Matrix of a linear map

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), with bases \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) of \(V\) and \(w_1,\dots,w_m\) of \(W\). The matrix \(\mathcal{M}(T)\) is the \(m \times n\) array of numbers \(A_{jk}\) defined by \(Tv_k = \sum_{j=1}^m A_{jk}w_j\). Column \(k\) records the coordinates of \(Tv_k\).

Statement 3.2.1 Composition is multiplication

Let \(S \in \mathcal{L}(U,V)\) and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), with bases of \(U\), \(V\) and \(W\). Then \(\mathcal{M}(T\circ S) = \mathcal{M}(T)\,\mathcal{M}(S)\), where \((AB)_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}\).

drag the images of e1 and e2 under S and under T

Show proof

Let \(u_1,\dots,u_p\) be a basis of \(U\), \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) of \(V\), and \(w_1,\dots,w_m\) of \(W\). Write \(\mathcal{M}(S) = B\) and \(\mathcal{M}(T) = A\), so \(Su_k = \sum_l B_{lk}v_l\) and \(Tv_l = \sum_j A_{jl}w_j\). Then, using linearity of \(T\) and interchanging a finite double sum,

\[ (T\circ S)u_k = T\Big(\sum_l B_{lk}v_l\Big) = \sum_l B_{lk}\sum_j A_{jl}w_j = \sum_j\Big(\sum_l A_{jl}B_{lk}\Big)w_j. \]

The coefficient of \(w_j\) is \(\sum_l A_{jl}B_{lk} = (AB)_{jk}\), which is the \((j,k)\) entry of the product. So \(\mathcal{M}(T\circ S) = AB\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 3.2.2 Multiplication is associative and distributive

For matrices of compatible sizes, \((AB)C = A(BC)\), and \(A(B+C) = AB + AC\).

pick a test triple of matrices

Show proof

Let \(A\) be \(m\times n\), \(B\) be \(n\times p\), and \(C\) be \(p\times q\). The \((i,j)\) entry of \((AB)C\) is \(\sum_k (AB)_{ik}C_{kj} = \sum_k\sum_l A_{il}B_{lk}C_{kj}\). The \((i,j)\) entry of \(A(BC)\) is \(\sum_l A_{il}(BC)_{lj} = \sum_l A_{il}\sum_k B_{lk}C_{kj}\). Both are the same finite double sum over \(l\) and \(k\), so they agree.

For distributivity, \((A(B+C))_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik}(B_{kj}+C_{kj}) = \sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj} + \sum_k A_{ik}C_{kj} = (AB+AC)_{ij}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 3.2.2 Rank of a matrix

The column rank of a matrix is the dimension of the span of its columns in \(\mathbb{F}^m\). The row rank is the dimension of the span of its rows in \(\mathbb{F}^n\).

Statement 3.2.3 Column rank equals row rank

For every matrix \(A\), the column rank of \(A\) equals its row rank.

drag the three columns of a 2 by 3 matrix

Show proof

Row rank is at most column rank. Let \(r\) be the column rank of \(A\), an \(m\times n\) matrix. Choose \(r\) columns that form a basis of the column space, and let \(C\) be the \(m \times r\) matrix with those columns. Each column of \(A\) is a combination of the columns of \(C\), so \(A = CR\) for some \(r\times n\) matrix \(R\). Row \(i\) of \(A\) equals \(\sum_k C_{ik}\cdot(\text{row } k \text{ of } R)\), so every row of \(A\) lies in the span of the \(r\) rows of \(R\). Hence the row rank is at most \(r\).

Equality. Applying the inequality to \(A^{\mathsf T}\) gives \(\text{row rank}(A^{\mathsf T}) \le \text{column rank}(A^{\mathsf T})\). Since the rows of \(A^{\mathsf T}\) are the columns of \(A\), this reads \(\text{column rank}(A) \le \text{row rank}(A)\). Together with the first part, the two ranks are equal.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Compute the matrix of the map \(T(x,y) = (x+y, x-y)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) in the standard basis, and the matrix of \(T\circ T\).
  2. Harder Show that the matrix product \(AB\) can be computed column by column: the \(k\)th column of \(AB\) is \(A\) times the \(k\)th column of \(B\).
  3. Toward 3.3 A square matrix represents an invertible map exactly when its columns are a basis. What does that say about its rank?

Home / Linear Algebra / 5.2
Linear Algebra · Part 5.2

The minimal polynomial

Every operator is killed by some polynomial, and the smallest such polynomial, the minimal polynomial, has exactly the eigenvalues as its zeros. That is enough to show that every operator on an odd-dimensional real space has an eigenvalue.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Eigenvalues were the roots of the operator's shift. The minimal polynomial is the canonical version of that idea: it is the lowest-degree polynomial that makes the operator vanish, so it captures exactly the information the operator carries. Its zeros are the stretch factors, and its factors show which real eigenvalues can exist.

Polynomials that kill an operator

The operator \(T = \operatorname{diag}(1,3)\) satisfies \((z-1)(z-3)\) at \(T\), because each diagonal entry is a zero of the polynomial. It does not satisfy the degree \(1\) polynomial \(z-1\).

The smallest one

For the identity, the minimal polynomial is \(z-1\). For \(\operatorname{diag}(1,3)\) it is \((z-1)(z-3)\). In both cases it is the monic polynomial of least degree that vanishes at the operator.

Odd dimensions

A real operator on \(\mathbb{R}^3\) always has a real eigenvalue. The minimal polynomial of a real operator can only fail to have a real zero when it is a product of quadratics, and an odd dimension rules that out.

2Play

The matrix \(T\) is upper triangular, with diagonal entries \(a, b\) and an off-diagonal entry \(s\). The graph of the minimal polynomial \(\mu\) is drawn with its zeros highlighted. Slide \(\lambda\) and test it: the two readouts, \(\mu(\lambda)\) and \(\det(T-\lambda I)\), vanish together.

slide the entries; test λ

  • Set \(a = b\) and \(s \ne 0\). The minimal polynomial becomes a square. Which eigenvalue does it have, and how many times does it appear?
  • Set \(a = b\) and \(s = 0\). What is the minimal polynomial now, and why is the square gone?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 5.2.1 Annihilating polynomial, minimal polynomial

For \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) and \(p(z) = \sum_k a_kz^k\), let \(p(T) = \sum_k a_kT^k\), where \(T^0 = I\). Then \((pq)(T) = p(T)q(T)\) and \((p+q)(T) = p(T)+q(T)\), because powers of \(T\) commute. We say \(p\) annihilates \(T\) if \(p(T) = 0\). A monic polynomial has leading coefficient \(1\). The minimal polynomial of \(T\) is the monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates \(T\); Statement 5.2.1 shows it exists and is unique.

Remark. If \(r \ne 0\) and \(\deg r < \deg \mu\), then \(r(T) \ne 0\) where \(\mu\) is the minimal polynomial. Dividing \(r\) by its leading coefficient gives a monic polynomial of smaller degree than \(\mu\), which would annihilate \(T\), contradicting minimality.

Statement 5.2.1 Existence and uniqueness

Let \(V\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then \(T\) has a unique minimal polynomial.

change the scale k of the candidate

Show proof

Existence. Let \(n = \dim V\). The space \(\mathcal{L}(V)\) has dimension \(n^2\), as the matrix description of Part 3.2 shows. So the \(n^2+1\) operators \(I, T, \dots, T^{n^2}\) are linearly dependent, and some nonzero polynomial \(q\) has \(q(T) = 0\). Dividing \(q\) by its leading coefficient gives a monic annihilating polynomial. Among all monic annihilating polynomials choose one of least degree.

Uniqueness. Let \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) be monic annihilating polynomials of the same least degree \(d\). Their difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) annihilates \(T\), because \((\mu_1 - \mu_2)(T) = \mu_1(T) - \mu_2(T) = 0\), and its degree is less than \(d\) since the leading terms cancel. By the Remark after Definition 5.2.1, \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.2.2 Annihilators are multiples of the minimal polynomial

Let \(\mu\) be the minimal polynomial of \(T\) and \(p \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\). Then \(p(T) = 0\) if and only if \(\mu\) divides \(p\).

set the coefficients of p

Show proof

Divide \(p\) by \(\mu\) using Statement 4.1.1: \(p = \mu s + r\) with \(\deg r < \deg \mu\). Then \(p(T) = \mu(T)s(T) + r(T) = r(T)\).

If \(\mu\) divides \(p\), then \(r = 0\), so \(p(T) = 0\). Conversely, if \(p(T) = 0\), then \(r(T) = 0\) with \(\deg r < \deg\mu\), so \(r = 0\) by the Remark after Definition 5.2.1. Hence \(p = \mu s\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.2.3 Eigenvalues are the zeros of the minimal polynomial

Let \(\mu\) be the minimal polynomial of \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\), with \(V\) nonzero and finite-dimensional. Then \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\) if and only if \(\mu(\lambda) = 0\).

test a value λ

Show proof

Eigenvalue implies zero. Let \(Tv = \lambda v\) with \(v \ne 0\). Then \(T^kv = \lambda^kv\) for every \(k\), so \(p(T)v = p(\lambda)v\) for every polynomial \(p\). With \(p = \mu\), we get \(0 = \mu(T)v = \mu(\lambda)v\). Since \(v \ne 0\), \(\mu(\lambda) = 0\).

Zero implies eigenvalue. Suppose \(\mu(\lambda) = 0\). By Statement 4.1.2, \(\mu = (z-\lambda)s\) for a polynomial \(s\), which is monic of degree \(\deg \mu - 1\). By the Remark after Definition 5.2.1, \(s(T) \ne 0\), so there is \(w\) with \(s(T)w \ne 0\). Then \((T-\lambda I)\bigl(s(T)w\bigr) = \mu(T)w = 0\). So \(s(T)w\) is a nonzero eigenvector of \(T\) for \(\lambda\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.2.4 Odd-dimensional real operators have eigenvalues

Every operator on an odd-dimensional real vector space has an eigenvalue.

change the dimension; drag the angle

Show proof

We prove by strong induction on odd \(n\) that every operator on a real \(n\)-dimensional space has an eigenvalue. For \(n = 1\), the space is spanned by one nonzero \(v\), and \(Tv\) lies in it, so \(Tv = \lambda v\) for some \(\lambda\). Now let \(n \ge 3\) be odd, let \(T\) act on \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\), and let \(\mu\) be the minimal polynomial of \(T\). Since \(V \ne 0\), \(\mu\) is not constant.

Case 1: \(\mu\) has a real zero \(\lambda\). Then \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue by Statement 5.2.3.

Case 2: \(\mu\) has no real zero. By Statement 4.1.5, \(\mu\) is a product of real polynomials of degree \(1\) or \(2\). A factor of degree \(1\) would give a real zero of \(\mu\), so there is a real factor of degree \(2\). Divide it to make it monic, and call it \(q(z) = z^2 + \beta z + \gamma\). Then \(\mu = qs\) for a real polynomial \(s\) of smaller degree than \(\mu\). Any real zero of \(q\) would be a real zero of \(\mu\), so \(\beta^2 < 4\gamma\). Put \(\delta = \sqrt{\gamma - \beta^2/4} > 0\).

Let \(R = \operatorname{range} q(T)\) and \(U = \operatorname{null} q(T)\). Since \(q(T)\) commutes with \(T\), both \(R\) and \(U\) are invariant under \(T\).

(a) \(R \ne V\). Otherwise \(q(T)\) is surjective, so it is invertible by Statement 3.3.2. From \(q(T)s(T) = \mu(T) = 0\) we get \(s(T) = q(T)^{-1}\cdot 0 = 0\). But \(\deg s < \deg \mu\) and \(s \ne 0\), which contradicts the Remark after Definition 5.2.1.

(b) \(\dim U\) is even. On \(U\), define \(J = \delta^{-1}(T|_U + \tfrac{\beta}{2}I_U)\). Since \((T + \tfrac{\beta}{2}I)^2 = q(T) - \delta^2 I\) and \(q(T) = 0\) on \(U\), we get \(J^2 = -I_U\). Lemma: a real space \(W\) with an operator \(J\) satisfying \(J^2 = -I\) has even dimension. Proof of the lemma: let \(U_0\) be a \(J\)-invariant subspace of largest even dimension. Suppose \(U_0 \ne W\), and pick \(w \notin U_0\). Let \(P = \operatorname{span}(w, Jw)\). It is \(J\)-invariant, because \(J(Jw) = -w\). It has dimension \(2\): if \(Jw = cw\) with \(c\) real, then \(-w = J^2w = c^2w\), impossible for \(w \ne 0\). The subspace \(U_0 \cap P\) is \(J\)-invariant. It is not all of \(P\), since \(w \notin U_0\). If it were a line \(\operatorname{span}(x)\), then \(Jx = dx\) with \(d\) real, and \(-x = J^2x = d^2x\) would be impossible. So \(U_0 \cap P = \{0\}\), and \(U_0 + P\) is \(J\)-invariant of dimension \(\dim U_0 + 2\), which is even and larger, a contradiction. Hence \(U_0 = W\).

(c) Conclusion. By the fundamental theorem of linear maps (Statement 3.1.2), \(n = \dim U + \dim R\). Since \(n\) is odd and \(\dim U\) is even, \(\dim R\) is odd. In particular \(R \ne \{0\}\), and by (a) \(\dim R < n\). So \(T\) restricted to \(R\) is an operator on an odd-dimensional real space of smaller dimension. By the induction hypothesis it has an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with eigenvector \(v \in R\), and then \(Tv = \lambda v\). So \(T\) has an eigenvalue.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the minimal polynomial of the identity on a nonzero space, and of \(\operatorname{diag}(2,2,5)\).
  2. Harder Let \(T\) be an operator on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with no real eigenvalue. Show that its minimal polynomial is \(z^2 + \beta z + \gamma\) with \(\beta^2 < 4\gamma\).
  3. Toward 5.3 On a complex space the minimal polynomial factors completely into linear factors. Which of these factors do you expect to see on the diagonal of a suitable matrix, and why might a basis making the matrix upper triangular exist?

Home / Linear Algebra / 8.1
Linear Algebra · Part 8.1

Generalised eigenvectors and nilpotent operators

An eigenvector is a direction that an operator only stretches. Some operators have too few of them, so we look at the powers of \(T - \lambda I\) instead: the null spaces of those powers form a chain that grows and then stops, and the operators that eventually send everything to zero are the nilpotent ones.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Eigenvectors can run out. The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\) has only one line of eigenvectors, yet the plane is still spanned by vectors that the operator moves in a controlled way. The fix is to ask a different question: which vectors does some power of \(T-\lambda I\) kill?

A shear in the plane

The map \(T-2I\) of the matrix above sends \((x,y)\) to \((y,0)\), and applying it twice gives \(0\). Every vector is killed by some power of \(T-2I\), even though only the \(x\)-axis is an eigenspace.

A staircase

The null spaces of \(T\), \(T^2\), \(T^3\), \(\dots\) get bigger and bigger, but they cannot grow forever. At some point the staircase levels off, and once it levels off it never climbs again.

Why it matters

Over the complex numbers the vectors killed by powers of \(T-\lambda I\) fill out the whole space. That is what makes a block form for \(T\) possible, and it is the reason this part exists.

2Play

Pick an operator and move the power \(k\). The shaded set is \(\operatorname{null}T^k\). Watch how it grows with \(k\), and notice the operators for which it never grows at all.

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • For which operators does \(\operatorname{null}T^k\) stop growing, and at which \(k\)?
  • Is the inclusion \(\operatorname{null}T^k\subseteq\operatorname{null}T^{k+1}\) ever violated? Why not?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 8.1.1 Nilpotent operator

An operator \(T\in\mathcal{L}(V)\) is nilpotent if \(T^m=0\) for some positive integer \(m\).

Definition 8.1.2 Generalised eigenvector

Let \(\lambda\in\mathbf{F}\). A vector \(v\neq 0\) is a generalised eigenvector of \(T\) for \(\lambda\) if \((T-\lambda I)^j v=0\) for some positive integer \(j\). Every eigenvector is one, taking \(j=1\).

Statement 8.1.1 Null spaces of powers grow

For every integer \(k\ge 0\), \(\operatorname{null}T^k\subseteq\operatorname{null}T^{k+1}\).

Try the statement on each operator:

choose T, then move k

Show proof

Let \(v\in\operatorname{null}T^k\), so \(T^kv=0\). Then \(T^{k+1}v=T(T^kv)=T(0)=0\), so \(v\in\operatorname{null}T^{k+1}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.1.2 Once level, always level

If \(\operatorname{null}T^m=\operatorname{null}T^{m+1}\) for some \(m\), then \(\operatorname{null}T^j=\operatorname{null}T^m\) for every \(j\ge m\).

Watch the dimensions of the null spaces once the staircase levels off:

choose T; the bars are dimensions

Show proof

It is enough to show that \(\operatorname{null}T^{j}=\operatorname{null}T^{j+1}\) implies \(\operatorname{null}T^{j+1}=\operatorname{null}T^{j+2}\), and then use induction on \(j\).

Suppose \(\operatorname{null}T^{j}=\operatorname{null}T^{j+1}\) and let \(v\in\operatorname{null}T^{j+2}\). Then \(T^{j+1}(Tv)=0\), so \(Tv\in\operatorname{null}T^{j+1}=\operatorname{null}T^{j}\). Hence \(T^{j}(Tv)=0\), that is \(T^{j+1}v=0\), so \(v\in\operatorname{null}T^{j+1}\). The reverse inclusion is 8.1.1.

Starting from \(j=m\) and repeating this gives \(\operatorname{null}T^{j}=\operatorname{null}T^{m}\) for all \(j\ge m\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.1.3 The staircase levels off by \(\dim V\)

Let \(d=\dim V\). There is some \(k\le d\) with \(\operatorname{null}T^k=\operatorname{null}T^{k+1}\). Consequently \(\operatorname{null}T^{d}=\operatorname{null}T^{d+1}=\operatorname{null}T^{d+2}=\cdots\).

Build a nilpotent operator from blocks and see where its staircase stops:

choose the shape, then move n

Show proof

Suppose \(\operatorname{null}T^j\neq\operatorname{null}T^{j+1}\) for every \(j=0,1,\dots,d\). By 8.1.1 the inclusions are then strict, and each strict inclusion of finite-dimensional subspaces raises the dimension by at least one. So \(\dim\operatorname{null}T^{d+1}\ge d+1\), which is impossible since \(\operatorname{null}T^{d+1}\subseteq V\) has dimension at most \(d\).

Hence there is a least \(k\le d\) with \(\operatorname{null}T^k=\operatorname{null}T^{k+1}\). By 8.1.2 the null spaces are equal from index \(k\) on, and since \(d\ge k\), this includes \(\operatorname{null}T^d\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.1.4 Nilpotent operators die by step \(\dim V\)

If \(T\) is nilpotent, then \(T^{\dim V}=0\).

Drag the upper triangle of a \(3\times 3\) matrix. Any matrix of this shape is nilpotent:

drag the three coloured dots up or down

Show proof

Let \(d=\dim V\) and let \(m\) be such that \(T^m=0\). Then \(\operatorname{null}T^m=V\).

If \(m\le d\), then \(V=\operatorname{null}T^m\subseteq\operatorname{null}T^d\subseteq V\) by 8.1.1, so \(\operatorname{null}T^d=V\). If \(m\gt d\), then 8.1.3 gives \(\operatorname{null}T^d=\operatorname{null}T^m=V\). Either way \(T^dv=0\) for every \(v\), so \(T^d=0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.1.5 A generalised eigenvector has one eigenvalue

If \(v\) is a generalised eigenvector of \(T\) for \(\lambda\) and also for \(\mu\), then \(\lambda=\mu\).

Here \(T=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\). Drag \(v\) and see which eigenvalue, if any, it belongs to:

drag v; near a line it snaps onto it

Show proof

Since \(v\) is generalised for \(\mu\), there is a least \(k\ge 1\) with \((T-\mu I)^kv=0\). Put \(w=(T-\mu I)^{k-1}v\). By minimality \(w\neq 0\), and \((T-\mu I)w=0\), so \(Tw=\mu w\).

Since \(T-\lambda I\) and \(T-\mu I\) commute, \((T-\lambda I)^jw=(T-\mu I)^{k-1}(T-\lambda I)^jv=0\), where \(j\) is an exponent that kills \(v\) for \(\lambda\). But \((T-\lambda I)w=(\mu-\lambda)w\), so by induction \((T-\lambda I)^jw=(\mu-\lambda)^jw\). Therefore \((\mu-\lambda)^jw=0\), and since \(w\neq 0\), \(\mu=\lambda\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 8.1.6 Generalised eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent

If \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) are generalised eigenvectors of \(T\) for distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\), then \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) is linearly independent.

Drag \(u\) and \(w\). Each snaps onto one of the two generalised eigenspaces, so you can test pairs with equal or distinct eigenvalues:

drag u and w

Show proof

Induct on \(m\). The case \(m=1\) holds because \(v_1\neq 0\). Let \(m\ge 2\) and suppose \(\sum_i a_iv_i=0\) with not all \(a_i\) zero. Choose \(j_i\ge 1\) with \((T-\lambda_iI)^{j_i}v_i=0\), and let \(N\ge\max_i j_i\). Put \(S=(T-\lambda_mI)^N\).

Then \(Sv_m=0\). For \(i\lt m\), the vector \(w_i=Sv_i\) is killed by \((T-\lambda_iI)^{j_i}\), because \(S\) commutes with it. If \(w_i=0\), then \(v_i\) is killed by \((T-\lambda_mI)^N\), so \(v_i\) is a generalised eigenvector for \(\lambda_m\) as well as \(\lambda_i\), contradicting 8.1.5. So \(w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}\) are nonzero generalised eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues, hence independent by the induction hypothesis.

Applying \(S\) to the relation gives \(\sum_{i\lt m}a_iw_i=0\). If all \(a_i\) with \(i\lt m\) vanished, then \(a_mv_m=0\) forces \(a_m=0\), a contradiction. So some \(a_i\) with \(i\lt m\) is nonzero, which contradicts the independence of the \(w_i\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Let \(T(x,y,z)=(0,x,y)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Show that \(T^3=0\), and compute \(\dim\operatorname{null}T^k\) for \(k=0,1,2,3\).
  2. Harder Show that the only eigenvalue of a nilpotent operator is \(0\), and that its eigenvectors are exactly the nonzero vectors killed by \(T\).
  3. Toward 8.2 Let \(\lambda\) be an eigenvalue of \(T\). Show that the set of all generalised eigenvectors for \(\lambda\), together with \(0\), is a subspace. This is the generalised eigenspace \(G(\lambda,T)\), studied in the next part.

Home / Linear Algebra / 4.1
Linear Algebra · Part 4.1

Polynomials

Polynomials can be divided, and their zeros are exactly their linear factors. Over the complex numbers every nonconstant polynomial has a zero, and over the real numbers every one splits into factors of degree one or two.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Over the real numbers, \(z^2 + 1\) has no zero, and a rotation of the plane by a right angle has no real invariant line. Over the complex numbers, the same polynomial has the zeros \(\pm i\), and the rotation has invariant lines after all. The next parts depend on exactly this: the zeros of a polynomial are the values where the polynomial can be factored, and they are the candidates for invariant lines of a map.

A polynomial as a function

A polynomial with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}\) is a function \(z \mapsto a_0 + a_1z + \dots + a_mz^m\). Its degree is the largest \(m\) with \(a_m \ne 0\).

Zeros are factors

The number \(2\) is a zero of \(z^2-4\), and indeed \(z^2-4 = (z-2)(z+2)\). The factor \(z-2\) is the reason the zero exists.

Why we need the complex numbers

The polynomial \(z^2+1\) has no real zero, yet over \(\mathbb{C}\) it factors as \((z-i)(z+i)\). Adding the complex numbers is what makes every nonconstant polynomial have a zero.

2Play

Each handle on the axis is a zero. The curve is the product of the factors \(x-r_i\) for the zeros shown, and the degree controls how many handles you get. Drag two handles onto each other, and see how the count of distinct zeros changes while the degree stays fixed.

drag the zeros along the axis

  • Drag two zeros onto the same point. How many distinct zeros remain, and how does that compare with the degree?
  • Could a degree \(3\) polynomial have four distinct zeros? What in the factored form forbids it?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 4.1.1 Polynomial, degree, zero

A polynomial with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}\) is a function \(p(z) = a_0 + a_1z + \dots + a_mz^m\) with \(a_0,\dots,a_m \in \mathbb{F}\). We write \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\) for the set of such polynomials. The degree \(\deg p\) is the largest \(k\) with \(a_k \ne 0\), and the zero polynomial has degree \(-\infty\). A zero of \(p\) is a \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\) with \(p(\lambda) = 0\).

Two facts about degree are used throughout. If \(p\) and \(q\) are nonzero, then \(pq\) is nonzero and \(\deg(pq) = \deg p + \deg q\), because the product of the leading coefficients is nonzero. Also \(\deg(p+q) \le \max(\deg p, \deg q)\).

Statement 4.1.1 Division algorithm

Let \(p, s \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\) with \(s \ne 0\). Then there are unique \(q, r \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\) with \(p = sq + r\) and \(\deg r < \deg s\).

change the divisor s

Show proof

Existence. Use strong induction on \(\deg p\). If \(p = 0\) or \(\deg p < \deg s\), take \(q = 0\) and \(r = p\). Otherwise let \(m = \deg p \ge n = \deg s\), with leading terms \(a z^m\) of \(p\) and \(b z^n\) of \(s\). The polynomial \(p_1 = p - (a/b)z^{m-n}s\) has its \(z^m\) terms cancelled, so \(p_1 = 0\) or \(\deg p_1 < m\). By induction \(p_1 = sq_1 + r\) with \(\deg r < n\), and then \(p = s\bigl((a/b)z^{m-n} + q_1\bigr) + r\).

Uniqueness. Suppose \(sq_1 + r_1 = sq_2 + r_2\) with both remainders of degree less than \(\deg s\). Then \(s(q_1 - q_2) = r_2 - r_1\). If \(q_1 \ne q_2\), the left side has degree at least \(\deg s\), while the right side has degree less than \(\deg s\) or is zero. This is a contradiction, so \(q_1 = q_2\) and then \(r_1 = r_2\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.1.2 Zeros are linear factors

Let \(p \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\). Then \(\lambda\) is a zero of \(p\) if and only if \(p(z) = (z-\lambda)q(z)\) for some \(q \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\).

slide λ along the axis

Show proof

If \(p = (z-\lambda)q\), then \(p(\lambda) = 0\) because the first factor vanishes.

Conversely, divide \(p\) by \(z - \lambda\) using Statement 4.1.1: \(p = (z-\lambda)q + r\) with \(\deg r < 1\), so \(r\) is a constant \(c\). Evaluating at \(\lambda\) gives \(0 = p(\lambda) = 0\cdot q(\lambda) + c\), so \(c = 0\) and \(p = (z-\lambda)q\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.1.3 At most as many zeros as the degree

Let \(p \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\) be a nonzero polynomial of degree \(m\). Then \(p\) has at most \(m\) zeros in \(\mathbb{F}\).

drag the zeros; choose the degree

Show proof

Let \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\) be distinct zeros of \(p\). We show by induction on \(k\) that \(p = (z-\lambda_1)\cdots(z-\lambda_k)\,r\) for some \(r \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\). The case \(k = 1\) is Statement 4.1.2. For the inductive step, write \(p = (z-\lambda_1)\cdots(z-\lambda_{k-1})\,q\). Substituting \(\lambda_k\) gives \(0 = \prod_{i

Since \(p \ne 0\), the factor \(r\) is nonzero, and \(\deg p = k + \deg r \ge k\). Hence \(k \le m\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.1.4 Fundamental theorem of algebra (cited)

Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a zero in \(\mathbb{C}\). Consequently, every nonconstant \(p \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{C})\) of degree \(m\) can be written as \(p(z) = c(z-\lambda_1)\cdots(z-\lambda_m)\) with \(c \ne 0\) and \(\lambda_i \in \mathbb{C}\).

drag the zeros in the plane

Show proof

The first statement is the fundamental theorem of algebra. I cite it rather than prove it here; standard proofs use complex analysis (for instance Liouville's theorem applied to \(1/p\)) or topology.

For the consequence, induct on \(m = \deg p\). If \(m = 1\), then \(p = a_1z + a_0 = a_1(z - \lambda)\) with \(\lambda = -a_0/a_1\). If \(m \ge 2\), the theorem gives a zero \(\lambda\), so \(p = (z-\lambda)q\) by Statement 4.1.2. Here \(\deg q = m - 1 \ge 1\), and induction factors \(q\), which gives the factorisation of \(p\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.1.5 Real polynomials split into degrees 1 and 2

Every nonconstant real polynomial is a product of real polynomials, each of degree \(1\) or \(2\).

drag the zeros; the pair is conjugate

Show proof

Induct on \(\deg p\). Degrees \(1\) and \(2\) need nothing. Let \(p\) be real of degree at least \(3\).

Case 1: \(p\) has a real zero \(\lambda\). Divide \(p\) by \(z - \lambda\) inside real polynomials. The quotient \(q\) and remainder \(r\) are real, and \(r\) is the constant \(p(\lambda) = 0\). So \(p = (z-\lambda)q\) with \(q\) real of smaller degree, and induction applies to \(q\).

Case 2: \(p\) has no real zero. By Statement 4.1.4, \(p\) has a complex zero \(\alpha\), which is not real. Since \(p\) has real coefficients, \(p(\bar\alpha) = \overline{p(\alpha)} = 0\), so \(\bar\alpha\) is also a zero. Let \(q(z) = (z-\alpha)(z-\bar\alpha) = z^2 - 2(\operatorname{Re}\alpha)z + |\alpha|^2\), which has real coefficients. Dividing \(p\) by \(q\) within real polynomials gives \(p = qs + r\) with \(s\) real and \(r = uz + v\) with \(u, v\) real. Evaluating at \(\alpha\) gives \(u\alpha + v = 0\). Since \(\alpha\) is not real, \(u = 0\) and then \(v = 0\). So \(p = qs\), and \(s\) is real. If \(\deg s = 0\), then \(p\) is itself a real polynomial of degree \(2\) times a constant, which is a valid factor. Otherwise \(\deg s \ge 1\) and induction applies to \(s\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Divide \(z^3 - 2z^2 + 3z - 1\) by \(z - 2\), and check that the remainder equals the value of the polynomial at \(2\).
  2. Harder Show that if a real polynomial has a zero \(\alpha\), then \(\bar\alpha\) is also a zero. Deduce that every real polynomial of odd degree has a real zero.
  3. Toward 5.1 For a linear map \(T\), define \(p(T)\) for a polynomial \(p\). Why do \((z-\lambda)(z-\mu)\) and \(z^2 - (\lambda+\mu)z + \lambda\mu\) give the same operator?

Home / Linear Algebra / 7.3
Linear Algebra · Part 7.3

Positive operators and isometries

A nonnegative number has exactly one nonnegative square root, and a positive operator does too. At the other end, isometries are the maps that keep lengths fixed. Both are built from the spectral theorem.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Among real numbers, the nonnegative ones are exactly the squares. So a nonnegative number has a square root that is itself nonnegative. The same idea works for operators, and the matrices that are squares of symmetric matrices are the positive ones. On the other side of the picture, a rotation keeps every length, and the theory of isometries says that this is the only way a map can do so.

Squares of numbers

The number \(4\) has two square roots, \(2\) and \(-2\). Exactly one is nonnegative. Positive operators will have the same kind of unique, well-behaved root.

Shapes

A positive matrix stretches the circle into an ellipse whose axes are perpendicular, and never flips a direction. Its square root has the same axes with each stretch replaced by its square root.

Rotations

A rotation of the plane keeps every length, and it keeps every angle. The theorem will show that a map with this one property, keeping lengths, is determined by a simple matrix identity.

2Play

Choose the two eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix and turn its eigen-axes. The first ellipse is the matrix, and the second ellipse is its square root. Then try the second root, the negative one. It squares to the same matrix, but it is not positive.

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Set \(\lambda_2 = 0\). Does the root still reach the matrix when squared?
  • Switch to the negative root. Which of the two readouts changes, and which stays the same?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 7.3.1 Positive operator

An operator \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) is positive if \(T\) is self-adjoint and \(\langle Tv, v\rangle \geq 0\) for every \(v \in V\). Write \(T \geq 0\).

Definition 7.3.2 Square root

A square root of \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) is an operator \(R\) with \(R^{2} = T\). If \(R\) is also positive, we call it a positive square root.

Definition 7.3.3 Isometry

A linear map \(S \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) is an isometry if \(\lVert Sv\rVert = \lVert v\rVert\) for every \(v \in V\).

Statement 7.3.1 Three ways to be positive

For \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) the following are equivalent: (a) \(T\) is positive; (b) \(T\) is self-adjoint and all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; (c) \(T = R^{*}R\) for some \(R \in \mathcal{L}(V)\).

positive: the quadratic form never goes negative

Show proof

(a) implies (b). If \(Tv = \lambda v\) with \(v \neq 0\), then \(\lambda\lVert v\rVert^{2} = \langle Tv,v\rangle \geq 0\), so \(\lambda \geq 0\).

(b) implies (c). By Statement 7.2.3 (or 7.2.4), \(V\) has an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) with \(Te_j = \lambda_j e_j\) and every \(\lambda_j \geq 0\). Define \(R\) by \(Re_j = \sqrt{\lambda_j}\, e_j\). In this basis \(R\) has real diagonal entries, so \(R^{*} = R\), and \(R^{*}R e_j = \lambda_j e_j = Te_j\). Hence \(T = R^{*}R\).

(c) implies (a). \((R^{*}R)^{*} = R^{*}R^{**} = R^{*}R\), so \(R^{*}R\) is self-adjoint, and \(\langle R^{*}Rv,v\rangle = \lVert Rv\rVert^{2} \geq 0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.3.2 Unique positive square root

Every positive operator \(T\) has exactly one positive square root, denoted \(\sqrt{T}\).

only the positive root is positive

Show proof

Existence. By Statement 7.3.1, the operator \(T\) has an orthonormal eigenbasis \(e_j\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_j \geq 0\), and \(R\) defined by \(Re_j = \sqrt{\lambda_j}\,e_j\) is positive with \(R^{2} = T\).

Uniqueness. Let \(R\) be any positive operator with \(R^{2} = T\). Let \(\lambda\) be an eigenvalue of \(T\) with eigenspace \(E = \operatorname{null}(T - \lambda I)\). Since \(R\) commutes with \(R^{2} = T\), for \(v \in E\) we have \(T(Rv) = R(Tv) = \lambda Rv\), so \(R\) maps \(E\) into \(E\). The restriction \(R|_E\) is self-adjoint on \(E\). If \(Rv = \mu v\) with \(v \in E\), \(v \neq 0\), then \(\lambda v = Tv = R^{2}v = \mu^{2}v\), so \(\mu^{2} = \lambda\); also \(\mu \geq 0\) because \(R\) is positive. Hence \(\mu = \sqrt{\lambda}\). By the spectral theorem, \(E\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(R|_E\), and all of them have eigenvalue \(\sqrt{\lambda}\). So \(Rv = \sqrt{\lambda}\, v\) for every \(v \in E\).

The spectral theorem also gives \(V = \bigoplus_\lambda E_\lambda\) over the eigenvalues \(\lambda\) of \(T\). Since \(R\) acts as \(\sqrt{\lambda}\) on each \(E_\lambda\), it is determined by \(T\). So any two positive square roots agree.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.3.3 Isometries

For \(S \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) the following are equivalent: (a) \(S\) is an isometry; (b) \(\langle Su,Sv\rangle = \langle u,v\rangle\) for all \(u,v \in V\); (c) \(S^{*}S = I\); (d) for some orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) of \(V\), the list \(Se_1,\dots,Se_n\) is orthonormal.

drag the columns, try the presets

Show proof

(a) implies (b). Polarisation: in a complex space \(\langle u,v\rangle = \frac14\sum_{k=1}^{4} i^{k}\lVert u + i^{k}v\rVert^{2}\), and in a real space \(\langle u,v\rangle = \frac14(\lVert u+v\rVert^{2} - \lVert u-v\rVert^{2})\). Since \(S\) is linear and preserves norms, it preserves each term, so it preserves \(\langle u,v\rangle\).

(b) implies (c). \(\langle (S^{*}S - I)u, v\rangle = \langle Su,Sv\rangle - \langle u,v\rangle = 0\) for all \(u,v\). Taking \(v = (S^{*}S-I)u\) gives \(S^{*}S = I\).

(c) implies (a). \(\lVert Sv\rVert^{2} = \langle S^{*}Sv,v\rangle = \langle v,v\rangle = \lVert v\rVert^{2}\).

(b) implies (d), because \(\langle Se_j, Se_k\rangle = \langle e_j,e_k\rangle\) for any orthonormal basis. (d) implies (a): if \(v = \sum_j\langle v,e_j\rangle e_j\), then \(\lVert Sv\rVert^{2} = \sum_j|\langle v,e_j\rangle|^{2} = \lVert v\rVert^{2}\) by orthonormality of the list \(Se_j\) and Parseval's identity for \(e_j\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) is positive and find its positive square root. Check by squaring.
  2. Harder Let \(T\) be positive with \(\langle Tv,v\rangle = 0\). Show that \(Tv = 0\). Hint: write \(T = R^{*}R\) and use \(\lVert Rv\rVert = 0\).
  3. Toward 7.4 Show that every isometry on a finite-dimensional space has all its singular values equal to \(1\). Why does this make the singular value decomposition a natural next step?

Home / Linear Algebra / 6.3
Linear Algebra · Part 6.3

Orthogonal complements and projections

Every subspace has a perpendicular partner, and together they split the whole space. The projection onto a subspace is the piece of a vector that lives in it, and it is the closest point of that subspace to the vector.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Drop a perpendicular from a point to a line: the foot of the perpendicular is the point of the line nearest to where you started. Every vector splits into a part along a line and a part perpendicular to it. The same picture works in any finite-dimensional inner product space.

In the plane

For a line \(U\), the perpendicular lines are the vectors \(w\) with \(\langle w,d\rangle=0\). Each vector is the sum of its component along \(U\) and its component perpendicular to \(U\).

Shadows

Projecting onto \(U\) is like casting a shadow with the light falling straight down. The shadow of a vector is the closest point of \(U\) to it.

The count

A line and its perpendicular make up the plane, with dimensions \(1+1=2\). The general statement says the dimensions always add up in this way.

2Play

Turn the line \(U\). The vector \(v\) splits into \(u\) on \(U\) and \(w\) on the perpendicular \(U^\perp\), and the parallelogram they form is shaded. Then see how a projection squashes a grid onto \(U\).

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

The projection as a map:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Find the angle at which \(v\) is already on \(U\). What is \(w\) then?
  • Apply the projection twice in your head. Why does \(P(Pv)\) always equal \(Pv\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 6.3.1 Orthogonal complement

For a subspace \(U\subseteq V\), its orthogonal complement is \(U^\perp=\{v\in V:\langle u,v\rangle=0\text{ for all }u\in U\}\).

Statement 6.3.2 Splitting into a subspace and its complement

If \(U\) is a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\), then \(U^\perp\) is a subspace, \(U\cap U^\perp=\{0\}\), and \(V=U\oplus U^\perp\). In particular every \(v\in V\) is uniquely \(v=u+w\) with \(u\in U\) and \(w\in U^\perp\).

the shaded parallelogram is u + w

Show proof

For each \(u\in U\), the map \(v\mapsto\langle u,v\rangle\) is conjugate-linear, and the set where it vanishes is a subspace. So \(U^\perp\), the intersection of these sets, is a subspace. If \(x\in U\cap U^\perp\), then \(\langle x,x\rangle=0\), so \(x=0\).

For the sum, let \(e_1,\dots,e_m\) be an orthonormal basis of \(U\) (6.2.4 applied to \(U\)). Given \(v\in V\), set \(u=\sum_k\langle v,e_k\rangle e_k\in U\) and \(w=v-u\). Then \(\langle w,e_j\rangle=\langle v,e_j\rangle-\langle v,e_j\rangle=0\) for each \(j\), so for any \(x=\sum_jc_je_j\in U\), \(\langle w,x\rangle=\sum_j\overline{c_j}\langle w,e_j\rangle=0\). Hence \(w\in U^\perp\) and \(v=u+w\in U+U^\perp\). Together with \(U\cap U^\perp=\{0\}\), the sum is direct, and uniqueness of the decomposition follows.

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 6.3.3 Orthogonal projection

For a subspace \(U\) of a finite-dimensional inner product space, the orthogonal projection \(P_U\in\mathcal L(V)\) sends \(v=u+w\) (with \(u\in U\), \(w\in U^\perp\), as in 6.3.2) to \(P_Uv=u\).

Statement 6.3.4 Properties of the orthogonal projection

For a subspace \(U\) of a finite-dimensional inner product space, with an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_m\) of \(U\): (a) \(P_U\) is linear; (b) \(\operatorname{range}P_U=U\) and \(\operatorname{null}P_U=U^\perp\); (c) \(P_U^2=P_U\); (d) \(P_Uv=\sum_k\langle v,e_k\rangle e_k\).

the grid is squashed onto U

Show proof

(a) If \(v=u+w\) and \(v'=u'+w'\) are the decompositions, then \(\alpha v+\beta v'=(\alpha u+\beta u')+(\alpha w+\beta w')\) with the two parts in \(U\) and \(U^\perp\). By uniqueness, \(P_U(\alpha v+\beta v')=\alpha P_Uv+\beta P_Uv'\).

(b) Every \(P_Uv\) lies in \(U\), and \(P_Uu=u\) for \(u\in U\) (take \(w=0\)), so the range is \(U\). If \(P_Uv=0\), then \(v=w\in U^\perp\); conversely \(P_Uw=0\) for \(w\in U^\perp\). So the null space is \(U^\perp\).

(c) Since \(P_Uv\in U\), we have \(P_U(P_Uv)=P_Uv\) by (b).

(d) Let \(u=\sum_k\langle v,e_k\rangle e_k\) and \(w=v-u\). The proof of 6.3.2 showed \(w\in U^\perp\) and \(u\in U\), so this is the decomposition and \(P_Uv=u\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 6.3.5 Closest point property

Let \(U\) be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space, \(v\in V\), and \(u\in U\). Then \(\|v-P_Uv\|\le\|v-u\|\), with equality if and only if \(u=P_Uv\).

drag the point u along U; the circle through u touches U only at P_U v

Show proof

Write \(v-u=(v-P_Uv)+(P_Uv-u)\). The first term lies in \(U^\perp\) by 6.3.2, and the second lies in \(U\) because both \(P_Uv\) and \(u\) do. So the two terms are orthogonal, and the Pythagorean theorem (6.1.6) gives \[\|v-u\|^2=\|v-P_Uv\|^2+\|P_Uv-u\|^2\ge\|v-P_Uv\|^2.\] This proves the inequality. Equality holds exactly when \(\|P_Uv-u\|=0\), that is, when \(u=P_Uv\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine In \(\mathbb R^3\), find \(P_U\) for the plane \(U=\{(x,y,z):x+y+z=0\}\) applied to \((1,2,3)\), using an orthonormal basis of \(U\).
  2. Harder Prove that \(\dim U^\perp=\dim V-\dim U\), and deduce that \((U^\perp)^\perp=U\).
  3. Toward 7.1 Projections are self-adjoint with respect to the inner product. Which properties of \(P_U\) above use that fact, and which do not?
