Home / Linear Algebra / 7.5
Linear Algebra · Part 7.5

QR and Cholesky factorisations

Gram–Schmidt turns any invertible matrix into an orthogonal matrix times a triangular one. For a positive definite matrix, the triangular factor can be chosen to be the matrix's own square root in a triangular form.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Solving \(Ax = b\) is much easier when \(A\) is triangular, and much more stable when \(A\) is orthogonal. A factorisation that gives one of each, multiplied together, is therefore useful. The QR factorisation gives this for any invertible matrix, and the Cholesky factorisation is the special form it takes for a symmetric positive definite matrix.

Two vectors in the plane

Take a vector \(a_1\) and a second vector \(a_2\). Keep the direction of \(a_1\) as the first axis, then keep only the part of \(a_2\) that is perpendicular to it as the second axis. Those two axes are the orthogonal matrix, and the numbers you used to get there are the triangular matrix.

The triangle

The second column of the triangular factor says how much of \(a_2\) lies along the first axis. Nothing lies along the second axis from the first column, so the zero below the diagonal appears automatically.

Positive matrices

A symmetric positive definite matrix \(A\) can be written \(A = R^{*}R\) with \(R\) upper triangular. Each entry of \(R\) has a meaning as a length or a projection, and the next sim draws it.

2Play

Drag the two column vectors \(a_1\) and \(a_2\). The orthonormal axes \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) come from Gram–Schmidt. The dashed segment is the part of \(a_2\) that is perpendicular to \(q_1\), and it sets the length \(r_{22}\). Move the columns to be almost parallel and see what happens to \(r_{22}\).

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Make \(a_2\) a multiple of \(a_1\). What does the verdict say, and why does the factorisation fail?
  • Which entries of \(R\) change when you move only \(a_1\)? Which change when you move only \(a_2\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 7.5.1 Positive definite

An operator (or matrix) \(A\) is positive definite if it is self-adjoint and \(\langle Av,v\rangle > 0\) for every \(v \neq 0\). A unitary matrix \(Q\) is one with \(Q^{*}Q = I\); in the real case these are called orthogonal.

Statement 7.5.1 QR factorisation

Let \(A\) be an invertible \(n\times n\) matrix. Then \(A = QR\), where \(Q\) is unitary and \(R\) is upper triangular with positive diagonal entries. This factorisation is unique.

Gram–Schmidt on the columns

Show proof

Existence. Let \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) be the columns of \(A\); they are linearly independent. Run Gram–Schmidt: set \(v_k = a_k - \sum_{j 0\), and \(R_{jk} = 0\) for \(j > k\). A square matrix with orthonormal columns is unitary.

Uniqueness. Suppose \(QR = Q'R'\) with both factorisations of the required kind. Then \(R\) is invertible, since \(A\) is, and \(U = Q'^{*}Q = R'R^{-1}\). The matrix \(U\) is unitary, and it is upper triangular with positive diagonal, because products and inverses of upper triangular matrices are upper triangular and the diagonal entries multiply. Now \(U^{-1} = U^{*}\) is lower triangular, since \(U\) is upper triangular, and \(U^{-1}\) is upper triangular. So \(U\) is diagonal, with diagonal entries of modulus \(1\) that are also positive. Hence \(U = I\), so \(Q = Q'\) and \(R = R'\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.5.2 Cholesky factorisation

Let \(A\) be positive definite. Then there is a unique upper triangular matrix \(R\) with positive diagonal entries such that \(A = R^{*}R\).

the ellipse of A, and the columns of R

Show proof

Existence. Since \(A\) is positive definite, its eigenvalues are real and positive: if \(Av = \lambda v\) with \(v \neq 0\), then \(\lambda\lVert v\rVert^{2} = \langle Av,v\rangle > 0\). By Statement 7.3.2 there is a positive square root \(B = \sqrt{A}\), with eigenvalues \(\sqrt{\lambda} > 0\) on the same eigenvectors. So \(B\) is invertible and \(B^{*}B = B^{2} = A\). By Statement 7.5.1, \(B = QR\) with \(Q\) unitary and \(R\) upper triangular with positive diagonal. Then \(A = B^{*}B = R^{*}Q^{*}QR = R^{*}R\).

Uniqueness. Suppose \(A = R^{*}R = S^{*}S\) with \(R\) and \(S\) upper triangular with positive diagonals. Both are invertible, and \(U = RS^{-1}\) satisfies \(U^{*}U = S^{-*}R^{*}RS^{-1} = S^{-*}S^{*}SS^{-1} = I\). So \(U\) is unitary. It is also upper triangular with positive diagonal, so \(U = I\) by the argument in the uniqueness part of Statement 7.5.1 (a unitary upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal is the identity). Hence \(R = S\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the QR factorisation of \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) by hand, and check that the diagonal of \(R\) is positive.
  2. Harder Let \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\). Find its Cholesky factor \(R\) and check \(R^{*}R = A\).
  3. Toward 8.1 Let \(N\) be upper triangular with zeros on its diagonal. Show that \(N^{n} = 0\) when \(N\) is \(n\times n\). Why is this the first step towards understanding operators that are not diagonalisable?

Home / Linear Algebra / 2.1
Linear Algebra · Part 2.1

Span and linear independence

Combining a list of vectors with scalars produces everything its span can reach. Independence asks whether each vector is really needed: a list is independent exactly when every vector in its span has only one way to be built.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Two arrows in the plane can reach a whole region if they point in different directions. If they point the same way, they reach only a line. The span is the set of all places you can reach, and independence measures whether some arrow is wasted.

Euclidean

The vectors \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) span \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The vectors \((1,0)\) and \((2,0)\) span only the \(x\)-axis, because the second is a multiple of the first.

Beyond the plane

The polynomials \(1, x, x^2\) span a space of polynomials of degree at most \(2\). Adding \(x+1\) to the list changes nothing: it was already there.

The question

Given a list, which vectors can be reached, and does any vector in the list repeat what the others already give? The statements below answer both.

2Play

Drag the two vectors \(u\) and \(v\). The shaded region is their span. Pick a candidate subspace \(X\) with the chips and see whether it contains the list, and whether it contains \(u+v\).

What to notice before reading the proof:

drag u and v; pick a candidate subspace X

  • Make \(u\) and \(v\) parallel. What does the span become, and does the line \(X\) still contain it?
  • For \(X\) equal to the line through \(u\), can \(v\) be off that line while \(X\) still contains the span? Why not?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 2.1.1 Linear combination and span

A linear combination of a list \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) in \(V\) is a vector \(a_1v_1+\cdots+a_mv_m\) with \(a_i \in \mathbb{F}\). The set of all such combinations is \(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_m)\). The span of the empty list is \(\{0\}\).

Statement 2.1.1 Span is the smallest subspace

\(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_m)\) is a subspace of \(V\) containing each \(v_j\). If \(X\) is any subspace of \(V\) containing each \(v_j\), then \(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_m) \subseteq X\).

drag u and v; test a subspace X

Show proof

The span contains \(0\), since taking all \(a_i=0\) gives \(0\). It is closed under addition: \((\sum a_iv_i)+(\sum b_iv_i) = \sum(a_i+b_i)v_i\). It is closed under scaling: \(\lambda\sum a_iv_i = \sum(\lambda a_i)v_i\). Each \(v_j\) is in the span by taking \(a_j=1\) and all other coefficients \(0\).

If \(X\) is a subspace containing every \(v_j\), then each \(a_jv_j\) lies in \(X\) by scaling, and the finite sum \(\sum a_jv_j\) lies in \(X\) by repeated addition. So the span is contained in \(X\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 2.1.2 Linear independence

A list \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) is linearly independent if the only choice of scalars with \(a_1v_1+\cdots+a_mv_m = 0\) is \(a_1=\cdots=a_m=0\). Otherwise the list is linearly dependent.

Statement 2.1.2 Linear dependence lemma

If \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) is a linearly dependent list and \(v_1 \neq 0\), then there is an index \(j \ge 2\) such that \(v_j\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{j-1})\). Moreover, the vector \(v_j\) can be removed without changing the span.

drag v1, v2, v3 in the plane

Show proof

Since the list is dependent, there are scalars \(a_1,\dots,a_m\), not all zero, with \(\sum a_iv_i = 0\). Let \(j\) be the largest index with \(a_j \neq 0\). Then \(a_jv_j = -\sum_{i

We have \(j \ge 2\): if \(j=1\), then \(a_1v_1 = 0\) with \(a_1 \neq 0\), which forces \(v_1 = 0\), contrary to assumption.

Removing \(v_j\) does not change the span: every combination that uses \(v_j\) can replace \(v_j\) by its expression in the earlier vectors.

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 2.1.3 Representation

A vector \(w\) has a representation \(w = a_1v_1+\cdots+a_mv_m\) for a fixed list. The representation is unique if no other choice of scalars gives the same \(w\).

Statement 2.1.3 Independence is unique representation

A list \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) is linearly independent if and only if every vector in its span has exactly one representation as a linear combination of the list.

drag u and v; move the target w

Show proof

Suppose the list is independent, and \(w = \sum a_iv_i = \sum b_iv_i\) is a vector in the span. Subtracting gives \(\sum (a_i-b_i)v_i = 0\), so every \(a_i-b_i=0\). The representation is unique.

Conversely, suppose every vector in the span has exactly one representation. The zero vector lies in the span and has the representation with all coefficients \(0\). Uniqueness says no other representation of \(0\) exists, which is independence.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Show that \((1,1,0),\,(0,1,1),\,(1,0,1)\) are linearly independent in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), and find the span of the first two.
  2. Harder Show that a list containing the zero vector is always dependent, and that a list of length \(1\) is independent exactly when its vector is nonzero.
  3. Toward 2.2 Suppose \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) spans \(V\) and is dependent. Show that some vector can be removed and the span stays \(V\). Give an example where removing a vector from a spanning list leaves a list that no longer spans.

Home / Linear Algebra / 7.2
Linear Algebra · Part 7.2

The spectral theorem

A symmetric matrix turns a circle into an ellipse whose axes point along perpendicular eigenvectors. The spectral theorem says this is always true for self-adjoint operators, and that normal operators behave the same way over the complex numbers.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

An eigenvector is a direction that the map keeps. For a general matrix there may be no such direction, or the directions may not be perpendicular. The spectral theorem says that for the operators of Part 7.1 the picture is as clean as it can be: a basis of perpendicular eigenvectors, which is also an orthonormal basis.

In the plane

A symmetric \(2\times 2\) matrix stretches the circle into an ellipse. The long and short axes of that ellipse are perpendicular, and they are the eigen-directions of the matrix.

Without symmetry

A shear has one eigen-direction and no perpendicular pair. A rotation has no real eigen-direction at all. The theorem will explain exactly which matrices avoid both problems.

Over the complex numbers

A rotation-and-scaling matrix has complex eigenvectors, and those eigenvectors are perpendicular. Normal operators are the class where this always works.

2Play

Press Animate and watch the eigen-axes turn with the matrix. The matrix is \(A = Q_\theta D Q_\theta^{T}\), where \(D\) is diagonal and \(Q_\theta\) is a rotation. The two glowing axes are the eigen-directions, and they stay perpendicular as they turn. Switch to Tilt to add a shear: the axes stop being perpendicular.

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Turn the rotation through a full circle. Do the eigen-axes ever stop being perpendicular while the matrix is symmetric?
  • Switch to Tilt. Which eigen-axes move apart from each other, and what does the readout say about perpendicularity?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 7.2.1 Eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator are real

If \(T\) is self-adjoint, then every eigenvalue of \(T\) is a real number. This holds over \(\mathbb{R}\) and over \(\mathbb{C}\).

real axis: real eigenvalues

Show proof

Let \(Tv = \lambda v\) with \(v \neq 0\). Then \(\lambda\lVert v\rVert^{2} = \langle Tv, v\rangle\). Also \(\langle Tv, v\rangle = \langle v, Tv\rangle = \overline{\langle Tv,v\rangle}\) because \(T\) is self-adjoint. So \(\langle Tv,v\rangle\) is real, and dividing by \(\lVert v\rVert^{2} \neq 0\) shows \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.2.2 Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal

Let \(T\) be self-adjoint, let \(Tu = \alpha u\) and \(Tv = \beta v\), and suppose \(\alpha \neq \beta\). Then \(u \perp v\).

distinct eigenvalues

Show proof

Using self-adjointness and the realness of \(\beta\) from Statement 7.2.1, \(\alpha\langle u,v\rangle = \langle Tu, v\rangle = \langle u, Tv\rangle = \langle u, \beta v\rangle = \beta\langle u,v\rangle\). So \((\alpha - \beta)\langle u,v\rangle = 0\), and since \(\alpha \neq \beta\), \(\langle u,v\rangle = 0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.2.3 Real spectral theorem

Let \(V\) be a real inner product space and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then \(T\) is self-adjoint if and only if \(V\) has an orthonormal basis made of eigenvectors of \(T\).

turn the matrix, watch the axes

Show proof

If \(V\) has such a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\), with \(Te_j = \lambda_j e_j\), then the matrix of \(T\) in this basis is the real diagonal matrix \(D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\). Because the basis is orthonormal, the matrix of \(T^{*}\) is the conjugate transpose \(D^{*} = D\) (Statement 7.1.3). So \(T^{*}\) and \(T\) have the same matrix, and \(T^{*} = T\).

If \(T\) is self-adjoint, we induct on \(\dim V\). The case \(\dim V = 0\) is empty. Let \(\dim V \geq 1\).

Step 1: there is an eigenvector. The unit sphere of a finite-dimensional real space is compact, so \(v \mapsto \langle Tv,v\rangle\) attains a maximum \(\lambda\) at some unit vector \(v_0\). Put \(S = T - \lambda I\). Then \(S\) is self-adjoint, \(\langle Sx,x\rangle \leq 0\) for every \(x\) (by scaling), and \(\langle Sv_0,v_0\rangle = 0\). For any \(w\) and real \(t\), \(0 \geq \langle S(v_0+tw), v_0+tw\rangle = 2t\operatorname{Re}\langle Sv_0,w\rangle + t^{2}\langle Sw,w\rangle\). Since this holds for all real \(t\), \(\operatorname{Re}\langle Sv_0,w\rangle = 0\). Replacing \(w\) by \(iw\) in the complex case gives \(\operatorname{Im}\langle Sv_0,w\rangle = 0\) too. Taking \(w = Sv_0\) shows \(Sv_0 = 0\), so \(Tv_0 = \lambda v_0\).

Step 2: split off the eigenvector. Let \(U = (\operatorname{span}v_0)^{\perp}\). For \(u \in U\), \(\langle Tu, v_0\rangle = \langle u, Tv_0\rangle = \lambda\langle u,v_0\rangle = 0\), so \(U\) is invariant under \(T\). The restriction \(T|_U\) is self-adjoint on the \((n-1)\)-dimensional space \(U\). By induction \(U\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and adding \(v_0\) gives one for \(V\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.2.4 Complex spectral theorem

Let \(V\) be a complex inner product space and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then \(T\) is normal if and only if \(V\) has an orthonormal basis made of eigenvectors of \(T\).

normal: perpendicular complex eigenvectors

Show proof

If there is an orthonormal eigenbasis, the matrix of \(T\) in it is diagonal, \(D\). Diagonal matrices commute with their conjugate transposes, so \(DD^{*} = D^{*}D\), which means \(TT^{*} = T^{*}T\).

If \(T\) is normal, we induct on \(\dim V\). Let \(\dim V \geq 1\). By the fundamental theorem of algebra, \(T\) has an eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Let \(E = \operatorname{null}(T - \lambda I)\).

Eigenvectors of \(T\) are eigenvectors of \(T^{*}\). The operator \(T - \lambda I\) is normal: \((T-\lambda I)(T-\lambda I)^{*} = TT^{*} - \bar\lambda T - \lambda T^{*} + |\lambda|^{2}I\) and \((T-\lambda I)^{*}(T-\lambda I) = T^{*}T - \lambda T^{*} - \bar\lambda T + |\lambda|^{2}I\), which agree because \(TT^{*} = T^{*}T\). By Statement 7.1.4, \(\lVert (T-\lambda I)v\rVert = \lVert (T^{*}-\bar\lambda I)v\rVert\) for all \(v\). So for \(v \in E\), \(\lVert (T^{*}-\bar\lambda I)v\rVert = 0\), that is \(T^{*}v = \bar\lambda v\). Hence \(E\) is invariant under \(T^{*}\).

Splitting off \(E\). Let \(W = E^{\perp}\). For \(w \in W\) and \(v \in E\), \(\langle Tw, v\rangle = \langle w, T^{*}v\rangle = \langle w, \bar\lambda v\rangle = 0\), so \(W\) is \(T\)-invariant. For \(w \in W\) and \(v \in E\), \(\langle T^{*}w, v\rangle = \langle w, Tv\rangle = \lambda\langle w,v\rangle = 0\), so \(W\) is also \(T^{*}\)-invariant. Therefore \((T|_W)^{*} = T^{*}|_W\), and \((T|_W)(T|_W)^{*} = TT^{*}|_W\) equals \(T^{*}T|_W = (T|_W)^{*}(T|_W)\). So \(T|_W\) is normal on a space of smaller dimension, and by induction \(W\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. An orthonormal basis of \(E\) consists of eigenvectors with eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Together they form an orthonormal basis of \(V\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine For the symmetric matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\), find the eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Check Statement 7.2.2 by computing the dot product of the eigenvectors.
  2. Harder Let \(T\) be self-adjoint on a real inner product space with \(\langle Tv,v\rangle = 0\) for all \(v\). Show that \(T = 0\). Does the same conclusion hold for a real operator that is not self-adjoint?
  3. Toward 7.3 Let \(T\) be self-adjoint with all eigenvalues nonnegative. Use the spectral theorem to show that \(\langle Tv,v\rangle \geq 0\) for every \(v\).

Linear Algebra · Part 7.4

Singular value decomposition

Every linear map, even between spaces of different dimensions, takes the unit ball to an ellipsoid. Its axes have lengths called singular values, and they are the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(T^{*}T\).

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Eigenvalues only make sense for an operator from a space to itself, and most maps are not like that. Singular values fix this. They measure how much a map stretches, and they are defined for every linear map. For a symmetric matrix they are the absolute values of the eigenvalues, and in general they tell you the whole shape of the image of the unit ball.

In the plane

Draw the unit circle and apply a \(2\times 2\) matrix. You get an ellipse. Its longest radius is the largest stretch of the matrix, and its shortest radius is the smallest.

Between different spaces

A map from \(\mathbb{R}^3\) to \(\mathbb{R}^2\) takes the unit ball of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) to a flat ellipse in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Singular values still say how wide each axis is, and they are defined without eigenvalues of the map.

Two bases

The ellipse has one perpendicular direction in the input and one in the output. The decomposition pairs them up, and this is the main result of the post.

2Play

Drag the two dots, which are the images of the standard basis vectors \(e_1\) and \(e_2\). Dragging them changes the entries of the matrix. The dashed circle is the unit circle, the blue shape is its image, and the two arrows are the semi-axes of the image, with lengths equal to the singular values.

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Drag the two dots until they are almost parallel. What happens to the smaller semi-axis?
  • Put them at right angles and make both the same length. What is the shape of the image, and what are its singular values?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 7.4.1 Singular values

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) with \(\dim V = n\). The operator \(T^{*}T\) is positive on \(V\) (Statement 7.3.1), so it has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n\), repeated with multiplicity. The singular values of \(T\) are \(s_j = \sqrt{\lambda_j}\).

Statement 7.4.1 Positive singular values count the range

The number of positive singular values of \(T\) equals \(\dim\operatorname{range}T\).

drag the columns, or try the rank presets

Show proof

First, \(\operatorname{null}T^{*}T = \operatorname{null}T\). Indeed \(\langle T^{*}Tv, v\rangle = \lVert Tv\rVert^{2}\), so \(T^{*}Tv = 0\) forces \(Tv = 0\), and the converse is clear.

In the orthonormal eigenbasis of Definition 7.4.1, the eigenspace for eigenvalue \(0\) is spanned by the basis vectors with \(\lambda_j = 0\). So its dimension is the number of zero singular values. The number of positive singular values is therefore \(n - \dim\operatorname{null}T^{*}T = n - \dim\operatorname{null}T\), which equals \(\dim\operatorname{range}T\) by the fundamental theorem of linear maps (Part 3.1).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.4.2 Singular value decomposition

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), with \(n = \dim V\), \(p = \dim W\), and \(k = \min(n,p)\). Let \(s_1 \geq \cdots \geq s_k\) be the \(k\) largest singular values of \(T\). Then there are orthonormal bases \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) of \(V\) and \(f_1,\dots,f_p\) of \(W\) such that \(Tv = \sum_{j=1}^{k} s_j\langle v, e_j\rangle f_j\) for every \(v \in V\).

drag the columns and the test point

Show proof

Let \(m\) be the number of positive singular values, so \(m = \dim\operatorname{range}T\) by Statement 7.4.1. Order the eigenbasis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) of \(T^{*}T\) so that \(T^{*}Te_j = s_j^{2}e_j\) with \(s_1,\dots,s_m > 0\) and \(s_j = 0\) for \(j > m\). For \(j > m\), \(\lVert Te_j\rVert^{2} = \langle T^{*}Te_j,e_j\rangle = 0\), so \(Te_j = 0\).

For \(j \leq m\) put \(f_j = s_j^{-1}Te_j\). Then \(\langle Te_j, Te_l\rangle = \langle T^{*}Te_j, e_l\rangle = s_j^{2}\delta_{jl}\), so \(f_1,\dots,f_m\) is orthonormal. For any \(v\), \(v = \sum_j\langle v,e_j\rangle e_j\), hence \(Tv = \sum_{j\leq m} \langle v,e_j\rangle Te_j = \sum_{j \leq m} s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j\).

Finally extend \(e_1,\dots,e_m\) to an orthonormal basis of \(V\) and \(f_1,\dots,f_m\) to one of \(W\). This is possible because \(m \leq \min(n,p)\). Define \(s_j = 0\) for \(m < j \leq k\). The formula still holds, since the new terms have coefficient zero.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.4.3 Polar decomposition

Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then there is an isometry \(S \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) with \(T = S\sqrt{T^{*}T}\). If \(T\) is invertible, \(S\) is orthogonal (in the real case) or unitary (in the complex case), and \(S = T(\sqrt{T^{*}T})^{-1}\).

the root P, then the isometry S, give T

Show proof

Let \(R = \sqrt{T^{*}T}\), a positive operator. For every \(v\), \(\lVert Tv\rVert^{2} = \langle T^{*}Tv,v\rangle = \langle R^{2}v,v\rangle = \lVert Rv\rVert^{2}\). So \(\operatorname{null}T = \operatorname{null}R\), and \(\dim\operatorname{range}T = \dim\operatorname{range}R =: k\).

Define \(S_0 : \operatorname{range}R \to \operatorname{range}T\) by \(S_0(Rv) = Tv\). It is well defined: if \(Rv = Rw\), then \(\lVert T(v-w)\rVert = \lVert R(v-w)\rVert = 0\). It is linear and preserves norms, since \(\lVert S_0(Rv)\rVert = \lVert Tv\rVert = \lVert Rv\rVert\).

The orthogonal complements \((\operatorname{range}R)^{\perp}\) and \((\operatorname{range}T)^{\perp}\) both have dimension \(n-k\). Choose an isometric isomorphism \(S_1\) between them, by sending an orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis. Define \(S(a+b) = S_0a + S_1b\) for \(a \in \operatorname{range}R\) and \(b \in (\operatorname{range}R)^{\perp}\). Since \(S_0a \in \operatorname{range}T\) and \(S_1b \in (\operatorname{range}T)^{\perp}\), these are orthogonal, so \(\lVert S(a+b)\rVert^{2} = \lVert S_0a\rVert^{2} + \lVert S_1b\rVert^{2} = \lVert a\rVert^{2} + \lVert b\rVert^{2} = \lVert a+b\rVert^{2}\). So \(S\) is an isometry, and \(S(Rv) = S_0(Rv) = Tv\). That is \(T = SR\).

If \(T\) is invertible, \(R\) is invertible and \(S = TR^{-1}\). An isometry of a finite-dimensional space is injective and therefore invertible, and \(S^{*}S = I\) by Statement 7.3.3, so \(S\) is orthogonal or unitary.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 7.4.4 The unit ball maps to an ellipsoid

Let \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\), let \(s_1 \geq \cdots \geq s_m > 0\) be its positive singular values, and let \(e_j, f_j\) be as in Statement 7.4.2. Let \(B\) be the closed unit ball of \(V\). Then (a) \(T(B) = \{\sum_{j=1}^{m} y_j f_j : \sum_{j=1}^{m}(y_j/s_j)^{2} \leq 1\}\), an ellipsoid in \(\operatorname{range}T\) whose semi-axes have lengths \(s_1,\dots,s_m\) along \(f_1,\dots,f_m\); and (b) \(\max_{v \in B}\lVert Tv\rVert = s_1\).

axes labelled by singular values

Show proof

(a). Let \(v \in B\) and \(x_j = \langle v, e_j\rangle\). By Bessel's inequality \(\sum_{j\leq m}|x_j|^{2} \leq \lVert v\rVert^{2} \leq 1\). The image is \(Tv = \sum_{j\leq m} s_jx_jf_j\), so \(y_j = s_jx_j\) satisfies \(\sum (y_j/s_j)^{2} \leq 1\). Conversely, given such \(y\), put \(v = \sum_{j\leq m}(y_j/s_j)e_j\). Then \(\lVert v\rVert^{2} = \sum (y_j/s_j)^{2} \leq 1\) and \(Tv = \sum y_jf_j\).

(b). For \(\lVert v\rVert \leq 1\), by orthonormality of the \(f_j\) and Bessel's inequality, \(\lVert Tv\rVert^{2} = \sum_{j\leq m}s_j^{2}|x_j|^{2} \leq s_1^{2}\sum_{j\le m}|x_j|^{2} \leq s_1^{2}\). Equality holds at \(v = e_1\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the singular values of \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). Check that exactly one is positive, as Statement 7.4.1 says.
  2. Harder Show that \(T\) and \(T^{*}\) have the same positive singular values. Hint: compare \(TT^{*}\) with \(T^{*}T\).
  3. Toward 7.5 Show that if \(A\) is an invertible matrix, then \(A^{T}A\) is positive definite. Why is this relevant to factoring \(A\) as a product of a triangular matrix and an orthogonal one?

Home / Linear Algebra / 5.3
Linear Algebra · Part 5.3

Upper-triangular matrices

Choose the basis well and an operator's matrix becomes triangular. Over the complex numbers, a basis like that always exists, and its diagonal lists the eigenvalues.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

An operator on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has one matrix in the standard basis, but many more in other bases. Some of those matrices are much simpler than others. The simplest useful shape is triangular: zeros below the diagonal, so that each basis vector is sent into the span of itself and the vectors before it.

In the plane

The first basis vector is sent to a multiple of itself exactly when it is an eigenvector. Then the lower-left entry of the matrix is \(0\), and the matrix is triangular.

Diagonal reading

When a matrix is triangular, its diagonal entries are the eigenvalues. Reading eigenvalues off a matrix becomes a matter of looking at the diagonal.

Over the complex numbers

A rotation of the plane has no real eigenvector, but over \(\mathbb{C}\) it still has a triangular matrix. The theorem below says every operator on a complex space works this way.

2Play

Drag the two basis vectors. The operator \(T\) is fixed, with the eigen-directions \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) drawn dashed. The matrix of \(T\) in your basis is computed live. Its lower-left entry vanishes exactly when \(Tv_1\) lies on the line through \(v_1\).

What to notice before reading the proof:

The simulation for this is set out under the statement below.

  • Snap \(v_1\) to an eigenvector. Why does the entry \(A_{21}\) become zero, and why does the second column never matter in dimension two?
  • Can you find a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) for which the matrix is triangular and \(v_1\) is not an eigenvector?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 5.3.1 Matrix of an operator

Let \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\) and let \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) be a basis of \(V\). The matrix \(\mathcal M(T)\) is the \(n\times n\) array \((A_{j,k})\) defined by \(Tv_k=A_{1,k}v_1+\dots+A_{n,k}v_n\). Column \(k\) lists the coefficients of \(Tv_k\).

Definition 5.3.2 Upper-triangular matrix

A square matrix is upper triangular if every entry below the diagonal is \(0\), that is, \(A_{j,k}=0\) whenever \(j\gt k\).

Definition 5.3.3 Invariant subspace

A subspace \(U\subseteq V\) is invariant under \(T\) if \(Tu\in U\) for every \(u\in U\). Then \(T\) restricts to an operator \(T|_U\) on \(U\).

Statement 5.3.4 Triangular criterion

Let \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\) and let \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) be a basis of \(V\). The matrix of \(T\) with respect to this basis is upper triangular if and only if \(Tv_j\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_j)\) for each \(j\).

the lower-left entry is the test

Show proof

The \(k\)th column of \(\mathcal M(T)\) holds the coefficients of \(Tv_k\) in the basis. The entries below the diagonal in that column are the coefficients of \(v_{k+1},\dots,v_n\). So those entries are all \(0\) exactly when \(Tv_k\) has no \(v_{k+1},\dots,v_n\) component, that is, when \(Tv_k\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\). Requiring this for every column gives the statement, since the matrix is upper triangular exactly when every column has zeros below the diagonal.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.3.5 Diagonal entries are the eigenvalues

Suppose \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\) has an upper-triangular matrix with respect to a basis \(v_1,\dots,v_n\), with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\). Then the eigenvalues of \(T\) are exactly \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\).

slide λ: the eigenlines appear at the diagonal entries

Show proof

Let \(A\) be the matrix, so \(Tv_k=\lambda_kv_k+\sum_{i\lt k}A_{i,k}v_i\).

Every \(\lambda_k\) is an eigenvalue. Fix \(k\) and let \(S=T-\lambda_kI\). For \(j\lt k\), \(Sv_j\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_j)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})\). For \(j=k\), the \(v_k\) term of \(Sv_k=\sum_{i\lt k}A_{i,k}v_i\) cancels, so \(Sv_k\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})\). Hence \(S\) maps the \(k\)-dimensional space \(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\) into the \((k-1)\)-dimensional space \(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})\). By the fundamental theorem of linear maps (Part 3.1), \(S\) has a nonzero vector \(w\) in \(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\) with \(Sw=0\). So \(Tw=\lambda_kw\).

There are no others. Let \(Tw=\lambda w\) with \(w\ne0\), and write \(w=\sum_{j\le m}c_jv_j\) with \(c_m\ne0\). Since \(Tv_j\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_j)\), only the terms with \(j=m\) contribute to the \(v_m\) coefficient of \(Tw\), and that coefficient is \(c_mA_{m,m}=c_m\lambda_m\). Comparing with the \(v_m\) coefficient \(\lambda c_m\) of \(\lambda w\) gives \(c_m(\lambda_m-\lambda)=0\), so \(\lambda=\lambda_m\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 5.3.6 Triangular form over \(\mathbb{C}\)

If \(V\) is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space and \(T\in\mathcal L(V)\), then \(V\) has a basis with respect to which \(T\) has an upper-triangular matrix.

real: a basis with the eigenvector first · complex: a rotation

Show proof

We induct on \(n=\dim V\). If \(n=1\) there is nothing to prove. Let \(n\ge2\) and assume the result for smaller dimensions. Since \(V\) is a nonzero complex space, \(T\) has an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) (a consequence of the fundamental theorem of algebra). Put \(W=\operatorname{range}(T-\lambda I)\).

Three facts about \(W\). First, \(T-\lambda I\) is not injective, so \(\dim W

If \(W=\{0\}\), take any basis \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) of \(V\); the third fact gives \(Tx_k\in\operatorname{span}(x_1,\dots,x_k)\) for all \(k\), and Statement 5.3.4 finishes. Otherwise, the induction hypothesis applied to \(T|_W\) gives a basis \(w_1,\dots,w_m\) of \(W\) with \(Tw_k\in\operatorname{span}(w_1,\dots,w_k)\). Extend it to a basis \(w_1,\dots,w_m,x_1,\dots,x_r\) of \(V\). For each \(k\), \(Tx_k=\lambda x_k+(T-\lambda I)x_k\) and \((T-\lambda I)x_k\in W=\operatorname{span}(w_1,\dots,w_m)\), so \(Tx_k\in\operatorname{span}(w_1,\dots,w_m,x_k)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(w_1,\dots,w_m,x_1,\dots,x_k)\). Together with \(Tw_k\in\operatorname{span}(w_1,\dots,w_k)\), Statement 5.3.4 shows the matrix is upper triangular.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) for which the operator \((x,y)\mapsto(2x+y,\,2y)\) has an upper-triangular matrix, and write that matrix down.
  2. Harder Show that the eigenvalues of an upper-triangular matrix are its diagonal entries, using only Statement 5.3.5 and no determinants.
  3. Toward 5.4 A triangular matrix can have repeated diagonal entries and still be far from diagonal. When can an upper-triangular operator be made diagonal by some other basis?

Home / Linear Algebra / 1.1
Linear Algebra · Part 1.1

Vector spaces

A vector space is any collection of objects where you can add and scale, and the usual rules hold. Subspaces are the pieces that stay inside themselves, and sums and direct sums are how we build bigger spaces from smaller ones.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In the plane, you can add two arrows and you can stretch an arrow by a number. The results are still arrows in the plane. Many other sets of objects behave the same way, and linear algebra studies all of them at once.

Euclidean

Two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) add coordinatewise, and any multiple of a vector is again in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). A line through the origin is closed under both operations; a line that misses the origin is not.

Beyond the plane

Polynomials add and scale just like vectors. So do functions from a set to \(\mathbb{R}\), added pointwise. The same rules apply.

The question

Which subsets are themselves closed under addition and scaling? Those are the subspaces, and the first statement below gives a test for them.

2Play

Below is a set \(S\) drawn as a green line. Drag the two handles \(u\) and \(v\) and the scalar slider. The readouts check whether \(u\), \(v\), \(u+v\) and \(s\,u\) stay in \(S\). Switch the set with the chips.

What to notice before reading the proof:

trials stream in: green stays in S, red escapes · drag u, v

  • For which choices of \(S\) does every readout say yes? Which one fails, and at which step?
  • Can you make \(u\) and \(v\) both in \(S\) while \(u+v\) leaves it? What does that tell you about the test?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 1.1.1 Vector space

Over a field \(\mathbb{F}\) (here \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\)), a vector space is a set \(V\) with an addition \(V \times V \to V\) and a scalar multiplication \(\mathbb{F} \times V \to V\) such that addition is commutative and associative, has a zero \(0\) and additive inverses, scalar multiplication is associative and has \(1\) as identity, and both distributive laws hold. Elements of \(V\) are called vectors.

Examples. \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\mathbb{C}^n\) with coordinatewise operations; the polynomials \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})\) with the usual addition and scaling; the set \(\mathbb{F}^S\) of all functions from a set \(S\) to \(\mathbb{F}\), with pointwise operations.

Definition 1.1.2 Subspace

A subset \(U\) of a vector space \(V\) is a subspace if \(U\) is itself a vector space under the operations of \(V\).

Statement 1.1.1 Subspace test

A subset \(U \subseteq V\) is a subspace if and only if \(0 \in U\), \(U\) is closed under addition, and \(U\) is closed under scalar multiplication.

the scalar ray s·u: red where it leaves S

Show proof

If \(U\) is a subspace, it has a zero, so \(0 \in U\), and it is closed under the operations by definition. Conversely, suppose the three conditions hold. The additive identity of \(V\) lies in \(U\), and additive inverses exist in \(U\) because \((-1)v = -v\) lies in \(U\) for each \(v \in U\). The vector space axioms are identities that hold in \(V\), so they hold for elements of \(U\) too.

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 1.1.3 Sum of subspaces

If \(U_1,\dots,U_m\) are subspaces of \(V\), their sum is \(U_1+\cdots+U_m = \{u_1+\cdots+u_m : u_i \in U_i\}\).

Statement 1.1.2 The sum is the smallest subspace

If \(U\) and \(W\) are subspaces of \(V\), then \(U+W\) is a subspace of \(V\) containing both \(U\) and \(W\). Any subspace containing \(U\) and \(W\) contains \(U+W\).

dust of sums u+w · drag the basis of U and W

Show proof

Both \(0 \in U\) and \(0 \in W\), so \(0 = 0+0 \in U+W\). If \(u_1+w_1\) and \(u_2+w_2\) lie in \(U+W\), their sum is \((u_1+u_2)+(w_1+w_2)\), which lies in \(U+W\) since \(U\) and \(W\) are closed under addition. Scaling by \(\lambda\) gives \((\lambda u_1)+(\lambda w_1)\in U+W\). So \(U+W\) is a subspace. It contains \(U\) because \(u = u+0\), and \(W\) because \(w = 0+w\).

If a subspace \(X\) contains \(U\) and \(W\), then every \(u+w\) is a sum of two elements of \(X\), so it lies in \(X\). Hence \(U+W \subseteq X\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Definition 1.1.4 Direct sum

The sum \(U_1+\cdots+U_m\) is a direct sum, written \(U_1\oplus\cdots\oplus U_m\), if every element of the sum can be written in exactly one way as \(u_1+\cdots+u_m\) with \(u_i \in U_i\).

Statement 1.1.3 Zero in a direct sum

The sum \(U_1+\cdots+U_m\) is direct if and only if the only way to write \(0\) as \(u_1+\cdots+u_m\), with \(u_i \in U_i\), is \(u_1=\cdots=u_m=0\).

drag U and W, watch the zero decomposition

Show proof

Suppose the sum is direct and \(0 = u_1+\cdots+u_m\). Also \(0 = 0+\cdots+0\) is a representation with each \(u_i=0\). By uniqueness, \(u_i = 0\) for all \(i\).

Conversely, suppose the only representation of \(0\) is the trivial one, and take \(v = u_1+\cdots+u_m = w_1+\cdots+w_m\) with \(u_i,w_i \in U_i\). Subtracting gives \(0 = (u_1-w_1)+\cdots+(u_m-w_m)\), with \(u_i-w_i \in U_i\). So each \(u_i-w_i = 0\), that is \(u_i = w_i\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 1.1.4 Direct sum of two subspaces

The sum \(U+W\) is direct if and only if \(U \cap W = \{0\}\).

drag U and W, watch their overlap

Show proof

Suppose the sum is direct and \(v \in U\cap W\). Then \(v = v + 0\) with \(v\in U\), \(0 \in W\), and also \(v = 0 + v\) with \(0 \in U\), \(v \in W\). Uniqueness gives \(v = 0\).

Conversely, suppose \(U \cap W = \{0\}\) and \(0 = u + w\) with \(u \in U\), \(w \in W\). Then \(u = -w\) lies in \(U\cap W\), so \(u = 0\) and \(w = 0\). By Statement 1.1.3, the sum is direct.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Decide whether \(\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x y = 0\}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  2. Harder Prove that \(\{p \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}) : p(3)=0\}\) is a subspace, and find a second subspace \(W\) with the sum of the two equal to all of \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})\).
  3. Toward 2.1 Given vectors \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) in \(V\), the set of all their linear combinations is a subspace. Which subspace is it, and why is it the smallest one containing the list?

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / Part 4
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 4 of 4

Other models of the hyperbolic plane

The upper half-plane is one picture of the hyperbolic plane. The disc, the Klein model and the hyperboloid are others, and they all describe the same geometry.

1Motivate

A model is a picture of an abstract geometry in a familiar space. Different models make different things easy to see. The upper half-plane makes the distance formulas simple, but its boundary is a line plus a point at infinity. The disc puts the boundary on a circle, and the Klein model makes geodesics straight.

Euclidean

The Euclidean plane has one natural picture: the plane itself. Every other description is a change of coordinates.

Hyperbolic

The hyperbolic plane has several standard pictures, and each one is a different bijection with a different metric. We prove that they agree, and that is what makes the subject one geometry rather than several.

What you will see

In the disc, geodesics are circular arcs. In the Klein model, they are straight chords, so the parallel postulate looks like Euclid's picture. On the hyperboloid, geodesics are plane sections through the origin.

2The models

Read them in order. Each one uses the previous.

  1. 4.1The Poincaré discThe Cayley map from the upper half-plane to the unit disc.
  2. 4.2Geodesics and distance in the discOrthogonal circles, and the distance formula.
  3. 4.3The Klein modelStraight chords, and the parallel postulate as a picture.
  4. 4.4The hyperboloidThe plane as a sheet in three-dimensional space.
  5. 4.5Comparing the modelsOne point, four distances, and why they agree.

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / Other models / 4.1
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 4.1 of 5

The Poincaré disc

A Möbius map carries the upper half-plane onto the unit disc, and puts the boundary on a circle.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

The upper half-plane has a boundary line, and points at infinity that are hard to picture. The disc has a boundary circle, and every point of it is a point of the circle. It is the model most often drawn in textbooks, because it is bounded and symmetric.

Euclidean

The plane is unbounded, and no map squeezes it into a disc without distorting it. Lines run off to infinity.

Hyperbolic

The hyperbolic plane is also unbounded, but a conformal map (one that keeps angles) can place it inside the unit disc. The boundary of the disc then plays the role of infinity.

The map

The Cayley map \(w = \dfrac{z-i}{z+i}\) does the job. It sends \(i\) to \(0\), and the real axis to the unit circle.

2Play

Drag the point \(z\) in the upper half-plane (left). The right panel shows its image \(w\) in the disc. The blue curves on the left are geodesics, and the purple ones on the right are their images under the Cayley map.

  • Drag \(z\) towards the real axis. Where does \(w\) go, and what does that say about the boundary?
  • Drag \(z\) far up. Where does \(w\) go? Which point of the disc is the image of \(\infty\)?
  • Which point of the upper half-plane goes to the centre \(0\) of the disc?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 4.1.1 The Poincaré disc and the Cayley map

The Poincaré disc is \(\mathbb{D} = \{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| \lt 1\}\). The Cayley map is \(c(z) = \dfrac{z - i}{z + i}\), defined for \(z \ne -i\).

Statement 4.1.1

The Cayley map is a bijection from \(\mathbb{H}^2\) onto \(\mathbb{D}\), with inverse \(c^{-1}(w) = \dfrac{i(1+w)}{1-w}\). It sends \(i\) to \(0\).

Show proof

For \(z\) in the plane, \(|z - i|^2 - |z + i|^2 = -4\operatorname{Im} z\), because \(|z \mp i|^2 = |z|^2 + 1 \mp 2\operatorname{Im} z\). So \(|c(z)| \lt 1\) exactly when \(\operatorname{Im} z \gt 0\), which shows that \(c\) maps \(\mathbb{H}^2\) into \(\mathbb{D}\).

To invert, solve \(w(z + i) = z - i\): \(z(w - 1) = -i(1 + w)\), so \(z = \dfrac{i(1+w)}{1-w}\). This is defined for \(w \ne 1\), and it has positive imaginary part whenever \(|w| \lt 1\), since \(\operatorname{Im} z = \operatorname{Re}\dfrac{1+w}{1-w} = \dfrac{1 - |w|^2}{|1-w|^2} \gt 0\). So \(c\) and \(c^{-1}\) are inverse bijections between \(\mathbb{H}^2\) and \(\mathbb{D}\). Finally \(c(i) = 0\).

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.1.2

The Cayley map sends the real line, together with \(\infty\), onto the unit circle.

Show proof

For real \(x\), \(|x - i|^2 = x^2 + 1 = |x + i|^2\), so \(|c(x)| = 1\). Also \(c(\infty) = 1\). Since \(c\) is a bijection and sends \(\mathbb{H}^2\) into the disc, its image of the boundary is exactly the circle.

\(\blacksquare\)

Remark. The disc is the picture in which the isometries of Part 4.2 become rotations and the geodesics become circular arcs. Statement 4.2.1 says what those arcs are.

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Compute \(c(2i)\), \(c(1+i)\) and \(c(-1)\). Check that the first two lie in the disc and the last on its boundary.
  2. Harder Show that \(c\) maps the vertical half-line \(\{x = 0\}\) onto the diameter \((-1,1)\) of the disc.
  3. Toward 4.2 Which circles in the disc are images of geodesics? Guess before you read Part 4.2.
← Other models 4.2 Geodesics and distance in the disc →
Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / Other models / 4.2
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 4.2 of 5

Geodesics and distance in the disc

The geodesics are circular arcs that meet the boundary at right angles, and the distance has a formula of its own.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

In the Euclidean plane the lines are straight. In the disc, the lines must bend, but they should still be the shortest curves. The right guess is circles that meet the boundary at right angles, and the proof confirms it.

Euclidean

A line is a circle of infinite radius, and it meets the point at infinity. Lines are the geodesics, and the distance is \(|z - w|\).

Disc

A geodesic is an arc of a circle orthogonal to the unit circle. The diameters are the limiting case. The distance is no longer \(|u - v|\), but a formula with the denominators \((1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)\).

Why it matters

The formula shows that distances blow up near the boundary, which is exactly the infinity of the hyperbolic plane.

2Play

Drag the two points \(u\) and \(v\) in the disc. The geodesic through them is the arc drawn in blue, and the panel gives its distance. Put the points on a diameter to see the degenerate case.

  • Move \(u\) and \(v\) close to the boundary. Does the distance grow quickly? Why?
  • Put \(u\) at the centre. What is the distance to \(v\) as a function of \(|v|\)?
  • Place \(u\) and \(v\) on one diameter. What is the geodesic now?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 4.2.1

The Cayley map sends each geodesic of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) to an arc of a circle orthogonal to the unit circle, or to a diameter.

Show proof

A geodesic is a vertical half-line or a semicircle centred on the axis, and it meets the real axis (or \(\infty\)) at right angles. The map \(c\) is holomorphic and injective, so it preserves angles between curves. It sends the real axis, including \(\infty\), into the unit circle (Statement 4.1.2). So the image of a geodesic meets the unit circle at the same angle as the geodesic meets the real axis, namely \(90^\circ\).

A circle or line that meets the unit circle at right angles is either a circle orthogonal to it or a diameter. The vertical line \(x = 0\) goes to the diameter \((-1,1)\), since \(c(iy) = \dfrac{y-1}{y+1}\) is real.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.2.2

For \(u, v \in \mathbb{D}\), the hyperbolic distance between \(u\) and \(v\) in the disc model, which is the distance of \(\mathbb{H}^2\) between \(c^{-1}(u)\) and \(c^{-1}(v)\), satisfies

\[\cosh d(u,v) = 1 + \frac{2|u-v|^2}{(1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)}.\]
Show proof

Let \(z = c^{-1}(u) = i\zeta\) with \(\zeta = \dfrac{1+u}{1-u}\), and similarly \(w = i\eta\) with \(\eta = \dfrac{1+v}{1-v}\). Then \(\operatorname{Im} z = \operatorname{Re}\zeta = \dfrac{1-|u|^2}{|1-u|^2}\), and likewise for \(w\). Also \(\zeta - \eta = \dfrac{2(u-v)}{(1-u)(1-v)}\), so \(|z - w|^2 = \dfrac{4|u-v|^2}{|1-u|^2|1-v|^2}\).

The distance formula in \(\mathbb{H}^2\) gives \(\cosh d = 1 + \dfrac{|z-w|^2}{2\operatorname{Im}z\,\operatorname{Im}w}\). Substituting,

\[\frac{|z-w|^2}{2\operatorname{Im}z\,\operatorname{Im}w} = \frac{4|u-v|^2}{|1-u|^2|1-v|^2}\cdot\frac{|1-u|^2|1-v|^2}{2(1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)} = \frac{2|u-v|^2}{(1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)}.\]

\(\blacksquare\)

Remark. Statement 4.2.2 is the formula used in the simulation. The geodesic through \(u\) and \(v\) is the orthogonal circle through them; its centre \(c\) solves \(2c\cdot u = |u|^2 + 1\) and \(2c\cdot v = |v|^2 + 1\), with radius \(\sqrt{|c|^2 - 1}\). Check these conditions numerically in the simulation.

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the hyperbolic distance from \(0\) to a point \(u\) of the disc, using Statement 4.2.2. Express it in terms of \(|u|\).
  2. Harder Show that the Möbius rotations \(w \mapsto e^{i\theta}w\) of the disc are isometries, using Statement 4.2.2.
  3. Toward 4.3 In the Klein model, geodesics are straight. Can you find a map from the disc to a disc in which the chords through two points are the geodesics?

Home / Hyperbolic Geometry / Other models / 4.3
Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 4.3 of 5

The Klein model

In the Klein model the geodesics are straight chords. The price is a messier distance formula, and the reward is a clear picture of the parallel postulate.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

The disc has curved geodesics, which are hard to picture when you are trying to see how lines behave. The Klein model is another disc, but its geodesics are straight. Euclid's picture of lines and points is exactly the picture we need.

Euclidean

Two distinct points lie on one line, and a line and a point off it give exactly one parallel.

Klein

Two distinct points in the disc lie on one chord, and a chord through a point that misses a given chord is a parallel. The chords through a point that miss a fixed chord form an interval of directions, so there are infinitely many of them.

The cost

The distance is no longer the simple formula of the disc, but an expression with a square root. The proof that the two models agree is a short algebraic check.

2Play

First, the chord and the distance. Drag \(P\) and \(Q\) inside the disc. The chord through them is a geodesic, and the panel gives the distance from the Klein formula.

  • Drag \(P\) and \(Q\) close to the boundary. Does the distance grow quickly, like in the disc?

Second, the parallel postulate. The solid chord is \(l\). Through \(P\) the simulation draws 24 geodesics, one for each direction. Green ones miss \(l\) inside the disc, and red ones meet it.

  • Move \(P\) towards \(l\) and then away. How does the count of green geodesics change?
  • Move the end of \(l\) close to the boundary. Does the count of green geodesics become larger?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 4.3.1 The Klein map

The Klein model is the unit disc \(\mathbb{K} = \{k : |k| \lt 1\}\). The map from the Poincaré disc is \(k(w) = \dfrac{2w}{1 + |w|^2}\). It has inverse \(w(k) = \dfrac{k}{1 + \sqrt{1 - |k|^2}}\).

Statement 4.3.1

The map \(w \mapsto k(w)\) is a bijection from the Poincaré disc onto the Klein model, with the inverse above.

Show proof

\(|k(w)| \lt 1\) is equivalent to \(2|w| \lt 1 + |w|^2\), that is \((1 - |w|)^2 \gt 0\), which holds for \(w \ne 1\), and that inequality is the only constraint. For the inverse, note that \(|k| = \dfrac{2r}{1+r^2}\) with \(r = |w|\), so \(1 - |k|^2 = \left(\dfrac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}\right)^2\), and \(\sqrt{1-|k|^2} = \dfrac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}\). Substituting back gives \(w = \dfrac{k}{1+\sqrt{1-|k|^2}}\). Both maps preserve the direction of their argument.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.3.2

For \(P, Q\) in the Klein model, the hyperbolic distance is given by

\[\cosh d(P,Q) = \frac{1 - P\cdot Q}{\sqrt{(1-|P|^2)(1-|Q|^2)}}.\]
Show proof

Let \(P = k(u)\) and \(Q = k(v)\). From \(1 - |k|^2 = \left(\dfrac{1-|u|^2}{1+|u|^2}\right)^2\),

\[\frac{1 - P\cdot Q}{\sqrt{(1-|P|^2)(1-|Q|^2)}} = \frac{(1+|u|^2)(1+|v|^2) - 4\,u\cdot v}{(1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)}.\]

The right-hand side of Statement 4.2.2 has numerator \((1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2) + 2|u-v|^2 = 1 + |u|^2 + |v|^2 + |u|^2|v|^2 - 4u\cdot v\), which is the same expression. So the two formulas agree.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.3.3

Through a point \(P\) not on a geodesic \(l\) of the Klein model, there are infinitely many geodesics that do not meet \(l\) in the disc.

Show proof

Geodesics are chords, so a geodesic through \(P\) is determined by its direction \(\theta\). Two chords meet in the disc exactly when their lines meet at a point of the open disc. As \(\theta\) turns, the point of intersection with the line \(l\) moves along \(l\). The set of directions for which it lies in the disc is an open interval of directions, and its complement is a closed interval of directions. That complement contains infinitely many directions, each giving a different geodesic that misses \(l\). This is the failure of Euclid's postulate.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the Klein model image of the Poincaré point \(w = \tfrac{1}{2}i\), and check that the hyperbolic distance from \(0\) is the same in both models.
  2. Harder Show that the midpoint of a chord in the Klein model is not, in general, the hyperbolic midpoint of its endpoints. What does that say about the Klein model?
  3. Toward 4.4 The Klein model is a projection of a sheet in three dimensions. Which sheet, and which direction does the projection come from?

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 4.4 of 5

The hyperboloid

The hyperbolic plane as a sheet in three-dimensional space, where geodesics are the sections by planes through the origin.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

The sphere is the set of points at distance \(1\) from the origin, and its great circles are the geodesics of the spherical geometry. The hyperboloid does the same job for the hyperbolic plane, with a different sign in the formula for distance.

Euclidean

The sphere lies in space, and its geodesics are great circles, which are the intersections with planes through the centre.

Hyperbolic

The hyperboloid \(x_0^2 - x_1^2 - x_2^2 = 1\) with \(x_0 \gt 0\) is a sheet in three-dimensional space. Its geodesics are the intersections with planes through the origin, and the distance is given by a sign-changed inner product.

Why it matters

Isometries become linear maps that preserve the sign-changed product, which is the cleanest description of the whole group of isometries.

2Play

The sheet is drawn in three dimensions. Drag the picture to turn it. The base point \(O\) is the bottom of the sheet, and the purple curve is a geodesic through \(O\), the intersection with a plane through the origin. Move \(\varphi\) to turn the plane and \(\tau\) to slide the point \(X\) along the curve.

  • Keep \(\varphi\) fixed and slide \(\tau\). Is the distance from \(O\) equal to \(|\tau|\) at every point?
  • Turn \(\varphi\) through \(180^\circ\). Do the curves cover every geodesic through \(O\)?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Definition 4.4.1 The hyperboloid

The hyperboloid is \(\mathbb{L} = \{x = (x_0,x_1,x_2) : x_0 \gt 0,\ x_0^2 - x_1^2 - x_2^2 = 1\}\). Define the Minkowski product \(\langle x, y\rangle = x_0y_0 - x_1y_1 - x_2y_2\).

Statement 4.4.1

The map \(w \mapsto x(w) = \left(\dfrac{1+|w|^2}{1-|w|^2},\ \dfrac{2\operatorname{Re} w}{1-|w|^2},\ \dfrac{2\operatorname{Im} w}{1-|w|^2}\right)\) is a bijection from the Poincaré disc onto \(\mathbb{L}\), with inverse \(w = \dfrac{x_1 + ix_2}{1 + x_0}\).

Show proof

Let \(r = |w|\). Then \(x_0^2 - x_1^2 - x_2^2 = \dfrac{(1+r^2)^2 - 4r^2}{(1-r^2)^2} = \dfrac{(1-r^2)^2}{(1-r^2)^2} = 1\), and \(x_0 \gt 0\) for \(r \lt 1\). Conversely, \(\dfrac{x_1 + ix_2}{1+x_0} = \dfrac{2w/(1-r^2)}{2/(1-r^2)} = w\), using \(1 + x_0 = \dfrac{2}{1-r^2}\). So the two maps are inverse to each other.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.4.2

For \(x, y \in \mathbb{L}\), the hyperbolic distance in the disc model satisfies \(\cosh d(x,y) = \langle x, y\rangle\).

Show proof

Let \(x = x(u)\) and \(y = x(v)\). Then

\[x_0y_0 - x_1y_1 - x_2y_2 = \frac{(1+|u|^2)(1+|v|^2) - 4\,u\cdot v}{(1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)} = 1 + \frac{2|u-v|^2}{(1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)} = \cosh d(u,v),\]

by the calculation in Statement 4.3.2 and Statement 4.2.2.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.4.3

Let \(O = (1,0,0)\). The geodesics through \(O\) are the curves \(\tau \mapsto (\cosh\tau,\ \sinh\tau\cos\varphi,\ \sinh\tau\sin\varphi)\), and \(d(O, X_\tau) = |\tau|\).

Show proof

The plane through the origin containing \(O\) and the direction \((0, \cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)\) consists of points \((s, t\cos\varphi, t\sin\varphi)\). On the hyperboloid this means \(s^2 - t^2 = 1\), so \(s = \cosh\tau\) and \(t = \sinh\tau\) for a unique real \(\tau\). This gives the curve above. By Statement 4.4.2, \(\cosh d(O, X_\tau) = \langle O, X_\tau\rangle = \cosh\tau\), so \(d(O, X_\tau) = |\tau|\). Hence the curve is parametrised by arc length from \(O\).

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the point of the hyperboloid over the Poincaré point \(w = \tfrac12\), and check its distance from \(O\) using Statement 4.4.2.
  2. Harder Show that a linear map of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) preserving the Minkowski product and the sheet is an isometry of \(\mathbb{H}^2\).
  3. Toward 4.5 Compare the three descriptions: the disc, the Klein model and the hyperboloid. Which quantity in each one is the hyperbolic distance?

Hyperbolic Geometry · Part 4.5 of 5

Comparing the models

One point, four pictures, and the same distance from the base point in every one. This is why we can say we have one geometry.

1Motivate2Play3Rigorous definitions and proofs4Look ahead

1Motivate

Four descriptions of the hyperbolic plane have appeared. Each has its own distance formula, and it is natural to ask whether they measure the same thing. They do, and the proof is a single calculation for each pair.

Euclidean

There is one plane, and one distance. Coordinates are a choice, and changing them does not change any distance.

Hyperbolic

Four pictures, four formulas, one distance. A point in the upper half-plane, its image in the disc, the Klein image, and the hyperboloid point all give the same number for the distance from the base point.

The test

Drag the point. The four readouts should agree at every position, and they do.

2Play

Drag the point \(z\) in the left panel. The middle and right panels show the same point in the Poincaré disc and the Klein model, with the geodesic from the base point \(i\) (or its image \(0\)) drawn in each.

  • Do the four distances agree everywhere you drag? Find a point where they are all about \(1\).
  • Take the point far up the left panel. Which of the four readouts grows fastest?

3Rigorous definitions and proofs

Try each statement before opening its proof.

Statement 4.5.1

Let \(z \in \mathbb{H}^2\), let \(w = c(z)\) be its Cayley image, and let \(d = d(i, z)\). Then \(|w| = \tanh\dfrac{d}{2}\), and the Klein image \(k\) of \(w\) satisfies \(|k| = \tanh d\). The hyperboloid point \(x\) of \(w\) satisfies \(x_0 = \cosh d\).

Show proof

Since \(c\) is an isometry from \(\mathbb{H}^2\) to the disc model, the disc distance from \(0 = c(i)\) to \(w\) is \(d\). By Statement 4.2.2 with \(u = 0\), \(\cosh d = \dfrac{1+|w|^2}{1-|w|^2}\). Solving for \(|w|^2\) gives \(|w|^2 = \dfrac{\cosh d - 1}{\cosh d + 1}\), that is \(|w| = \tanh\dfrac{d}{2}\).

For the Klein model, \(|k| = \dfrac{2|w|}{1+|w|^2}\). With \(\tau = \tanh\tfrac{d}{2}\), this is \(\dfrac{2\tau}{1+\tau^2} = \tanh d\), by the double-angle identity for \(\tanh\). For the hyperboloid, \(x_0 = \dfrac{1+|w|^2}{1-|w|^2} = \cosh d\) by Statement 4.4.1.

\(\blacksquare\)

Statement 4.5.2

The hyperbolic distance from \(i\) to \(z\) can be computed in four ways:

\[\cosh d = 1 + \frac{|z-i|^2}{2\operatorname{Im}z} = \frac{1+|w|^2}{1-|w|^2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-|k|^2}} = x_0.\]
Show proof

The first equality is the distance formula of Part 3.3 in the upper half-plane with \(z = i\). The second is Statement 4.2.2 with \(u = 0\) and \(v = w\). The third holds because \(1 - |k|^2 = \left(\dfrac{1-|w|^2}{1+|w|^2}\right)^2\), so \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-|k|^2}} = \dfrac{1+|w|^2}{1-|w|^2}\). The last equality is Statement 4.5.1.

\(\blacksquare\)

4Look ahead

  1. Routine Find the hyperbolic distance from \(i\) to \(2i\) in each of the four models, and check that the answers agree.
  2. Harder Show that the distance from the base point to a point of the Klein model is \(\operatorname{artanh}|k|\), and derive the formula of Part 4.3 for \(\cosh d(P,Q)\) from it.
  3. Looking back Return to the parallel postulate in Part 3.3. Which of the four models shows it most clearly, and why?
